schema_promotion_candidates.description: Zero-temperature Ginzburg-Landau coherence length in nm, extracted from dirty-limit temperature dependence ξ(T) = ξGL(0)(1-T/Tc)^(-1/2)
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: ξGL(0) relative to constriction dimensions directly determines CPR skewness and junction nonlinearity — the key parameter for designing ScS junctions as qubit elements. Tracking ξGL(0) across samples would allow systematic comparison of nonlinearity achievable with different constriction materials and geometries.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Main text, page 4; Supporting Information Figure S15

schema_promotion_candidates.description: First nonlinear Maclaurin coefficient of the current-phase relation, a1 = IJ'''(0)/IJ'(0); equals -1 for sinusoidal CPR
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: a1 quantifies the anharmonicity of the Josephson inductance, which directly determines the qubit anharmonicity (α = EC × a1 for ScS transmons). Tracking this across junction geometries would enable systematic comparison of junction types for qubit applications.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Main text, page 4-5: 'the overall SQUID arm CPR has a relatively low nonlinearity, with a1 ≈ -0.02 (for ξ ≈ 60 nm and T = 0.4 K)... the constriction itself is substantially more nonlinear, having a1 = -0.2'

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Mean critical current Ic of a Josephson junction in µA, extracted from averaged V-I sweeps
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Ic sets the Josephson energy EJ = Ic × Φ0 / (2π), which together with charging energy EC determines qubit frequency and anharmonicity. For ScS transmon compatibility, Ic must be in the nA range; current PtSi values (~µA) indicate ~2 orders of magnitude gap.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table 1, main text; Supporting Information Tables S1-S3

catchall.free_notes: This paper characterizes PtSi constriction Josephson junctions as a candidate platform for silicon-compatible superconducting electronics/qubits. No qubit coherence (T1, T2) measurements are reported — devices are Josephson junctions and SQUIDs only, not full qubits. The paper explicitly notes that current Ic values (~µA) are ~2 orders of magnitude too large for transmon qubits at GHz frequencies, requiring further dimensional scaling. The ξGL(0) = 45 nm extracted from constrictions is shorter than the bulk PtSi film value (76 nm), attributed to shorter mean free path within the constriction. All six device types (ScS-25, ScS-50, ScS-100, SSQ-25, SSQ-50, ASQ-50/100) were fabricated from the same wafer using the same process flow.

Both TaN_nanowire_39nm and TaN_Cu_bilayer_nanowire_39nm are explicitly stated to use the same TaN film deposition (actual thickness 39 nm confirmed by TEM for both), with distinct post-deposition integration flows (RIE-based for TaN; CMP-based TaN/Cu). TaN_Cu_bilayer_nanowire_39nm.profile_notes: Primary superconducting material is TaN (same stoichiometry N/Ta=0.53 as the other sample); Cu is a normal-metal encapsulant added for heat sinking, not the superconductor. The paper explicitly correlates Cu proximity effect with Tc reduction (~0.9 K), justifying Tc_to_operating_margin. No microwave or qubit device is measured, so coherence_tier is not_applicable.

substrate_material.source: Appendix A, page 12: 'We grow our films on a 2-inch annealed HEMEX sapphire wafer with a thickness of 650 µm.'

film_material.source: Appendix A, page 12: 'We grow niobium nitride (NbN) films using atomic layer deposition (ALD)'

film_thickness_nm.source: Appendix A, page 12: 'The final NbN thickness is typically 20 nm, unless otherwise noted.'

deposition_method.source: Appendix A, page 12: 'We grow niobium nitride (NbN) films using atomic layer deposition (ALD) in an Ultratech/Cambridge Fiji G2 plasma system.'

deposition_temperature_C.source: Appendix A, page 12: 'reaction is facilitated by a high chamber and chuck temperature, in our case 400 °C'

Tc_K.source: Page 7, prose: 'We take the critical temperature to be Tc = 12 K based on the measurement of the films in Section I.'

film_etch_chemistry.value: ALE in RIE-ICP system: SF6 diluted with H2, low-power plasma at 30 W for 10 seconds per cycle; main chamber at 15°C; removes less than 1 nm per cycle on average
film_etch_chemistry.source: Appendix A, page 12: 'The ALE process is carried out in a reactive ion etching inductively coupled plasma (RIE–ICP) system. In the first cycle we introduce SF6 diluted with H2 into the chamber. Subsequently, a low-power plasma is applied at 30 W for 10 seconds...The main chamber is maintained at 15°C. Each cycle removes, on average, less than one nanometer of material.'

post_fabrication_surface_treatment.value: Global ALE treatment removing approximately 3 nm of NbN and oxide combined to improve surface roughness
post_fabrication_surface_treatment.source: Appendix A, page 12: 'Unless otherwise noted, all samples undergo a global ALE treatment that removes approximately 3 nm of NbN and oxide combined. This step improves surface roughness and results in minimal microwave losses.'

additional_measurements.description: Thickness-driven SIT critical thickness for ALD NbN films
additional_measurements.value: dc ~ 2.5–3 nm; RN ~ RQ = 6.45 kΩ at critical thickness
additional_measurements.source: Page 2–3, prose and Fig. 1a,b caption: 'indicating a critical thickness, dc ~ 2.5 − 3 nm that separates the superconducting...and the insulating...regimes. At the critical thickness, the normal-state sheet resistance per square, RN, is close to the expectation RN ~ RQ = h/4e2'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Establishes the SIT regime exploited for the weak link; proximity to SIT affects disorder, mean free path, and quasiparticle behavior which directly influence qubit coherence

additional_measurements.description: Mattis-Bardeen relation between kinetic inductance LK and normal-state sheet resistance RN: LK = hbar*RN / (pi*Delta), with Delta_NbN = 2.03 meV inferred from Tc
additional_measurements.value: Agreement with Mattis-Bardeen confirmed; kinetic inductance ranges from 10 pH/sq to 250 pH/sq across chips
additional_measurements.source: Page 3, prose and Fig. 1d: 'We find that the extracted values of kinetic inductance, LK, and the RN measured at DC follow closely the Mattis-Bardeen relation using Delta_NbN = 2.03 meV'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Kinetic inductance (and hence sheet resistance) directly sets the participation ratio of the superconductor in the circuit, affecting qubit frequency, anharmonicity, and loss

additional_measurements.description: ALE reduces RMS surface roughness by over 50% compared to untreated NbN films
additional_measurements.source: Appendix B, page 13: 'the ALE process reduces the root-mean-square (RMS) roughness by over 50% compared to untreated NbN films'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Reduced surface roughness lowers TLS density at interfaces, directly improving Qi and qubit coherence

correlations_observed.description: Authors state ALE treatment plays a critical role in improving surface quality, and this improvement correlates with higher measured quality factors in CPW resonators
correlations_observed.measurement_b: Internal quality factor Qi of CPW resonators
correlations_observed.nature: Positive correlation: ALE-treated films show Qi > 10^6, untreated films show Qi ~ 10^5 and gap-dependent Qi

fabrication_details.description: ALD precursor: tris(diethylamido)(tert-butylimido)niobium(V) (TBTDEN); plasma: H2/N2
Substrate wafer preparation and anneal recipe referenced to Ref. [57] (Ganjam et al., Nature Communications 2024)
fabrication_details.source: Appendix A, page 12: 'Wafer preparation and anneal recipe is detailed in Ref. [57].'

fabrication_details.description: Post-etch cleaning: BOE (buffered oxide etch) compatible with NbN, used to remove residual carbon and fluoride contaminants
fabrication_details.source: Appendix A, page 12: 'all samples are NbN only, they are compatible with aggressive cleaning methods, such as Buffered Oxide Etching (BOE). This is used as a final step to remove residual carbon and fluoride contaminants'

fabrication_details.description: Multi-patch chip layout: four patches of different thickness per 7x7 mm chip, each made by e-beam lithography + ALE; Hall bars co-fabricated alongside CPW resonators on each patch
fabrication_details.source: Appendix B, page 12: 'There are four different patches on every 7 x 7 mm chip. Each patch is made by an e-beam lithography step followed by ALE...'

fabrication_details.description: Measurement packaging: copper package with air gap above and below chip, mounted on gold-plated copper brackets; light-tight shield closed with indium seals; mu-metal shield; Eccosorb filters + attenuators on input; HERD filters on output; base temperature ~23 mK
fabrication_details.source: Appendix B, page 12: 'The chip is mounted in a copper package with an air gap below and above the chip...shielded from thermal photons by a light tight shield closed tightly with indium seals and a µ-metal shield...Eccosorb filters...HERD filters'

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Kinetic inductance per square (LK, in pH/sq) of the superconducting film, extracted from CPW resonator frequency measurements and correlated with DC sheet resistance via Mattis-Bardeen
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: LK directly sets participation ratios and qubit frequency; it is the key material parameter for kinetic-inductance-heavy films (NbN, TiN, NbTiN) and its variation with disorder/thickness drives the SIT. Tracking LK alongside Qi, Tc, and RRR would enable systematic comparison across disordered superconductor platforms.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Fig. 1d and Appendix B, page 12: 'Kinetic inductance ranges from 10 pH/□ to 250 pH/□ within a single chip'

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Electron mean free path le in the weak link material, in nm, extracted from IcRN product and diffusion model fits
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Mean free path relative to coherence length determines clean vs. dirty limit; in this paper le = 0.03–0.5 nm (sub-atomic, indicating localization). Tracking this across NbN weak link devices would characterize the transport regime and its impact on anharmonicity and coherence.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Page 4: 'This results in le = 0.03 − 0.5 nm, comparable to NbN inter-atomic distance.'

film_material.source: Page 3 and Appendix B: CPW resonators fabricated from ALE-thinned NbN films

film_thickness_nm.source: Appendix A, page 12: 'The final NbN thickness is typically 20 nm, unless otherwise noted.' — resonators are ALE-thinned versions of the 20 nm base film; exact post-ALE thickness varies by patch

Tc_K.source: Page 7: 'We take the critical temperature to be Tc = 12 K based on the measurement of the films in Section I.' Borrowed from bulk film measurement; paper confirms these resonators share the same ALD NbN process and same 2-inch wafer.

film_etch_chemistry.value: ALE in RIE-ICP system: SF6/H2, 30 W plasma, 10 s per cycle, 15°C chamber; global ~3 nm removal + selective patterning via e-beam lithography + ALE to define CPW gaps
film_etch_chemistry.source: Appendix A, page 12 and Appendix B, page 12

post_fabrication_surface_treatment.value: Global ALE treatment (~3 nm NbN + oxide removal); BOE cleaning as final step

junction_present.source: Page 3, Section I: these are CPW resonators, no Josephson junctions

Qi_single_photon.source: Page 3, prose and Fig. 1d: 'internal quality factors in the single-photon regime...exceed 10^6 at base temperature (~23 mK), independent of RN in the range of investigation.' Also Fig. S7a shows up to ~3×10^6 for ALE-treated films.

resonator_type.source: Page 3: 'coplanar waveguide (CPW) resonators'; Appendix B, page 13: 'coplanar waveguide (CPW) resonators'

resonator_gap_width_um.source: Appendix B, page 13: 'We use 6µm, 24 µm, 48 µm and 72 µm' — multiple gaps used; 6 µm is the smallest. Fig. 1d and S7 show Qi independent of gap for ALE films.

additional_measurements.description: Qi of ALE-treated resonators is independent of CPW gap (6, 24, 48, 72 µm) and independent of kinetic inductance (RN), up to LK = 250 pH/sq
additional_measurements.value: Qi > 10^6 across all gaps and LK values for ALE-treated films; up to ~3×10^6 for best devices (Fig. S7a)
additional_measurements.source: Page 3 and Fig. S7a, Appendix B page 13
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Gap-independence of Qi indicates dissipation is NOT dominated by lossy material interfaces (since gap sets participation ratio); instead ALE surface quality improvement is the dominant factor. This directly connects surface roughness to microwave loss.

additional_measurements.description: Unetched (no ALE) NbN films show reduced Qi that depends on gap (gap-dependent loss)
additional_measurements.value: Qi ~ 10^5 for no-ALE films (LK = 10 pH/sq), gap-dependent; Fig. S7b red line
additional_measurements.source: Fig. S7b, Appendix B page 13: 'The red line represents data from resonators fabricated on a patch of film whose kinetic inductance is 10 pH and has not been treated with ALE.'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Gap-dependent Qi for untreated films implies surface/interface TLS loss dominates; after ALE treatment the gap independence shows TLS loss is suppressed, confirming ALE improves material interfaces relevant to qubit T1

correlations_observed.description: Authors state ALE surface treatment improves surface quality (>50% RMS roughness reduction) and this correlates with higher and gap-independent Qi
correlations_observed.measurement_b: Internal quality factor Qi and its gap-dependence
correlations_observed.nature: Positive correlation with treatment; ALE removes gap-dependence of Qi, indicating elimination of interface TLS loss

fabrication_details.description: CPW resonator design: 3–4 resonators per patch, target frequencies 5–9 GHz, resonators ~200 MHz apart within a patch; gaps of 6, 24, 48, 72 µm; one additional 6 µm gap resonator intentionally over-coupled (Qc ~10^4) for identification; others designed for Qc ~10^6
Resonator frequencies targeted using finite-element simulations (Sonnet) based on geometry and kinetic inductance
Qi extracted by circle fit procedure (Probst et al., Rev. Sci. Instrum. 2015 [Ref. 60], modified by Chan U. Lee, Suhas Ganjam and Yanhao Wang [Ref. 61])

film_material.source: Page 4, Section III: 'a transmon qubit fabricated from a single film of NbN'

film_thickness_nm.source: Appendix A, page 12: 'The final NbN thickness is typically 20 nm, unless otherwise noted.' Starting thickness before weak link ALE; planaron uses same base film.

deposition_method.source: Appendix G, page 15: 'The planaron qubit is fabricated from a single NbN film.'; Appendix A: all NbN films grown by ALD

Tc_K.source: Page 7: 'We take the critical temperature to be Tc = 12 K based on the measurement of the films in Section I.' Borrowed from bulk film measurement; paper states planaron uses same NbN ALD process.

film_etch_chemistry.value: ALE (SF6/H2, RIE-ICP, 30 W, 10 s/cycle, 15°C chamber) used for all patterning: weak link trench first, then capacitor pads and lead geometry
film_etch_chemistry.source: Appendix G, page 15: 'All structures are defined via electron-beam lithography followed by etching with ALE. First, we define a trench by exposing and etching a narrow constriction into the NbN film...After defining the weak link, the capacitor pads and large-scale lead geometry are patterned and etched'

post_fabrication_surface_treatment.value: BOE 6:1 for ~20 min after all ALE etching; BOE does not attack NbN; removes residual contaminants, organics, and native oxides
post_fabrication_surface_treatment.source: Appendix G, page 15: 'the sample is then cleaned in buffered oxide etch (BOE 6:1) for an extended period (~20 min). BOE does not attack NbN, allowing for effective removal of residual contaminants, organics and native oxides'

junction_present.source: Page 4: weak link serves as the nonlinear element (Josephson weak link) in the transmon qubit

junction_material.value: NbN (locally thinned to ~2.5 nm via ALE, forming SIT-based weak link — no oxide barrier)
junction_material.source: Page 4: 'we locally thin a uniform NbN film near the SIT and define a weak link in a fully planar geometry'; weak link thickness dI ~2.5 nm per Fig. 2b caption

junction_fabrication_method.value: Single-film planar weak link: local ALE thinning via e-beam lithography + ALE to define narrow constriction (w ~1 µm, l ~30 nm) in NbN film to insulating thickness (~2.5 nm); no metal deposition or liftoff
junction_fabrication_method.source: Page 4: 'We implement a weak link of dimensions w ~ 1 µm and l ~ 30 nm'; Appendix G: 'define a trench by exposing and etching a narrow constriction into the NbN film'

qubit_frequency_GHz.source: Page 6 and Fig. 3b/d: 'based on the designed charging energy of EC/ℏ = 2π × 293 MHz and measured frequency fq = 7.945 GHz'

additional_measurements.description: Measured anharmonicity of planaron qubit
additional_measurements.source: Page 4/5 and Fig. 3e: 'a second peak appears 235 MHz below the |0⟩→|1⟩ transition, which is attributed to the presence of the second excited state'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Anharmonicity determines qubit addressability; α/2π = 235 MHz is sufficient for two-level operation (α >> κt where κt/2π ≈ 15 MHz). Reduced from predicted 306 MHz, possibly due to transparent transport channels in NbN weak link.

additional_measurements.description: Total linewidth (decoherence rate) of planaron qubit
additional_measurements.source: Page 5: 'We extract the total linewidth of the qubit to be κt/2π ≈ 15 MHz'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: κt sets the coherence time scale; κt/2π = 15 MHz corresponds to T ~ 10 ns, much worse than state-of-the-art transmons (~100 µs). Authors attribute this to junction loss not yet understood.

additional_measurements.description: Coupling rate to transmission line
additional_measurements.source: Page 5: 'the coupling to the transmission line κc/2π ≈ 75 kHz'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: κt >> κc implies the qubit is strongly undercoupled; most decoherence is intrinsic (junction loss), not radiative. This ratio (κt/κc ~ 200) means only ~0.5% of decays go to the measurement port.

additional_measurements.description: Designed charging energy
additional_measurements.source: Page 6 and Appendix H: 'designed charging energy of EC/ℏ = 2π × 293 MHz, corresponding to a shunt capacitance of CS = 68.7 fF'

additional_measurements.description: Estimated Josephson energy from transmon formula
additional_measurements.source: Page 6: 'we extract an estimated Josephson energy of EJ/ℏ = 2π × 26.15 GHz...EJ/EC ~ 90'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: EJ/EC ~ 90 confirms deep transmon regime (charge noise insensitive); Josephson inductance LJ = 6.25 nH from this value.

additional_measurements.description: Predicted anharmonicity from transmon model (low-transparency S-I-S junction assumption)
additional_measurements.source: Page 6 and Appendix H: 'The anharmonicity, α ≃ −EC, is thus predicted to be 306 MHz where additional ~4% comes from numerical diagonalization'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Discrepancy between measured (235 MHz) and predicted (306 MHz) anharmonicity, not explained by stray inductance (~12 MHz reduction), attributed to transparent channels in NbN weak link reducing anharmonicity. This is a novel physics result.

additional_measurements.description: Stray inductance from leads (estimated from FEM)
additional_measurements.value: LS ~ 0.2 nH; LK = 17.5 pH/sq for the NbN film in planaron; stray inductance reduces α/2π by only ~12 MHz
additional_measurements.source: Page 6 and Appendix H: 'we estimate that the inductance of our leads reduces α/2π by only ~12 MHz'; 'LK = 17.5 pH/□, resulting in a total stray inductance of LS ~ 0.2 nH'

additional_measurements.description: Single-photon internal quality factor of L2UnA (linear lumped resonator with similar NbN weak link geometry, l=20nm, w=0.3µm, on second chip)
additional_measurements.value: Qi = 3.8 × 10^5 at single-photon power, resonant frequency ~9.433 GHz
additional_measurements.source: Appendix J, page 17: 'the devices displaying low anharmonicity had a much higher single-photon internal quality factor Qi = 3.8 × 10^5'; Fig. S12c: f0 = 9.433 GHz

additional_measurements.description: Anharmonicity of L2UnA (linear lumped resonator with l=20nm, w=0.3µm weak link)
additional_measurements.source: Appendix J, page 17: 'We estimate α/2π ≈ 10 Hz'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Orders of magnitude lower anharmonicity than planaron (235 MHz) despite similar LJ, not explained; geometry-dependent anharmonicity suppression in NbN weak links is a key open question.

additional_measurements.description: Half-integer Shapiro steps observed in NbN weak links, indicative of non-sinusoidal current-phase relation and highly transparent channels
additional_measurements.value: Half-integer Shapiro steps at fRF = 12.75 GHz (Device B, S2); also at 6.2 GHz and other frequencies
additional_measurements.source: Page 8, Fig. 5e-h and Appendix F, Fig. S10
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Non-sinusoidal CPR from transparent channels reduces anharmonicity (known to reduce α by up to 4x); these channels may also introduce additional loss mechanisms affecting qubit T1

anomalous_observations.description: The planaron qubit has κt/2π ≈ 15 MHz (T ~ 10 ns coherence), while CPW resonators from the same NbN process show Qi > 10^6 (photon lifetime ~100 µs equivalent). This is a ~4 orders of magnitude discrepancy in dissipation rate.
anomalous_observations.hypothesis: Author hypothesis: 'In a marked difference from the coplanar waveguide resonators, the transmon we studied here have relatively large dissipation, which is currently not understood...We leave a detailed investigation of intrinsic junction loss, spurious mode coupling, and design optimization to future studies.'

anomalous_observations.description: Measured anharmonicity α/2π = 235 MHz is significantly reduced from predicted 306 MHz for a low-transparency S-I-S junction with the same inductance. Stray inductance accounts for only ~12 MHz reduction.
anomalous_observations.hypothesis: Author hypothesis: The discrepancy is more likely due to the microscopic nature of the NbN weak link — transparent transmission channels in the link are known to reduce anharmonicity by up to a factor of four.

anomalous_observations.description: IcRN product is ~3x lower than Ambegaokar-Baratoff prediction: IcRN ≈ 0.3·π∆/2e vs expected π∆/2e.
anomalous_observations.hypothesis: Author hypothesis: Electrons dwell in the weak link over a time ~ℏ/ETh exceeding ℏ/∆, due to proximity to Anderson localization transition. Both diffusive and localization models are partially consistent with data; system is likely near the localization transition.

fabrication_details.description: Planaron fabrication sequence (S1-type): (1) E-beam lithography + ALE to etch narrow trench defining weak link constriction (w ~1 µm, l ~30 nm); (2) E-beam lithography + ALE to etch capacitor pads and lead geometry; (3) BOE 6:1 ~20 min final clean
fabrication_details.source: Appendix G, page 15 and Section II, page 4

fabrication_details.description: Qubit coupled directly to transmission line in hanger geometry (no readout resonator); omitting readout resonator facilitates characterization of unknown frequency/anharmonicity
fabrication_details.source: Page 4: 'we directly couple it to a transmission line in a hanger geometry without a readout resonator'

fabrication_details.description: Measurement setup identical to CPW resonator setup: copper package, light-tight + mu-metal shields, Eccosorb + HERD filters, ~23 mK base temperature
fabrication_details.source: Appendix B, page 12: 'We note that the transmon qubit is measured using the same setup.'

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Total decoherence linewidth κt/2π in MHz for a qubit coupled to a transmission line (or resonator), measured from power-dependent S21 lineshape fitting
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: For qubits without a readout resonator (hanger-coupled directly to TL), κt is the primary coherence metric reported — not T1 or T2. Tracking κt alongside κc allows extraction of intrinsic loss rate (κint = κt - κc), analogous to Qi for resonators. Without this field, the planaron's coherence data cannot be represented accurately.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Page 5: 'We extract the total linewidth of the qubit to be κt/2π ≈ 15 MHz'

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Qubit anharmonicity α/2π in MHz, defined as the difference f01 - f12
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Anharmonicity directly determines gate speed and addressability; for NbN weak-link qubits it is a key indicator of junction transparency (highly transparent channels reduce α). Systematic tracking of α alongside junction geometry would reveal the transparency-anharmonicity relationship in disordered superconductors.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Page 4: 'a measured anharmonicity of α/2π = 235 MHz'

fabrication_groups.evidence: Appendix A (page 12) describes a single ALD NbN deposition process on 2-inch annealed HEMEX sapphire wafers at 400°C using the Ultratech/Cambridge Fiji G2 system, producing 20 nm NbN films. Appendix B describes multi-patch chips cut from these wafers where NbN_ALD_SIT_films_bulk (bulk film transport) and CPW_resonators_ALE_treated (CPW resonators) are co-fabricated on the same 7×7 mm chips: 'The Hall bars and microwave CPW resonators are fabricated by etching multiple patches of different thicknesses on a single chip.' Appendix G (page 15) states the planaron_qubit 'is fabricated from a single NbN film' using 'the same way as detailed in Sec. II,' which uses the same ALD NbN deposition process and wafer substrate. Appendix B further states 'the transmon qubit is measured using the same setup.' All three sample types share the same ALD deposition run conditions, wafer, and base film.
fabrication_groups.source: Appendix A page 12, Appendix B page 12, Appendix G page 15

NbN_ALD_SIT_films_bulk.profile_notes: This sample record covers bulk film characterization (SIT critical thickness, kinetic inductance, Mattis-Bardeen relation, surface roughness after ALE) with no patterned microwave device measured; classified film_only and not_applicable. Mean free path le = 0.03–0.5 nm (sub-atomic) confirms extreme dirty/localized limit.

CPW_resonators_ALE_treated.profile_notes: Qi > 10^6 (up to ~3e6) places this in state_of_the_art for resonators. The gap-independence of Qi after ALE and gap-dependence before ALE directly implicates interface/surface TLS as the dominant pre-treatment loss channel; ALE surface treatment is mapped to anneal_to_Qi as the closest available correlation for surface treatment improving Qi.

planaron_qubit.profile_notes: Total linewidth κt/2π ≈ 15 MHz corresponds to T ~ 10 ns, well below 10 µs threshold, placing this in early_exploration. Loss mechanisms are unattributed (authors explicitly state intrinsic junction loss is not understood) with quasiparticle loss plausible given proximity to SIT and transparent channels; TLS_unattributed included because the large κt vs. resonator Qi discrepancy implies junction-localized loss not yet identified.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Methods Section V.A paragraph 3 describes one room-temperature deposition process for Si substrates: 'The second method involved sputtering tantalum at room temperature onto Si(100) substrates... We first deposited a 6 nm niobium seed layer, followed by either 60 nm or 100 nm of tantalum. The DC sputtering powers were set to 510 W for Nb and 310 W for Ta. Both materials were deposited under an argon process pressure of 3 mTorr, yielding a deposition rate of approximately 15 nm per minute.' Table I confirms all Si-substrate samples (Table I Row 1, Table I Row 3 through Table I Row 16) share this Si/Nb-seed/room-temperature process. However, the paper does not state whether all these samples came from a single physical deposition run or multiple separate runs — it is likely they were deposited in separate runs since different oxidation experiments were conducted on different days, but this is not stated explicitly.
fabrication_groups.source: Methods Section V.A paragraph 3; Table I

fabrication_groups.evidence: Methods Section V.A paragraph 2 describes the high-temperature sapphire process: '150 nm of Ta was deposited on sapphire substrates held at 500 °C' with thermal degassing at 500°C for 2 hours. Table I Row 1.profile_notes: Control sample with native oxide only; no microwave device measured. Loss mechanisms inferred from paper's stated motivation linking surface roughness and oxide to TLS density at metal-vacuum and metal-substrate interfaces.

Table I Row 2.profile_notes: Control sample on sapphire with native oxide; no microwave device measured. Higher roughness than Si-substrate control attributed to tri-domain grain structure from hexagonal sapphire alignment.

Table I Row 3.profile_notes: Tube furnace oxidation at 400°C for 10 min; oxide identified as Ta2O5 by XPS. No microwave device fabricated; surface roughness and oxide thickness are the primary characterization targets.

Table I Row 4.profile_notes: Tube furnace oxidation at 400°C for 30 min; oxide thickness increases with time. No microwave device fabricated.

Table I Row 5.profile_notes: Tube furnace oxidation at 400°C for 60 min; Ta2O5 confirmed by XPS with large grain structure. No microwave device fabricated.

Table I Row 6.profile_notes: RTA oxidation at 700°C for 1 min produces extreme roughness (7.28 nm); XRR not measurable. Authors explicitly conclude RTA is unfavorable for Josephson junction barrier formation.

Table I Row 7.profile_notes: RTA oxidation at 700°C for 5 min; roughness of 16.38 nm is the highest in the study. XRR not measurable. No microwave device fabricated.

Table I Row 8.profile_notes: RTA oxidation at 700°C for 10 min; non-uniform roughness (15.7 nm at 10 µm², 5.4 nm at 1 µm²). XRR not measurable due to excessive roughness. No microwave device fabricated.

Table I Row 9.profile_notes: Room-temperature plasma oxidation for 10 min; roughness (0.572 nm) nearly identical to control. XPS shows incomplete oxidation within 10 nm probe depth. No microwave device fabricated.

Table I Row 10.profile_notes: Room-temperature plasma oxidation for 30 min; roughness (0.613 nm) comparable to control and 10-min sample, indicating time-insensitive thermodynamic control. No microwave device fabricated.

Table I Row 11.profile_notes: Plasma oxidation at 200°C for 60 min yields lowest roughness in study (0.108 nm); identified as optimal condition for Josephson junction barrier. No microwave device fabricated.

Table I Row 12.profile_notes: Plasma oxidation at 200°C for 120 min; negligible change in thickness or roughness vs 60-min sample, confirming thermodynamic saturation. No microwave device fabricated.

Table I Row 13.profile_notes: Plasma oxidation at 300°C for 60 min; oxide thicker (~10 nm) than 200°C samples with moderate roughness (0.463 nm). No microwave device fabricated.

Table I Row 14.profile_notes: Plasma oxidation at 300°C for 120 min; roughness drops markedly vs 60-min (0.125 vs 0.463 nm) while thickness barely changes, showing time controls smoothness not thickness at this temperature. Ta2O5 confirmed by XPS.

Table I Row 15.profile_notes: Plasma oxidation at 400°C for 60 min produces thickest oxide (~15 nm) confirmed by SEM cross-section; moderate roughness (0.342 nm) suitable for thicker SIS barrier applications. No microwave device fabricated.

Table I Row 16.profile_notes: This is a film-only sample focused on controlled plasma oxidation to grow Ta2O5; no microwave device or qubit is measured. Transport regime is unknown as no RRR or mean free path data are provided for this specific sample.

schema_evolution_proposals.why_important: Table 2 and Section 5.4 systematically compare five different capping materials (Ta, Al, TiN, Au, Ru) on Nb films and show that T1 varies from 40 µs (uncapped) to >300 µs (Ta-capped on Si) — a 7x range driven entirely by encapsulation choice. Without a structured field for this parameter, the corpus cannot distinguish encapsulated from unencapsulated devices or compare encapsulant types across studies.
schema_evolution_proposals.supporting_text: Various in situ metal capping layers — Ta, Al, TiN, and Au — were systematically investigated for their ability to suppress native oxide formation at the Nb–air interface... Ta-capped Nb qubits that were fabricated on Si substrate demonstrated marked improvements in coherence, with energy relaxation times (T1) exceeding 300 µs, significantly outperforming other capping strategies.

schema_evolution_proposals.description: Thickness of the encapsulation or capping layer deposited on top of the superconducting film, in nanometers.
schema_evolution_proposals.why_important: Table 2 reports capping layer thicknesses (5–15 nm) alongside T1 values for each encapsulant. Without this field, quantitative comparison of encapsulation effectiveness across studies is impossible — a 5 nm Ru cap and a 10 nm Ta cap are physically different interventions that need to be distinguished.
schema_evolution_proposals.supporting_text: Table 2: Capping layer Thickness (nm) [values: 10 for Ta/Al/Au, 10–15 for TiN, 5 for Ru]

schema_evolution_proposals.description: Chemical identity of the dominant surface oxide species present on the superconducting film (e.g., Nb2O5, NbO2, NbO, NbOx, Ta2O5, AlOx, TiOx, RuOx). Free text.
schema_evolution_proposals.why_important: Multiple sections (4.3, 4.4, 4.5, 5.1) show that Nb surface oxide composition — specifically the ratio of Nb2O5 to suboxides NbO2 and NbO — directly determines TLS density and dielectric loss. Nb2O5 is a high-k dielectric that hosts oxygen vacancies, while suboxides have different defect densities. Tracking oxide composition alongside Qi and T1 would allow the corpus to test whether oxide stoichiometry predicts loss, independent of thickness.
schema_evolution_proposals.supporting_text: At a microscopic level, microwave dissipation in Nb thin films arises from the complex hierarchy of surface native oxide (Nb2O5) and suboxides (e.g., NbO2, NbO) that form upon air exposure... These oxides are structurally disordered and host oxygen vacancies and dangling bonds that give rise to electric-dipole TLS.

schema_evolution_proposals.description: Mean grain size of the superconducting film measured by TEM or XRD, in nanometers.
schema_evolution_proposals.why_important: Figure 5 and Section 3 show that HiPIMS films have smaller grains (44±14 nm) than DC magnetron sputtered films (65±22 nm), and this difference correlates with reduced RRR and lower resonator quality factors. Grain size determines grain boundary density, which controls oxygen diffusion pathways into the film and hence TLS density. A structured field would allow systematic corpus-wide analysis of the grain size → RRR → Qi chain.
schema_evolution_proposals.supporting_text: Nb films grown by HiPIMS often display smaller grains and increased roughness compared to conventional sputtering (Figure 5), which correlates with reduced RRR and lower resonator quality factors.

schema_evolution_proposals.description: Post-deposition surface engineering method applied to the superconducting film before or after patterning, distinct from standard BOE/piranha cleans. Examples: ANAB (Accelerated Neutral Atom Beam), CMP (Chemical Mechanical Polishing), nitrogen plasma passivation, in situ capping. Free text including method name and key parameters.
schema_evolution_proposals.why_important: Section 5 documents four distinct surface treatment strategies (BOE, nitrogen plasma, ANAB, encapsulation) that each produce measurably different oxide compositions and TLS densities. The existing post_fabrication_surface_treatment field captures chemistry for standard wet treatments but does not accommodate beam-based (ANAB) or plasma-based treatments with their specific process parameters (fluence, gas mixture, pressure). A dedicated field with controlled vocabulary would allow treatment-type comparisons across the corpus.
schema_evolution_proposals.supporting_text: Chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) and accelerated neutral atom beam (ANAB) processing have been shown to yield smoother surfaces and more stable suboxide layers with reduced hydrogen incorporation... Nitrogen plasma passivated Nb resonators exhibit a marked reduction in TLS participation and higher internal quality factors (Qi) even after device aging compared to untreated controls.

schema_evolution_proposals.description: Boolean or descriptive field indicating whether hydrogen or niobium hydride (NbHx) species were detected in the film, typically by SIMS. Values: true/false or 'NbHx detected by SIMS', 'H- signal present', 'none detected'.
schema_evolution_proposals.why_important: Sections 4.5 and 5 document that NbHx precipitation suppresses superconductivity below 1.3 K and is directly linked to qubit decoherence. SIMS detection of H- and NbH- signals is a reported measurement in multiple cited studies. Tracking hydrogen contamination as a structured field would allow the corpus to identify which processing steps (wet etch, plasma exposure) introduce hydrogen and correlate them with T1 degradation.
schema_evolution_proposals.supporting_text: Lee and Sung et al. discovered hydride precipitation in Nb transmon devices. SIMS data showed strong H− and NbH− signals, confirming hydrogen trapping during processing. Combined with microscopy, this provided a direct evidence of niobium hydride (NbHx) phases that suppress superconductivity below 1.3 K.

schema_evolution_proposals.description: Out-of-plane crystallographic orientation of the superconducting film as determined by XRD (e.g., (110), (111), polycrystalline). Already partially captured in the existing schema via film_crystal_phase, but orientation is a distinct and separately reportable quantity.
schema_evolution_proposals.why_important: Table 1 shows that Nb film orientation ((110) vs (111)) is systematically controlled by deposition temperature on sapphire substrates, and orientation determines grain boundary density, epitaxial quality, and RRR. The review documents a clear trend: (111)-oriented films grown at high temperature have RRR up to 12.5, while room-temperature polycrystalline films have RRR of 2.3. A structured orientation field (separate from crystal phase) would allow corpus-wide analysis of orientation effects on coherence.
schema_evolution_proposals.supporting_text: Table 1: Film orientation column shows (110) to (111) for [67], (111) for [65], (110) all cases for [91]. On c-plane sapphire, films grown at low temperatures (<700 K) typically adopt a (110) out-of-plane texture, whereas higher growth temperatures (>750 K) favor (111) orientation.

schema_evolution_proposals.description: Base pressure of the deposition chamber before film growth begins, in Torr. Distinct from the working/process pressure during deposition (already captured in deposition_pressure_torr).
schema_evolution_proposals.why_important: Table 1 reports base pressures (P_Base) as a separate column from deposition pressures (P_deposition) for all reviewed studies. Oxygen contamination during Nb growth is identified as the primary limitation of film quality — base pressure directly controls residual oxygen partial pressure and hence interstitial oxygen incorporation and RRR degradation. The existing deposition_pressure_torr field captures working pressure but not base pressure; conflating them would lose critical information.
schema_evolution_proposals.supporting_text: Table 1: P_Base (mTorr) column lists >1.5×10^-7 for [67], ~10^-6 for [91], <5×10^-5 for [87]. Among the most persistent challenges in Nb film growth is its strong affinity for oxygen. Even trace oxygen contamination in the growth environment leads to interstitial incorporation of oxygen or formation of Nb oxides.

schema_evolution_proposals.description: Boolean or descriptive field indicating whether an interfacial silicide layer (NbSix) was detected at the Nb-Si interface, typically by TEM/EDS/EELS. Values: true/false, or description of detection method and silicide phase if known.
schema_evolution_proposals.why_important: Section 3 identifies NbSix interlayer formation as a critical Nb-on-Si specific decoherence mechanism: 'Interfacial silicide formation in Nb-on-Si devices introduces amorphous or polycrystalline NbSix layers that increase electric-field participation at the metal–substrate interface and degrade coherence.' Whether silicide is present or absent depends on processing conditions (thermal budget, patterning chemistry) and directly determines MS interface participation ratio. Tracking this as a binary field would allow the corpus to identify which Nb-on-Si processes successfully suppress silicide.
schema_evolution_proposals.supporting_text: Interfacial silicide formation in Nb-on-Si devices introduces amorphous or polycrystalline NbSix layers that increase electric-field participation at the metal–substrate interface and degrade coherence... Altoe and collaborators performed a wafer-scale analysis... Their results revealed that, under optimized conditions, the Nb–Si interface can remain atomically sharp and chemically abrupt, with no detectable silicide or interfacial carbon.

primary_paper_queue.citation: M. Tuokkola, Y. Sunada, H. Kivijärvi, et al., 'Methods to achieve near-millisecond energy relaxation and dephasing times for a superconducting transmon qubit,' Nature Communications 16 (2025): 5421
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Reports median T1 = 425 µs and T2,echo = 541 µs in Nb transmons on high-resistivity Si, with maximum T1 above 660 µs — among the highest reported for Nb-based qubits. Contains fabrication details, film deposition conditions, and materials optimization strategies directly relevant to the Nb qubit coherence database.

primary_paper_queue.citation: A. Premkumar, C. Weiland, S. Hwang, et al., 'Microscopic relaxation channels in materials for superconducting qubits,' Communications Materials 2 (2021): 72
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Comprehensive study combining transmon qubit T1 measurements with PES depth profiling comparing DC sputtering vs HiPIMS Nb films on sapphire. Reports RRR values (8.9±0.1 vs 2.9–5.0), Tc values, oxide depth profiles by HAXPES, and correlates deposition method with qubit relaxation. High-value primary paper with quantitative materials-to-performance data.

primary_paper_queue.citation: J.-S. Oh, C. J. Kopas, J. Marshall, et al., 'Exploring the relationship between deposition method, microstructure, and performance of Nb/Si-based superconducting coplanar waveguide resonators,' Acta Materialia 276 (2024): 120153
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Systematic study of HiPIMS vs DC magnetron sputtered Nb films on Si with grain size distributions (44±14 nm vs 65±22 nm), TEM cross-sections, and resonator quality factor measurements. Contains quantitative microstructure-to-Qi correlations for Nb-on-Si CPW resonators.

primary_paper_queue.citation: M. Bal, A. A. Murthy, S. Zhu, et al., 'Systematic improvements in transmon qubit coherence enabled by niobium surface encapsulation,' npj Quantum Information 10 (2024): 43
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Systematic comparison of five Nb encapsulation strategies (uncapped, Ta, Al, TiN, Au) on both sapphire and Si substrates with T1 measurements ranging from 40 µs to >300 µs. Contains STEM-EDS and ToF-SIMS characterization of each interface alongside qubit performance data — directly links surface chemistry to T1.

primary_paper_queue.citation: A. A. Murthy, P. Masih Das, S. M. Ribet, et al., 'Developing a Chemical and Structural Understanding of the Surface Oxide in a Niobium Superconducting Qubit,' ACS Nano 16 (2022): 17257–17262
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Atomic-level characterization of Nb surface oxide structure using FEM and EDS in transmon qubit devices. Identifies oxygen vacancies in suboxides as TLS sources and correlates columnar grain structure with NbOx interspersion and decoherence. Key primary paper for the Nb surface oxide → TLS loss chain.

primary_paper_queue.citation: M. V. P. Altoé, A. Banerjee, C. Berk, et al., 'Localization and Mitigation of Loss in Niobium Superconducting Circuits,' PRX Quantum 3 (2022): 020312
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Wafer-scale analysis of Nb/Si coplanar resonators using XPS, EELS, and STEM showing atomically sharp Nb-Si interface under optimized conditions with no silicide, and quantifying process-induced oxides as dominant TLS sources. Reports BOE etch effects on oxide thickness and correlation with resonator Q > 10^6.

primary_paper_queue.citation: M. Drimmer, S. Telkamp, F. L. Fischer, et al., 'The effect of niobium thin film structure on losses in superconducting circuits,' Materials for Quantum Technology 5 (2025): 041001
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Systematic XRD study of Nb films sputtered on c-plane sapphire at temperatures from 300 K to 975 K, reporting RRR range 2.3–12.5 and Tc = 9.25±0.1 K alongside STEM confirmation of epitaxial quality. Directly correlates deposition temperature with crystal orientation, grain boundary elimination, and RRR — a key materials optimization study.

primary_paper_queue.citation: K. M. Ryan, C. G. Torres-Castanedo, D. P. Goronzy, et al., 'Characterization of Nb films for superconducting qubits using phase boundary measurements,' Applied Physics Letters 121 (2022): 202601
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Characterizes Nb films deposited by HiPIMS on Si(001), a-plane and c-plane Al2O3 at 300 K and on a-plane Al2O3 at 1273 K, reporting RRR (~5 and 2.59), Tc (8.5–9.0 K and 7.01 K), film orientation (110), and thickness (40/150 nm). Uses phase boundary measurements as a materials characterization approach relevant to qubit applications.

primary_paper_queue.citation: H. Wang, T. Banerjee, T. Farinha, et al., 'Impact of etches on thin-film single-crystal niobium resonators,' arXiv: 2402.18051 (2024)
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Studies single-crystal Nb films grown by MBE on c-plane sapphire at 1073 K with RRR 20–40 and Tc 7.9–9.2 K, and measures the impact of different etch chemistries on resonator quality. Directly relevant to the surface treatment → Qi chain in high-crystallinity Nb films.

primary_paper_queue.citation: S. K. Karuppannan, D. Huang, N. M. Kommanaboina, et al., 'Improved Interface of Niobium Superconducting Resonator With Ruthenium as a Capping Layer,' ACS Applied Electronic Materials 6 (2024): 7372–7379
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Reports Ru encapsulation reducing Nb surface oxide thickness from ~5.3 nm to ~0.6 nm and achieving >80% loss reduction in Nb/Si resonators in the low-photon regime. Contains quantitative TEM oxide thickness measurements and resonator Qi data — a key encapsulation study.

primary_paper_queue.citation: K. Zheng, D. Kowsari, N. J. Thobaben, et al., 'Nitrogen plasma passivated niobium resonators for superconducting quantum circuits,' Applied Physics Letters 120 (2022): 102601
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Demonstrates nitrogen plasma passivation forming ~5 nm NbN surface layer on Nb films, showing reduced TLS participation and higher Qi in resonators after aging compared to untreated controls. Contains quantitative Qi vs aging data and Tc preservation data for a scalable passivation approach.

primary_paper_queue.citation: B. Abdisatarov, D. Bafia, A. Murthy, et al., 'Direct measurement of microwave loss in Nb films for superconducting qubits,' Applied Physics Letters 125 (2024): 124002
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Directly measures microwave loss in Nb films for superconducting qubits, providing quantitative loss tangent or Qi data that would populate key database fields. Cited in the review as a key reference for HiPIMS film characterization.

primary_paper_queue.citation: J. A. Dhas, E. Bhatia, K. P. Koirala, et al., 'Tailoring the Physicochemical Properties of Nb Thin Films via Surface Engineering Methods,' ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces 17 (2025): 24502–24512
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Compares CMP and ANAB surface treatments on Nb films using TOF-SIMS depth profiling and 3D ion mapping, quantifying hydrogen-related species (NbOH-, NbH-, H-) reduction. Reports normalized NbOH- signal dropping from 0.16% to 0.06–0.09% after treatment — directly relevant to hydrogen contamination tracking.

primary_paper_queue.citation: Z. Sung, A. Cano, A. Murthy, et al., 'Direct observation of nanometer size hydride precipitations in superconducting niobium,' Scientific Reports 14 (2024): 26916
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Provides direct SIMS evidence of NbHx precipitation in Nb transmon devices, with depth profiles showing H- and NbH- signals. Establishes hydrogen incorporation during processing as a qubit decoherence mechanism — a primary paper for the hydrogen contamination → T1 loss chain.

primary_paper_queue.citation: A. A. Murthy, J. Lee, C. Kopas, et al., 'TOF-SIMS analysis of decoherence sources in superconducting qubits,' Applied Physics Letters 120 (2022): 044002
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: TOF-SIMS study of Nb-Si interfacial silicide formation during lithographic patterning and plasma processing in transmon qubits. Demonstrates that process-induced silicide at Nb-Si boundaries has implications for decoherence — directly relevant to the silicide_interlayer_detected schema proposal.

primary_paper_queue.citation: M. C. de Ory, V. Rollano, D. Rodriguez, M. T. Magaz, D. Granados, and A. Gomez, 'Low Loss Hybrid Nb/Au Superconducting Resonators for Quantum Circuit Applications,' Advanced Quantum Technologies 8 (2025): 2400699
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Reports Au-capped Nb lumped element resonators on Si achieving Q > 10^6, with Au encapsulation reducing TLS density. Contains quantitative Qi data and surface characterization for the Nb/Au bilayer system — a key encapsulation result for the database.

primary_paper_queue.citation: K. R. Joshi, S. Ghimire, M. A. Tanatar, et al., 'Quasiparticle Spectroscopy, Transport, and Magnetic Properties of Nb Films Used in Superconducting Qubits,' Physical Review Applied 20 (2023): 024031
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Comprehensive transport and spectroscopy study of Nb films specifically intended for superconducting qubits, covering quasiparticle properties, RRR, and magnetic response. Directly relevant to the Nb film materials database with quantitative transport measurements.

primary_paper_queue.citation: R. D. Chang, N. Shumiya, R. A. McLellan, et al., 'Eliminating Surface Oxides of Superconducting Circuits With Noble Metal Encapsulation,' Physical Review Letters 134 (2025): 097001
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Studies noble metal encapsulation of superconducting circuits (including Ta resonators) and identifies sidewall oxidation during etching as a loss channel not addressed by top-surface encapsulation alone. Quantitative loss reduction data and sidewall oxide characterization relevant to encapsulation strategy comparison.

primary_paper_queue.citation: A. Anferov, K.-H. Lee, F. Zhao, J. Simon, and D. I. Schuster, 'Improved coherence in optically defined niobium trilayer-junction qubits,' Physical Review Applied 21 (2024): 024047
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Reports improved coherence in Nb trilayer junction qubits using optically defined processes. Contains qubit T1/T2 measurements and fabrication details for Nb-based qubits with specific process optimization — directly relevant to the Nb qubit coherence database.

primary_paper_queue.citation: J.-S. Oh, R. Zaman, A. A. Murthy, et al., 'Structure and Formation Mechanisms in Tantalum and Niobium Oxides in Superconducting Quantum Circuits,' ACS Nano 18 (2024): 19732–19741
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Comparative EELS study of surface oxide formation on both Ta and Nb films in superconducting quantum circuits, providing structural and chemical characterization of NbOx-Nb interface. Directly relevant to surface oxide composition tracking across Nb and Ta film systems.

primary_paper_queue.citation: S. Kar, C. Weiland, C. Zhou, et al., 'Engineering of niobium surfaces through accelerated neutral atom beam technology for quantum applications,' Journal of Applied Physics 134 (2023): 025301
primary_paper_queue.why_relevant: Quantitative characterization of ANAB-treated Nb films showing tunable oxide thickness (2.2–5.5 nm) as a function of oxygen fluence, with XRR and XPS depth profiling. Reports stratified oxide structure and reduced hydrogen incorporation — key data for the surface treatment → oxide composition → Qi chain.

fabrication_details.description: Device is a 6-qubit Xmon transmon chip fabricated by MIT Lincoln Laboratory SQUILL Foundry, funded by LPS Qubit Collaboratory. Three qubits used in experiments (Q1, Qa, Q2). Common X-shaped transmon design per reference [44] (Chen et al., PRL 113, 220502, 2014). Flux-tunable transmons.
fabrication_details.source: Supplementary Section VII page 11 and Acknowledgments page 7

fabrication_details.description: Measurement setup: Bluefors LD250 dilution refrigerator, base temperature ~10 mK at MXC stage. Additional MXC shield for IR radiation protection. Amuneal magnetic shielding can with inner surface painted with Stycast 1266, Carbon Black and Silicon Carbide for IR suppression. TWPA at MXC stage, HEMT at 4K stage. RF lines filtered with K&L 12 GHz LPF, Marki 9.6 GHz LPF, Eccosorb LPF. OPX+ system with Lab Brick and Windfreak microwave sources. Bias tee ZFBT-4R2GW-FT+ for flux control; Yokogawa 7651 DC source. MIT Lincoln Laboratory TWPA provided for measurements.
Qubit control: I-Q modulation for readout resonators and transmons. 10 MHz reference for phase-locking all RF instruments including ADC.

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Relaxation time for the |f>->|e> transition of a transmon qutrit, in µs. Distinct from T1^ge (|e>->|g> decay).
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: For g-f erasure qubits, T1^ef sets the erasure rate (detectable leakage timescale). The ratio T1^ge / T1^ef ~2 determines whether the erasure hierarchy (erasure errors >> Pauli errors) is satisfied. This is the primary figure of merit for erasure qubit performance and cannot be derived from T1^ge alone.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table S1, |f>->|e> decay T1^ef rows; page 3 paragraph 2

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Ramsey coherence time between ground state |g> and second excited state |f> of a transmon qutrit, in µs.
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: T2^gf characterizes dephasing of the g-f logical qubit encoding directly; it sets the fundamental limit on phase-flip lifetime in the absence of dynamical decoupling and cannot be inferred from T2^ge alone.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table S1, g-f Ramsey T2^gf rows

schema_promotion_candidates.description: The timescale for detectable leakage out of the code subspace into |e>, in µs. Characterizes the rate of erasure errors in the g-f qubit.
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: The erasure lifetime (not T1 or T2) is the primary figure of merit for erasure qubit QEC benefit. The ratio erasure_lifetime / bit_flip_lifetime determines how much QEC threshold improvement erasure encoding provides. This is a fundamentally new performance metric for the erasure qubit paradigm.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Page 4 paragraph 1: 'erasure lifetime (45 µs) which characterizes the timescale for detectable leakage'; Figure 3b,d,f

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Logical qubit bit-flip lifetime achieved via mid-circuit erasure detection and post-selection, in µs. Distinct from physical T1.
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: The logical T1 (post-selected) is the operationally relevant coherence for erasure-based QEC and can be 10x or more longer than the physical T1. Tracking this alongside physical T1 and erasure lifetime would enable systematic comparison of erasure qubit performance across platforms.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Page 4 paragraph 1 and Figure 3b: logical bit-flip lifetimes 549(56) µs and 610(46) µs

catchall.free_notes: This paper reports two fridge cooldowns (A and B) for the same three-qubit device. Table S1 lists parameters for both cooldowns side by side. The main experiment results (memory lifetimes >500 µs, RB) appear to be from cooldown B based on the T1^ge ~55 µs stated in the main text matching the cooldown B range (40-80 µs) better than cooldown A (30-70 µs). The parity measurement data (Fig. 5) was taken during a period of 'slightly lower coherence performance' (noted in Figure 5 caption and Supplementary Section XI). Cooldown A and B share the same physical device but represent separate cooldowns with distinct measured values. Q2 is mentioned as having 'relatively short coherence time' in the context of the parity measurement experiment (page 5). The g-f coherence time T2^gf ≈ 47 µs (XY4) in the supplementary refers to the physical g-f dephasing without erasure detection benefit.

Three qubits were used in this experiment.' Table S1 explicitly lists parameters for all three qubits (Q1^A, Qa^A, Q2^A, Q1^B, Qa^B, Q2^B) across two cooldowns (A, B) of the same physical device. Q1_cooldown_A.profile_notes: Material class assigned as aluminum based on standard MIT Lincoln Laboratory Xmon transmon fabrication with Al/AlOx junctions; growth method is 'other' as foundry fabrication details are not specified. TLS is implicated via the transient TLS dip anomaly; flux noise and charge noise are implied by flux-tunable operation and dephasing noise PSD measurements.

Q1_cooldown_B.profile_notes: Same device as cooldown A, second thermal cycle. T1 ~60 µs places this in the competitive tier (10–100 µs qubit_state context). Logical T1 >500 µs is a post-selected logical metric, not the physical qubit T1 used for coherence_tier assignment.

Qa_cooldown_A.profile_notes: Ancilla qubit with T1 ~17.5 µs at sweet spot falls in competitive range, but when operated away from flux sweet spot for the FWM erasure gate its effective coherence drops below 1 µs; sweet-spot T1 used for coherence_tier, giving competitive. Flux noise is a primary identified loss channel due to operation away from the flux sweet spot.

Qa_cooldown_B.profile_notes: Ancilla T1 ~12.5 µs at sweet spot; early_exploration threshold is T1 < 10 µs, so this is borderline competitive, but given the range reported (could be below 10 µs at times) and it being the weakest qubit, competitive is assigned based on the nominal value of 12.5 µs.

Q2_cooldown_A.profile_notes: Q2 T1 ~20 µs places it in the competitive tier (>10 µs); however it is described as having relatively short coherence. Assigned competitive based on nominal T1 value of 20 µs meeting the threshold.

Q2_cooldown_B.profile_notes: Q2 in cooldown B has T1 ~25 µs, placing it in the competitive tier. Authors note 'relatively short coherence time' compared to Q1, consistent with it being the weakest data qubit but still above the early_exploration threshold.

fabrication_details.description: Photoresist: MP S1813 spun at 3000 rpm, baked 1 min at 90°C. Patterned using G-line stepper. Developed in MP 321 MIF developer for 1 min.

Deposition chamber: AJA International Inc. magnetron sputtering chamber with 7 × 2-inch gun assemblies; base pressure 3×10⁻⁸ Torr without gettering; used for magnetic depositions (Fe, Co, Ni) for >20 years
Nb target purity: 3N5 (99.95%), 2-inch diameter, 1/8-inch thick, from AJA International Inc. Certificate of analysis impurities: Co 0.001 ppm, Fe 0.08 ppm, Ni 0.004 ppm, Cr 0.05 ppm

Measurement setup: resonators packaged in enclosures with Berkeley black coated copper shim to absorb stray photons and prevent quasiparticle generation. Meehl fridge: Bluefors LD dilution refrigerator with bottom loader, base T=17 mK. Eccosorb filters on input and output.
Resonator design: Boulder Cryogenic Quantum Testbed open-source design (Kopas et al. arXiv:2204.07202); hangar configuration with 8 λ/4 resonators at 4-8 GHz; 3 µm gap CPW

Supp Table I Row 1: DP1-BOE-1165-noHF.profile_notes: RRR of ~5 places this firmly in the dirty limit. Qi of ~33,600 is early_exploration by resonator thresholds. The paper explicitly links Cl residues from 1165 strip (without HF) to ~15x higher LP loss, supporting surface_oxide_to_Qi correlation.

Supp Table I Row 2: DP1-Anneal-1165-noHF.profile_notes: RRR of ~4 confirms dirty limit. Qi ~32,000 is early_exploration. In situ anneal did not improve performance without HF post-treatment, consistent with the dominant loss being post-etch Cl contamination rather than substrate bulk quality.

Supp Table I Row 3: DP1-Thermal-1165-noH.profile_notes: RRR ~4.3 confirms dirty limit. Qi ~31,000 is early_exploration. Thermal oxidation + BOE substrate prep did not improve over BOE-only without HF, confirming that post-etch Cl residue is the dominant loss driver in the 1165-noHF condition.

Supp Table I Row 4: DP1-BOE-1165-HF.profile_notes: No Tc/RRR reported for this aggregated row; dirty_limit inferred from the same deposition conditions as rows 1-3 (RRR ~5). Qi ~641,000 falls in the competitive tier (1e5–1e6). HF post-treatment removes Cl/oxide residues enabling near-SOTA performance.

Supp Table I Row 5: DP1-Anneal-1165-HF.profile_notes: Dirty limit inferred from deposition conditions consistent with rows 2 and 3 (RRR ~3.65 after fabrication). Qi ~637,000 is competitive. HF post-treatment recovers performance despite Anneal substrate prep showing no independent advantage.

Supp Table I Row 6: DP1-Thermal-1165-HF.profile_notes: Dirty limit inferred from DP1 deposition conditions (RRR ~3.37 for Thermal condition). Qi ~833,000 is competitive but below 1e6 threshold. Best among 1165+HF substrate variants though authors note distributions are not well-separated.

Supp Table I Row 7: DP1-BOE-AZ-noHF.profile_notes: Dirty limit inferred from DP1 deposition conditions. Qi ~690,000 is competitive. Key result: AZ300T strip removes Cl without HF, achieving near-SOTA performance; XPS confirms no detectable Cl after AZ strip, directly correlating with ~20x loss improvement vs 1165-noHF.

Supp Table I Row 8: DP2-BOE-AZ-noHF.profile_notes: DP2 chamber co-loaded with magnetic targets (permalloy, Co, CoFeB); RRR ~5.03 still places film in dirty limit. Qi ~568,000 is competitive. Result demonstrates magnetically contaminated chamber does not preclude high-Qi resonators, making deposition_conditions_to_film_purity relevant.

Supp Table I Row 9: DP1-BOE-AZ-HF.profile_notes: Dirty limit inferred from DP1 conditions. Qi ~1,189,000 exceeds 1e6 threshold placing this in state_of_the_art for resonators. AZ+HF combination consistently outperforms 1165+HF, attributed to AZ providing a cleaner surface template before HF treatment.

Supp Table I Row 10: DP2-BOE-AZ-HF.profile_notes: DP2 magnetically contaminated chamber with AZ+HF post-treatment achieves Qi ~1,311,000, state_of_the_art. Slightly exceeds DP1+AZ+HF, confirming magnetic chamber contamination is not a loss-limiting factor when strip chemistry is optimized.

Supp Table I Row 11: DP1-BOE-AZ-BOE.profile_notes: Best-performing sample in the study: Qi ~2,000,000 (state_of_the_art). Post-fabrication 20 min BOE outperforms HF treatment; authors suggest HF may introduce hydrogen/hydride contamination in Nb. Aging study (Row 13) tracks oxide regrowth degradation over 4 weeks.

Supp Table I Row 12: DP2-BOE-AZ-BOE.profile_notes: DP2 magnetically contaminated chamber with AZ+BOE achieves Qi ~2,100,000, state_of_the_art and comparable to DP1+AZ+BOE. Confirms magnetic chamber contamination is not performance-limiting; BOE post-treatment is the dominant determinant of this result.

Supp Table I Row 13: DP1-BOE-AZ-Aged.profile_notes: Same chip as Row 11 re-measured after 4 weeks ambient aging; Qi degraded from ~2,000,000 to ~610,000, dropping from state_of_the_art to competitive. Directly demonstrates SiO2 and NbOx regrowth as the dominant loss mechanism recovering toward un-treated baseline.

Supp Table I Row 14: DP2-BOE-AZ-Aged.profile_notes: Same chip as Row 12 re-measured after 6 weeks aging; Qi ~847,000 remains competitive but degraded from state_of_the_art initial value. Slightly better retention than DP1 aged sample but very small sample (2 resonators); oxide regrowth confirmed as degradation mechanism.

Supp Table I Row 15: LPS-BOE-AZ-noHF.profile_notes: E-beam evaporated Nb with RRR 2.29 and Tc 8.15 K — worse film quality than sputtered samples yet Qi ~943,000 is comparable, supporting the conclusion that post-etch surface chemistry (not deposition method) dominates loss. TLS_metal_vacuum included because higher roughness (1.2 nm RMS vs <300 pm for sputtered) was noted as potentially elevating metal-air interface TLS.

Supp Table I Row 16: LPS-Anneal-AZ-noHF.profile_notes: RRR of 2.36 firmly places this in the dirty_limit despite the improved crystallinity from the in situ 800°C anneal. Qi of ~8.3e5 falls in the competitive tier by resonator Qi thresholds; loss mechanisms are inferred from the CPW resonator context typical of TLS-dominated Nb films, consistent with paper framing comparing surface/interface treatments.

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Fundamental Josephson energy EJ1/h in GHz; governs the Josephson inductance and determines transmon EJ/EC regime
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: EJ1 directly sets the Josephson inductance, the qubit frequency, and the inductive contribution to higher harmonics (EJ2,L ∝ EJ1²). Tracking EJ1 per device is essential for understanding harmonic scaling and circuit Hamiltonian accuracy across devices.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table 1, column E(L)J1/h (GHz)

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Ratio of second-harmonic Josephson energy to fundamental, EJ2/EJ1, expressed as a percentage
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: This ratio quantifies the magnitude of higher-order corrections to the cosine potential that affect qudit processors, coupler architectures, and supercurrent diode physics. Without this field, harmonic characterization data cannot be systematically compared across devices and papers.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Fig. 4 and main text discussion of ODR fit

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Series inductance L of the metallic trace connecting the junction to circuit elements, in pH
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Series inductance generates inductance-induced harmonics (EJ2,L ≈ EJ1²/4EL) that alter circuit Hamiltonians in flux-biased devices. Systematic tracking of this quantity across labs and processes would allow quantitative comparison of harmonic contributions and inform trace geometry design rules.

schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: SQUID arm asymmetry determines the suppression of the fundamental harmonic at half-flux bias and therefore the sensitivity to second-harmonic effects. It also sets the residual flux dependence of qubit frequency and is a key fabrication quality metric.

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Chemical identity of the insulating tunnel barrier in the S-I-S junction stack, distinct from the superconducting electrode film
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: The tunnel barrier material determines TLS loss, barrier uniformity, aging stability, and critical current density — all directly affecting qubit frequency stability and coherence. Tracking barrier material separately from electrode material enables systematic comparison across junction types (AlOx vs TaN vs Al2O3 vs AlN)
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Abstract page 1; Introduction page 2

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Atomic ratio of nitrogen to metal (N/Ta) in the nitride film, determined by XPS depth profiling
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: N/Ta ratio determines whether TaN is insulating (N-rich, e.g. Ta5N6 at N/Ta~1.2) or conducting (N-poor). The insulating vs conducting character of the tunnel barrier is binary from a device function perspective — off-stoichiometry TaN would short the junction. Tracking N/Ta ratio enables process control monitoring across wafers and fabrication runs
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Page 19: 'The N/Ta ratio is ~1.2 at all depths within the TaN'

schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Crystal phase of TaN tunnel barrier determines whether the film is insulating (Ta5N6 hexagonal) or conducting (cubic TaN). Phase assignment is required to confirm barrier suitability and predict aging/stability behavior
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Page 16: 'The diffraction spots in the SAD pattern of TaN...show the crystalline structure of Ta5N6'; page 18: 'XRD analysis supports a hexagonal TaNx structure'

catchall.free_notes: This paper characterizes ALD TaN as a prospective tunnel barrier material for Ta-based Josephson junctions. No actual junction devices, qubits, or resonators are fabricated — the paper is a materials characterization study of the barrier film only. The companion paper (Bhatia et al., arXiv:2511.20266) apparently reports integration of this TaN barrier into actual Josephson junctions. The 13 nm and 25 nm TaN samples are both deposited on 300 mm wafers using the same ALD process and proprietary chemistry; they are distinguished only by thickness (number of ALD cycles). The paper notes that ALD TaN preferentially induces alpha-Ta phase formation in subsequently sputtered Ta electrodes, which is relevant for superconducting qubit electrodes.
