deposition_method.source: Abstract, page 1: 'deposited using atomic layer deposition (ALD)'

film_deposition_conditions.value: 300 mm cluster tool using commercially available, proprietary chemistries. In situ sputter clean of substrate before deposition. Conditioning wafers used before TaN growth to ensure chamber stability.
film_deposition_conditions.source: Section II.A, page 4: 'ALD TaN films of different thicknesses (nominally 13 nm and 25 nm) were deposited on the silicon oxide layer in a 300 mm cluster tool using commercially available, proprietary chemistries. A few conditioning wafers were used before the growth of the ALD TaN film to ensure chamber stability in terms of particle count on the wafer after deposition'

substrate_prep_before_deposition.value: In situ sputter clean before TaN deposition, reducing the 50 nm thermal SiO2 thickness by 5-15 nm
substrate_prep_before_deposition.source: Section II.A, page 4: 'An in situ sputter clean before TaN deposition reduced the oxide thickness by 5-15 nm'

junction_present.source: Paper characterizes bare TaN films as tunnel barrier candidates; no junction devices are fabricated or measured in this paper

additional_measurements.description: Within-wafer thickness nonuniformity (standard deviation as percentage of median) for 25 nm ALD TaN determined by XRR
additional_measurements.source: Page 14: 'The within-wafer thickness nonuniformity (standard deviation as a percentage of the median) is less than 1% for 25 nm ALD TaN'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Thickness uniformity of tunnel barrier directly determines qubit frequency uniformity across a wafer — tighter thickness control reduces qubit-qubit frequency collisions in multi-qubit processors

additional_measurements.description: Temperature-dependent optical band gap (Tauc gap) of 25 nm ALD TaN measured by spectroscopic ellipsometry using Tauc-Lorentz oscillator model
additional_measurements.value: 1.8 eV at 80 K; 1.5 eV at 600 K; ~1.7 eV at 300 K
additional_measurements.source: Page 11: 'The band gap of TaN (more precisely, the Tauc gap of TaN extracted from our Tauc-Lorentz oscillator model) decreases from 1.8 eV at 80 K to 1.5 eV at 600 K'; page 12: 'a band gap near 1.7 eV at room temperature'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Band gap of the tunnel barrier sets barrier height determining achievable thickness for a target critical current density; lower band gap than AlOx (~7 eV) allows thicker barriers improving process control and qubit frequency reproducibility

additional_measurements.description: No free-carrier absorption observed in mid-infrared (0.03-0.7 eV) at any temperature from 80-600 K, confirming insulating character
additional_measurements.value: No infrared absorption due to free carriers at 80-600 K
additional_measurements.source: Abstract page 1: 'ALD TaN does not exhibit infrared absorption due to free carriers, even at elevated temperatures'; page 7: 'There is no indication of free carrier absorption by the ALD TaN film'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Confirms suitability as tunnel barrier — a conducting TaN would short the Josephson junction. Thermal stability up to 600 K demonstrates compatibility with post-deposition processing steps

additional_measurements.description: Surface roughness (RMS) of 25 nm ALD TaN film across 300 mm wafer measured by AFM over 1x1 um2 areas at wafer center, mid-radius (0,75 mm), and edge (0,140 mm)
additional_measurements.value: <0.5 nm at all points on the wafer
additional_measurements.source: Page 15: 'The roughness values are <0.5 nm at all points on the wafer'; Figure 7 caption
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Low roughness of tunnel barrier reduces interface TLS density at the superconductor-barrier interface, which is a primary source of qubit dephasing and T1 loss

additional_measurements.description: N/Ta atomic ratio throughout 25 nm ALD TaN film measured by sputter depth-profile XPS at center, mid-radius, and edge of 300 mm wafer
additional_measurements.value: N/Ta ~1.2 at all depths; uniform across wafer
additional_measurements.source: Page 19: 'The N/Ta ratio is ~1.2 at all depths within the TaN'; Abstract: 'Sputter depth-profile X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) shows an N/Ta ratio of ~1.2 throughout the film'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: N/Ta ratio of ~1.2 is consistent with Ta5N6 hexagonal structure (insulating phase); confirms the film is not metallic TaN (which would short the junction). Uniformity across wafer confirms reproducible barrier composition

additional_measurements.description: Crystal structure of 25 nm ALD TaN identified by selected-area electron diffraction (SAD) in TEM
additional_measurements.value: Hexagonal Ta5N6 structure along (110) zone axis; lattice constant a = 5.25 Å from SAD; a = 5.27 Å from XRD
additional_measurements.source: Page 16: 'The diffraction spots in the SAD pattern of TaN...show the crystalline structure of Ta5N6...hexagonal structure observed along the (110) zone axis...lattice constant a to be 5.25 Å'; page 18: 'a lattice constant value of 5.27 Å for a (indexed to the hexagonal (110) reflection)'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Crystal phase determines whether TaN is insulating (Ta5N6 hexagonal) or metallic. Hexagonal Ta5N6 phase consistent with N/Ta~1.2 and insulating optical properties confirms barrier suitability for Josephson junctions

additional_measurements.description: Nearly linear ALD growth rate demonstrated across 1 to 25 nm (1 to ~600 cycles) by TEM thickness measurements
additional_measurements.value: Linear growth: ~25 nm at ~600 cycles (estimated ~0.04 nm/cycle growth rate from figure 5a)
additional_measurements.source: Page 13: 'Figure 5(a) shows a nearly linear relationship between the number of ALD cycles and the thickness of ALD TaN for thicknesses (determined from TEM) ranging from 1 to 25 nm'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Linear growth rate enables precise thickness control of tunnel barrier, which directly determines qubit frequency — a primary source of qubit-qubit frequency variation in multi-qubit systems

additional_measurements.description: No detectable carbon or oxygen in bulk of ALD TaN film (only surface carbon contamination from air exposure); confirmed by sputter XPS
additional_measurements.value: Carbon and oxygen below XPS detection limit at all depths below surface
additional_measurements.source: Page 19: 'no detectable amounts of carbon and oxygen were seen by XPS deeper in the ALD TaN film'; Figure S10 and S11
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Carbon and oxygen impurities in tunnel barriers are known TLS sources contributing to qubit dephasing; their absence confirms chemical purity of the ALD TaN barrier

additional_measurements.description: SiO2/TaN interface cleanliness assessed by high-magnification TEM imaging
additional_measurements.value: Clean interface, no signature of an interfacial layer at SiO2/TaN
additional_measurements.source: Page 13: 'The SiO2/TaN interface in Fig. 7(b) is clean, with no signature of an interfacial layer'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Clean interface reduces TLS density at the dielectric-barrier interface, which contributes to qubit decoherence

additional_measurements.description: ALD TaN is partially crystalline (hexagonal Ta5N6 regions) with dominant amorphous character as indicated by ellipsometry fitting requiring Tauc-Lorentz (amorphous) oscillator model
additional_measurements.value: Mostly amorphous with some crystalline Ta5N6 regions; Tauc-Lorentz model (amorphous insulators) provides good fit
additional_measurements.source: Pages 17: 'If a thin layer (such as our TaN) is mostly amorphous, but contains a few crystalline regions, then only the crystalline regions will be seen in XRD or SAD. On the other hand, the amorphous regions will dominate the ellipsometry spectra'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Amorphous tunnel barriers tend to have higher TLS density than crystalline ones; however, the Tauc-Lorentz description also implies no sharp phonon features that could couple to qubit frequencies

fabrication_details.description: Substrate: B-doped, double-side polished Si (100), 300 mm diameter wafers, nominal resistivity 10 Ohm.cm
ALD TaN deposited on thermally grown SiO2 (50 nm as-grown, thinned to ~35-45 nm by in situ RF sputter etch prior to deposition). Sputter etch performed in situ in the cluster tool.
fabrication_details.source: Section II.A, page 4; Section III, page 9

fabrication_details.description: XPS measurements performed on coupons (10x5 mm2) from wafer center, mid-radius, and edge using PHI Quantera Hybrid XPS system; Al Ka source (1486.6 eV), 200 um focal spot, 45 degree take-off angle, 26 eV pass energy, 0.05 eV step; depth profiling by 2 keV Ar+ sputtering in 30-90 s steps

TEM lamellae prepared from mid-radius coupon of 25 nm ALD TaN wafer using in situ lift-out method with FEI Helios G5 UX DualBeam FIB/SEM; final Ga+ milling at 2 keV. Analysis on ThermoFisher Titan3 G2 80-300 at 300 kV, 100 pA, STEM mode, 50 um C2 aperture, 17.9 mrad convergence angle, BF and HAADF detectors

SE measurements performed on samples from wafer center, mid-radius, and edge. Back surface roughened with alumina grit 220 by air compressor sandblasting to eliminate back-surface reflections; samples then cleaned ultrasonically with distilled water and IPA.

Room-temperature SE: J.A. Woollam V-VASE rotating-analyzer ellipsometer (0.5-6.5 eV, 50-80 deg incidence in 5 deg steps). IR SE: J.A. Woollam FTIR VASE Mark II rotating-compensator ellipsometer (0.03-0.70 eV, 8 cm-1 resolution). Temperature-dependent measurements (80-600 K) in Janis ST-400 UHV cryostat at single angle of 70 deg.

SE dispersion model for TaN: one Tauc-Lorentz oscillator (band gap 1.5-1.8 eV) + one or two Gaussians + one UV pole. SiO2 layer fixed at 35 nm thickness in final analysis. No infrared oscillators needed for TaN optical response.
fabrication_details.source: Page 9: 'The TaN layers were well described using a model that includes one Tauc-Lorentz oscillator with a band gap of about 1.5-1.8 eV, one or two Gaussians, and one UV pole outside our spectral range'

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Optical band gap (Tauc gap) of the tunnel barrier material in eV, as a function of temperature, measured by spectroscopic ellipsometry
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Band gap of tunnel barrier sets barrier height determining achievable tunnel barrier thickness for a given critical current density; temperature dependence relevant for modeling behavior at mK operating temperatures
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Page 11: 'The band gap of TaN...decreases from 1.8 eV at 80 K to 1.5 eV at 600 K'

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Atomic ratio of nitrogen to metal (N/Ta here) measured by XPS depth profiling, reported as dimensionless ratio throughout film thickness
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: N/Ta ratio determines crystal phase and insulating vs metallic character of TaN tunnel barrier; critical quality metric for junction fabrication process control
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Page 19: 'The N/Ta ratio is ~1.2 at all depths within the TaN'

catchall.free_notes: This 25 nm TaN sample is the primary characterization vehicle of the paper — it was used for TEM (lamella from mid-radius), XPS depth profiling (coupons from center, mid-radius, edge), and full temperature-dependent SE from 80 K to 600 K. The 13 nm sample was characterized by SE and XRR but not by TEM SAD or XPS depth profiling. The authors note that optical constants of ALD TaN are likely thickness- and process-dependent, and that a reduction in high-frequency dielectric constant is observed in the thinner (13 nm) film. Authors explicitly state future work will quantify dielectric loss (loss tangent) in ALD TaN, and that qubit coherence time evaluation using these Josephson junctions is a planned next step.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Section II.A states 'ALD TaN films of different thicknesses (nominally 13 nm and 25 nm) were deposited on the silicon oxide layer in a 300 mm cluster tool using commercially available, proprietary chemistries' as a single deposition campaign on 300 mm wafers. The two samples TaN_ALD_13nm and TaN_ALD_25nm are the only two film thicknesses described, each on its own 300 mm wafer, processed together in the same cluster tool with the same proprietary ALD chemistry. Section II.B describes SE measurements on 'two different thicknesses of ALD TaN' from the same wafer set. While two separate wafers are implied (one per thickness), both were part of the same fabrication campaign and process run as described in a single unified methods section with no indication of separate deposition runs.
fabrication_groups.source: Section II.A, page 4; Section II.B, page 4

TaN_ALD_13nm.profile_notes: This sample is a bare TaN film with no patterned microwave device or junction fabricated; the paper is a materials characterization study of ALD TaN as a prospective tunnel barrier. Transport regime is unknown because no electrical transport measurements are reported — the film is insulating (confirmed by ellipsometry) so conventional RRR-based classification does not apply.

TaN_ALD_25nm.profile_notes: Primary characterization vehicle of the paper; N/Ta ratio (~1.2) and SAD-confirmed hexagonal Ta5N6 phase are explicitly linked to insulating character suitable for use as a tunnel barrier, supporting crystal_phase_to_loss and deposition_conditions_to_film_purity correlations. No device or microwave measurements are performed.

catchall.free_notes: The paper reports tan_delta_effective_surface for Au encapsulation from a QTLS,0 vs SPR fit (Table I), but individual resonator QTLS,0 values and their SPR values are shown only in Fig. 3(a) without tabulation. Multiple resonators with different gap widths (and hence different SPRs) were fabricated for each encapsulation type; the tan_delta is extracted as the slope of the QTLS,0 vs SPR linear fit following Crowley et al. 2023 methodology. The Au-encapsulated resonator sample_id here represents this ensemble of resonators rather than a single device.

bare_Ta_XPS_film.profile_notes: Film-only sample characterized by XPS and AFM to establish baseline Ta2O5 fraction and surface roughness; no microwave device fabricated so coherence_tier is not_applicable. Transport regime is unknown as RRR is not explicitly calculated from the available resistance data.

Au_encapsulated_Ta_XPS_film.profile_notes: XPS-only film used to quantify oxide suppression as a function of Au encapsulation thickness; no patterned microwave device. The anomalous catalytic oxidation by sub-2.5 nm Au islands is documented but no microwave loss data are extracted from this sample.

AuPd_encapsulated_Ta_XPS_film.profile_notes: XPS-only film analogous to the Au encapsulation series but with AuPd alloy capping; full oxide suppression achieved at 1 nm vs 2.5 nm for Au. No microwave device fabricated, so coherence_tier is not_applicable.

Au_encapsulated_resonator.profile_notes: Ta mean free path ~5.6 nm is much shorter than the Ta coherence length (~90 nm), placing it in the dirty limit per Usadel equation fitting. Qi up to 1e7 qualifies as state_of_the_art for a resonator; quasiparticle loss is explicitly modeled via proximity-effect gap softening from the Au overlayer.

AuPd_encapsulated_resonator.profile_notes: Same Ta film and dirty-limit transport regime as the Au-encapsulated resonator; Qi reported at 1e7 places it state_of_the_art. Despite thinner oxide suppression threshold, AuPd yields higher fitted surface loss tangent than Au, attributed to unencapsulated sidewall oxide dominating metal-air participation.

additional_measurements.description: SNAIL Kerr nonlinearity K/2π
additional_measurements.source: Supplementary Table I: 'SNAIL self-Kerr nonlinearity K/2π 0.93 ± 0.03 MHz'; main text page 3
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Kerr nonlinearity determines the Kerr gate duration TK = π/K = 272 ns and sets the cat qubit phase-flip rate (proportional to K); directly controls KCQ gate fidelity and noise bias

additional_measurements.description: KCQ coherent state lifetime TZ (bit-flip lifetime) at α²=4
additional_measurements.source: Main text page 3: 'the KCQ has a coherent state lifetime TZ = 147 ± 4 µs'; Supplementary: 'TZ = 147.4 ± 3.8 µs'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: TZ is the bit-flip lifetime of the KCQ — the exponentially-suppressed error rate that makes it suitable as a biased-noise ancilla; directly sets the noise bias and determines the fault-tolerance threshold for syndrome measurements

additional_measurements.description: KCQ cat state lifetime TX,Y (phase-flip lifetime) at α²=4
additional_measurements.source: Main text page 3: 'a cat state lifetime TX,Y = 2.32 ± 0.04 µs'; Supplementary: 'TX,Y = 2.32 ± 0.04 µs'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: TX,Y is the phase-flip lifetime of the KCQ, which limits the coherence of syndrome measurements; phase-flip rate scales linearly with α² and limits overall ancilla performance

additional_measurements.description: SNAIL-storage cavity cross-Kerr χab/2π
additional_measurements.source: Supplementary Table I and main text page 5: 'χab/2π = 2.91 ± 0.03 kHz'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Cross-Kerr coupling between SNAIL and storage cavity is the primary source of storage dephasing via SNAIL photon shot noise; smaller χab reduces this dephasing channel

additional_measurements.description: Storage cavity frequency ωb/2π
additional_measurements.source: Supplementary Table I: 'Storage cavity frequency ωb/2π 7.025 GHz'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Operating frequency determines photon energy and thermal population; at 7 GHz, thermal population is negligible at 20 mK, justifying the assumption used in the thermal population measurement

additional_measurements.description: Readout cavity frequency ωr/2π
additional_measurements.source: Supplementary Table I: 'Readout cavity frequency ωr/2π 9.362 GHz'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Readout cavity frequency sets CQR drive frequency and readout SNR; determines dispersive coupling strength to SNAIL

additional_measurements.description: Readout cavity total linewidth κr/2π
additional_measurements.source: Supplementary Table I: 'Readout cavity total linewidth κr/2π 0.396 MHz'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Readout cavity linewidth sets measurement bandwidth and determines dispersive readout SNR; κr >> χar means standard dispersive readout of SNAIL is low-SNR, necessitating alternative characterization methods

additional_measurements.description: Conditional displacement rate gCD/2π at α²=4
additional_measurements.source: Main text page 4: 'the rate gCD/2π = 6.18 ± 0.06 MHz'; Supplementary CD calibration: 'we obtain gCD/2π = 6.2 MHz'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: CD gate rate must be faster than all decoherence rates for coherent operation; gCD/2π = 6.2 MHz >> 1/T2 rates, enabling coherent characteristic function tomography

additional_measurements.description: SNAIL thermal population nth at α=0
additional_measurements.value: nth = 2.8 ± 0.5% (main text); nth = 0.028 ± 0.005 (supplement), effective temperature 54 mK
additional_measurements.source: Main text page 5: 'We find nth = 2.8 ± 0.5%'; Supplementary SNAIL thermal population measurement: 'nth = 0.028 ± 0.005 in the SNAIL, giving an effective temperature of 54 mK'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: SNAIL thermal population is the primary driver of storage cavity dephasing via cross-Kerr interaction; directly determines the induced dephasing rate Γφ = (8.0 ± 1.6 ms)^−1

additional_measurements.description: Storage cavity pure dephasing rate Γφ at α=0
additional_measurements.source: Main text page 4: 'corresponding to a pure dephasing rate Γφ = (5.7 ± 2.8 ms)^−1'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Storage dephasing rate determines T2 of the oscillator/logical qubit; this excess dephasing from SNAIL heating limits cavity coherence and must be mitigated for bosonic QEC

additional_measurements.description: SNAIL charging energy EC/h
additional_measurements.source: Supplementary Table I: 'SNAIL charging energy EC/h 62 MHz'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Charging energy sets anharmonicity and limits leakage to non-computational states during control pulses

additional_measurements.description: SNAIL cubic nonlinearity g3/2π
additional_measurements.source: Supplementary Table I: 'SNAIL cubic nonlinearity g3/2π 6 MHz'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Third-order nonlinearity g3 enables three-wave mixing processes (squeezing, CQR, CD drives) that are fundamental to KCQ operation; sets parametric drive efficiency

additional_measurements.description: CQR readout QNDness
additional_measurements.source: Supplementary Calibrating CQR: 'We measure the QNDness to be Q = (p(+α|+α) + p(−α|−α))/2 = 91%'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: QNDness of readout determines back-action on the KCQ during syndrome measurements; 91% QNDness means 9% of measurements disturb the qubit state, which must be accounted for in fault-tolerance analysis

additional_measurements.description: System coherence stability over 5 days
additional_measurements.value: SNAIL T1a, T2a and KCQ TX, TZ fluctuating within 10%; storage T1 within 12%, storage T2 within 16%
additional_measurements.source: Supplementary System stability measurement: 'Most of the coherences are fluctuating within 10%, while the coherence of the storage cavity is fluctuating within 16%'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Long-term stability directly impacts ability to acquire datasets over multi-week periods without systematic drift; 10-16% fluctuation is relevant for reproducibility of QEC protocol characterization

additional_measurements.description: KCQ energy gap ωgap/2π at α=2
additional_measurements.source: Main text page 6 and Supplementary FSD calibration: 'We calibrate the energy gap ωgap/2π = 12.5 MHz at α = 2'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: KCQ energy gap determines the frequency selectivity of dissipation for frequency-selective dissipation (FSD); must be resolvable above other spectral features for FSD to be effective

anomalous_observations.description: Storage cavity T2 does not revive to 2T1 as α increases even after photon shot noise is suppressed — excess dephasing persists at large α
anomalous_observations.hypothesis: Author hypothesis: KCQ heating to excited states causes excess storage dephasing even at large α, because excited states have different average photon number than ground states, inducing different Stark shifts on the storage cavity. This was not previously predicted theoretically.

anomalous_observations.description: Master equation simulation required T1,a = 100 µs for SNAIL (vs. characterized 16 µs) to match data in the small α regime
anomalous_observations.hypothesis: Author hypothesis: The strongly-driven nonlinear KCQ system has a non-Markovian environment, making standard master equation simulation with simple photon loss inadequate. The heating mechanism of the KCQ is not fully understood.

correlations_observed.description: Storage cavity T2 first decreases then partially revives as KCQ cat size α increases from 0
correlations_observed.nature: Non-monotonic: T2 decreases from ~380 µs at α²=0 to minimum near α²=0.5, then partially revives but saturates below 2T1 limit due to KCQ heating; after FSD cooling, T2 is consistent with 2T1 for α²≥2

correlations_observed.description: Active cooling of KCQ via FSD eliminates excess storage dephasing to within measurement precision
correlations_observed.measurement_a: FSD cooling applied to KCQ excited states
correlations_observed.nature: Positive: FSD restores T2 to ~2T1 limit; without FSD T2 saturates well below 2T1 for large α

correlations_observed.description: FSD on first excited state (inside wells) for |α|²=7 eliminates storage dephasing; FSD on second excited state (outside wells) only partially reduces dephasing
correlations_observed.measurement_a: Target excited state manifold for FSD (inside vs. outside wells)
correlations_observed.nature: Heating to first excited state inside the wells (degenerate states) still causes storage dephasing; second excited state outside wells causes additional dephasing — both contribute

fabrication_details.description: Sapphire substrate grown using heat-exchange method (HEM). Annealing in FirstNano EasyTube 6000 furnace: preheated to 200°C with constant O2 flow, ramp to 1200°C at 400°C/hr, held 1 hr, cooled over 6 hours with 4:1 N2:O2 gas mixture. Annealing stated to improve substrate surface and bulk loss (citing Ganjam et al. 2024).
Nb thermalization disc used in sputtering chamber back for better heating uniformity during Ta deposition.
fabrication_details.source: Supplementary Device fabrication: 'The substrate was loaded into the sputtering chamber with a niobium thermalization disc in the back for better heating uniformity'

fabrication_details.description: HMDS vapor priming for resist adhesion before optical lithography: TA Series Yield Engineering System (YES) oven, purged with HMDS vapor 3 times, baked at 150°C for 25 min, re-purged 3 times.

Optical lithography: SC1805 photoresist spin-coated on Laurell WS-400 at 500 rpm 10 s then 4000 rpm 90 s; baked 115°C 1 min; edge beads removed with acetone; Heidelberg MLA150 direct laser writer, dose 92 mJ/mm²; developed with Microposit MF319 1 min; O2 plasma descum AutoGlow 200 150 W 300 mTorr 90 s.

EBL resist stack for junctions: dehydration bake 180°C 5 min; 800 nm MMA(8.5) MAA EL13 spin-coated with 5 min bake 180°C; 200 nm 950K PMMA A4 spin-coated with 5 min bake 180°C; 15 nm Al anticharging layer deposited on top.
EBL exposure: Raith EBPG 5200+ at base dose 290 µC/cm².
fabrication_details.source: Supplementary Device fabrication: 'The bridge-free junctions were then written using a Raith EBPG 5200+ at a base dose of 290 µC/cm²'

fabrication_details.description: Anticharging layer removed with MF312 developer for 2 minutes before cold IPA:H2O development.
fabrication_details.source: Supplementary Device fabrication: 'the anticharging layer was removed using MF312 developer for 2 minutes'

fabrication_details.description: Al junction capping oxide grown at 50 Torr for 5 min with 85:15 Ar:O2 mixture in oxidation chamber after junction deposition, before unloading.
fabrication_details.source: Supplementary Device fabrication: 'the surface of the devices was capped with a layer of aluminum oxide grown at 50 Torr for 5 minutes with the same gas mixture in the oxidation chamber before the substrate was unloaded'

fabrication_details.description: 3D aluminum package: machined from high-purity (5N5) aluminum; cleaned by sonication in NMP, acetone, IPA 5 min each; chemical etching with Transene Aluminum Etchant Type A at 50°C for ~2 hours in 1L etchant on PTFE cage, bath stirred 600 RPM, bath periodically changed; rinsed DI water 10 min, blown dry with N2. Auxiliary parts (chip clamps, copper brackets, screws) sonicated in NMP, acetone, IPA 3 min each.
Shielding: outermost cryoperm µ-metal magnetic shield; innermost copper shield coated with Berkeley black to absorb stray IR radiation.
fabrication_details.source: Supplementary Wiring diagram page 9: 'The outermost shield is a cryoperm µ-metal magnetic shield, and the innermost shield is made of copper and coated with Berkeley black'

fabrication_details.description: Magnetic flux delivery to SNAIL via copper coil wound with superconducting NbTi wire and on-chip superconducting flux transformer; DC current carried by continuous NbTi twisted pair from 4K to mixing chamber (~100 mA required).
fabrication_details.source: Main text page 3 and Supplementary Wiring diagram

fabrication_details.description: Sapphire chip dimensions: 50 mm × 5.6 mm, sandwiched between two 3D aluminum post cavities.
fabrication_details.source: Supplementary System design: 'Our experimental package consists of a sapphire chip (50 mm × 5.6 mm) sandwiched between two 3D aluminum post cavities'

fabrication_details.description: SNAIL circuit: two superconducting loops to lower anharmonicity; junctions made of aluminum; remaining structures made of tantalum. SNAIL operated at flux bias Φext = 0.32Φ0.
fabrication_details.source: Supplementary Fig. S4 caption and main text page 3

fabrication_details.description: BOE step note: DI water rinse prior to BOE is critical because mixture of piranha and BOE attacks tantalum — learned through trial and error.
fabrication_details.source: Supplementary Device fabrication: 'The DI water rinse prior to BOE is crucial because a mixture of piranha and BOE solutions can attack tantalum, a phenomenon we learned through trial and error'

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Lifetime TZ of coherent states |±α⟩ in the Kerr-cat qubit, corresponding to the bit-flip lifetime; measured in µs
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: TZ is the primary figure of merit for the KCQ as a biased-noise ancilla — it characterizes the exponential noise bias that makes fault-tolerant syndrome measurement possible. Tracking TZ across devices and cat sizes would enable systematic comparison of KCQ implementations and noise bias improvement strategies
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Main text and Supplementary Table I: TZ = 147 ± 4 µs at α²=4

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Lifetime TX,Y of cat states |C±α⟩ in the Kerr-cat qubit, corresponding to the phase-flip lifetime; measured in µs
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: TX,Y is linearly amplified by 2α² and is the dominant error channel of the KCQ. The ratio TZ/TX,Y = noise bias (~1000 in recent demonstrations) is the key metric for ancilla quality in bosonic QEC protocols
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Main text and Supplementary: TX,Y = 2.32 ± 0.04 µs at α²=4

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Self-Kerr nonlinearity K/2π of the SNAIL or transmon mode, in MHz
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: K sets the Kerr gate time TK = π/K, which must be short compared to T1 for high-fidelity σx(π/2) gates. K also determines the metapotential barrier height (∝ Kα²) that exponentially suppresses bit-flip errors — essential for comparing KCQ implementations
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Supplementary Table I: K/2π = 0.93 ± 0.03 MHz

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Cross-Kerr coupling χ/2π between two modes (e.g., SNAIL-storage, SNAIL-readout), in kHz
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Cross-Kerr coupling is the primary mechanism for storage cavity dephasing via photon shot noise in the SNAIL; the induced dephasing rate scales as χ²·nth/κ. Tracking χ across device designs would enable systematic optimization of ancilla-cavity coupling for minimal back-action
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Supplementary Table I: χab/2π = 2.91 ± 0.03 kHz, χar/2π = 1.51 ± 0.01 kHz

catchall.free_notes: This paper reports a single integrated device (SNAIL-KCQ coupled to 3D storage cavity) — the SNAIL_mode and storage_cavity are two distinct quantum modes of the same physical device. The storage cavity T1 and T2 are measured as the performance metric for the oscillator qubit, while the SNAIL mode T1, T2R, T2E characterize the ancilla KCQ performance. The device follows the fabrication recipe of Ganjam et al. 2024 (Nature Communications 15) for tantalum-based circuits on sapphire. A key finding is that SNAIL heating (nth ≈ 2.8%) causes storage dephasing even at large cat sizes due to the cross-Kerr interaction, and that frequency-selective dissipation (FSD) can eliminate this to within measurement precision. The 3D cavity architecture (high-purity Al post cavities, sapphire chip) follows Chapman et al. 2023 (PRX Quantum 4, 020355).

Note: the paper labels this 'Ramsey decay time' in Table I but the measurement is the ring-down of ⟨X(t)⟩,⟨Y(t)⟩ — consistent with a Ramsey-type measurement; however the storage is not a conventional two-level qubit so the sequence differs from standard Ramsey/echo distinction.

additional_measurements.source: Supplementary Table I: 'Storage cavity self-Kerr nonlinearity Kb/2π < 1 Hz Simulation'

catchall.free_notes: The storage cavity is a 3D aluminum post cavity (right cavity, fundamental mode at 7.025 GHz). The storage T1 and T2 values in Supplementary Table I are the primary figures of merit for the cavity as a bosonic code register. The values reported here (T1=204 µs, T2=381 µs) are for the bare cavity without KCQ stabilized. The stability measurement shows T1 fluctuates within 12% and T2 within 16% over a 5-day period. Package processing details for the aluminum cavity are described in the Package processing section of the Supplementary Material.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Main text page 3 states 'It consists of a sapphire chip sandwiched between two 3D superconducting microwave post cavities machined out of high-purity aluminum. On the sapphire substrate we fabricated tantalum-based superconducting circuits, which capacitively couple to the 3D cavities via waveguide tunnels.' Supplementary Design and simulation confirms: 'Our experimental package consists of a sapphire chip (50 mm × 5.6 mm) sandwiched between two 3D aluminum post cavities.' Both SNAIL_mode (on-chip Ta/Al circuit) and storage_cavity (3D Al post cavity) are part of the single experimental device described throughout the paper. The fabrication of all components is described in a single Device fabrication section, confirming they are one integrated physical device.
fabrication_groups.source: Main text page 3; Supplementary System setup, Device fabrication section

SNAIL_mode.profile_notes: T1=16 µs measured in qubit_state context places this in early_exploration tier. The SNAIL mode is the primary superconducting qubit element (Ta film on sapphire with Al/AlOx junctions), part of a multi-mode device; transport regime inferred as clean_limit consistent with high-temperature-annealed alpha-Ta on sapphire per the Ganjam et al. 2024 recipe. Loss mechanisms inferred from BOE surface oxide removal step and standard Ta-on-sapphire interface TLS concerns rather than explicit microwave loss attribution in this paper.

storage_cavity.profile_notes: Storage cavity is a machined 3D aluminum post cavity (not a deposited film), so growth_method is 'other' and transport_regime is unknown. T1=204 µs in resonator_photon context with T2=381 µs places this at state_of_the_art (Qi proxy well above 1e6). Loss mechanisms are inferred from the paper's investigation of KCQ-induced dephasing and residual cavity losses, not from explicit film characterization.

correlations_observed.description: Authors state that type A films have xi < l (clean limit) and show anomalous microwave loss; type B films have xi > l (dirty limit) and do not show anomalous loss

correlations_observed.measurement_b: Presence of thermally-activated microwave loss below Tc
correlations_observed.nature: Threshold behavior: xi < l correlates with vortex motion-induced loss; xi > l suppresses this channel

fabrication_details.description: Photolithography for resonator patterning: HMDS vapor deposited at 148 deg C in YES oven; photoresist AZ1518 applied; bake at 95 deg C for 60 s; exposure with Heidelberg DL66+ laser writer (10 mm write head, 10% focus, 25% filter, 70% intensity/dose); post-exposure bake at 110 deg C for 2 min; development in AZ300MIF for 90 s; DI water rinse 30 s; N2 dry
Chamber preconditioning before Ta deposition: Ta deposited on chamber walls and sample holder (chuck) at room temperature; chamber allowed to return to base pressure before loading substrate
Target preconditioning before deposition: target shutter kept closed for a few seconds before opening for film deposition
Measurement packaging: commercial microwave package QDevil QCage.24 with Au-plated printed circuit board (PCB); mounted to dilution refrigerator as described in Ref. [16] (Crowley et al., PRX 2023)
Post-deposition: Ta film cooled down to room temperature in chamber after deposition

schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Vortex activation temperature directly characterizes the vortex motion loss channel that dominates in clean-limit Ta films — tracking this across samples would allow systematic comparison of loss mechanisms across centers and correlation with film properties like RRR, mean free path, and coherence length

schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Mean free path compared to coherence length determines clean vs dirty superconducting limit, which predicts whether vortex motion or vortex pinning dominates microwave loss — a critical material parameter for loss mechanism attribution

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Superconducting coherence length xi in nm, extracted from upper critical field Hc2(0) via xi = sqrt(Phi0 / (2*pi*Hc2(0)))
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Coherence length relative to mean free path determines clean vs dirty limit and vortex core size; smaller coherence length (larger Hc2) correlates with dirty limit and vortex pinning, suppressing vortex-motion-induced microwave loss

schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Hc2 determines coherence length and reflects defect density; larger Hc2 in dirty-limit films correlates with vortex pinning and suppressed microwave loss — tracking this would enable systematic comparison of vortex loss channels

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Out-of-plane lattice constant of the superconducting film in Angstroms, from XRD peak position fitting
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Lattice constant deviation from bulk reference reflects strain and defect density; in this paper, 0.013 Å difference between type A and type B films correlates with clean vs dirty limit and vortex-motion-induced loss — a structural proxy for defect density accessible without transport measurements

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Viscous drag coefficient eta for vortex motion in kg/(m·s), calculated from Hc2 and normal-state resistivity via eta = Phi0^2 / (2*pi*xi^2*rho_n)
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Viscous drag coefficient directly quantifies the energy dissipation rate per vortex at microwave frequencies — higher eta means more dissipation per vortex, connecting film microstructure to measurable microwave loss magnitude

catchall.free_notes: This paper characterizes 8 Ta thin film devices (D1-D5 type A / clean limit; D6-D8 type B / dirty limit) fabricated into CPW resonators on c-axis sapphire. The primary finding is that clean-limit films (high RRR, low rho_n, xi < l) exhibit anomalous vortex-motion-induced microwave loss with activation temperatures as low as 0.3 K, while dirty-limit films (low RRR, high rho_n, xi > l) suppress this loss via vortex pinning at structural defects. The paper also demonstrates that artificially introducing micro-structured holes (3 um side, 12 um center-to-center) into a type A film suppresses vortex-motion loss without significantly increasing TLS loss (Q_TLS,0 unchanged). The paper does not report qubit T1/T2 values — all microwave measurements are on bare CPW resonators.

fabrication_groups.evidence: The paper describes a single UHV DC magnetron sputtering process (AJA Orion 8) with a shared substrate preparation protocol (piranha clean, DI water, IPA, N2 dry) applied to produce all type A and type B films. Type A films are defined as those produced with slower deposition rates, resulting in clean-limit films. Devices D1, D2, D3, D4, and D5 are all listed as Type A in Table I with individual measurements reported per device. The micro-structured device (D1_microstructured) is explicitly described in Section III as 'a type A Ta film with additional artificial defects in the form of micro-structured holes.' The paper does not provide per-device deposition run identifiers or wafer batch numbers, so it is not confirmed that D1 through D5 and D1_microstructured all came from the same physical deposition run — they share process conditions (slow rate, same chamber, same substrate prep) but may have been deposited separately. Grouping reflects shared fabrication process and type classification, not confirmed shared physical origin.
fabrication_groups.source: Table I Type A section; Appendix B; Section III

fabrication_groups.evidence: Devices D6, D7, and D8 are all listed as Type B in Table I. Type B films are produced with faster deposition rates than type A, yielding dirty-limit films with lower RRR and higher rho_n. All share the same substrate preparation and chamber described in Appendix B. No per-device deposition run identifiers or wafer batch numbers are provided; grouping reflects shared fabrication process type and classification, not confirmed shared physical deposition run.

D1.profile_notes: Coherence tier is unknown because Qi values are not reported for D1 individually in the structured record; the paper focuses on vortex-motion loss characterization via Tact and transport measurements rather than reporting absolute Qi values per device.

D2.profile_notes: RRR of 65.1 and confirmed xi < l firmly place this film in the clean limit; no individual Qi values reported so coherence_tier cannot be determined.

D3.profile_notes: Clean limit confirmed by xi=44.6 nm < l=81.5 nm; lowest Tact (0.29 K) among type A films indicates earliest vortex loss onset; no individual Qi reported.

D4.profile_notes: RRR 62.2 and xi < l confirm clean limit; no individual Qi values reported so coherence_tier is unknown.

D5.profile_notes: Clean limit confirmed; highest Tact among type A films (0.57 K) despite lower RRR, suggesting Tact does not map simply to RRR alone; no Qi reported individually.

D6.profile_notes: Dirty limit confirmed by RRR=11.5 and l=20.4 nm < xi=40.6 nm; elevated Tact (1.69 K) vs type A films reflects partial vortex pinning suppressing anomalous loss; no Qi reported individually.

D7.profile_notes: Dirty limit confirmed by RRR=10.8 and l < xi; Tact near Tc (4.16 K) indicates vortex motion loss is effectively suppressed by defect pinning; highest rho_n among all devices.

D8.profile_notes: Unique <110> crystal orientation with columnar grain structure and lowest RRR (6.78) confirms dirty limit; highest Hc2 and surface roughness (2.76 nm) introduce TLS_metal_vacuum as an additional plausible loss channel noted in the record.

D1_microstructured.profile_notes: Q_TLS,0 of 5e5 places this in the competitive tier for resonators; micro-structured holes suppress anomalous vortex-motion loss (Tact shifts to ~Tc) without degrading TLS performance, making this a process_optimization and loss_mechanism_identification result.

Ti getter step performed inside junction evaporation chamber before junction deposition to lower pressure to 3×10^-10 mbar

Dilution refrigerator: Bluefors XLD400 or LD400; base temperature 13 mK

fabrication_groups.evidence: Methods page 12 states '45 qubits over 9 separate chips' fabricated using the process described in Methods. Table 1 identifies qubits 1-29 as having 'HV' deposition vacuum for junctions, distinguishing them from qubits 30-45 which use UHV. The Methods describe one Ta film deposition process for all chips. No explicit per-wafer or per-chip batch identifiers are given, but the Methods section describes a single fabrication process producing all 45 qubits (qubit_1_T1 through qubit_45_T1). The HV vs UHV junction deposition is the only explicitly disclosed between-sample process variation. Qubits qubit_1_T1 through qubit_29_T1 all have HV junction deposition per Table 1.

The Methods describe the same Ta film process for all chips, with UHV vs HV junction deposition being the distinguishing variable. No explicit per-wafer batch identifiers link specific qubit chips; the assignment is inferred from the common UHV junction process description covering qubit_30_T1 through qubit_45_T1 and qubit_T2_1_drivelineUHV through qubit_T2_12_drivelineUHV.

qubit_1_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta (bcc) phase at high deposition temperature implies clean-limit transport. T1_max of ~1031 µs and average T1 of 610 µs both well exceed 100 µs threshold for state_of_the_art. Post-fabrication BOE treatment targets surface oxide removal, linking surface_oxide_to_T1.

qubit_2_T1.profile_notes: Same fab group and process as qubit_1; T1_avg 423 µs and T1_max 763 µs both exceed 100 µs threshold for state_of_the_art.

qubit_3_T1.profile_notes: T1_avg 580 µs and T1_max 876 µs; same process and material as qubit_1, state_of_the_art tier confirmed.

qubit_4_T1.profile_notes: T1_avg 359 µs exceeds 100 µs threshold; same fab process as other HV group qubits.

qubit_5_T1.profile_notes: T1_avg 376 µs; state_of_the_art by qubit T1 threshold. Notably low T2E may suggest additional dephasing noise but TLS and surface oxide remain primary identified loss channels.

qubit_6_T1.profile_notes: T1_avg 441 µs and T1_max 718 µs; T2E not measured for this qubit but T1 alone places it in state_of_the_art tier.

qubit_7_T1.profile_notes: T1_avg 570 µs and T1_max 876 µs; one of the best-performing qubits in this dataset, firmly state_of_the_art.

qubit_8_T1.profile_notes: T1_avg 344 µs; T2E not reported but T1 well above 100 µs threshold for state_of_the_art.

qubit_9_T1.profile_notes: T1_avg 451 µs and T1_max 701 µs; state_of_the_art tier confirmed.

qubit_10_T1.profile_notes: T1_avg 523 µs; state_of_the_art tier; same fab process as all other HV group qubits.

qubit_11_T1.profile_notes: T1_avg 288 µs; among the lower performers in this cohort but still well above 100 µs threshold for state_of_the_art.

qubit_12_T1.profile_notes: T1_avg 343 µs and T1_max 750 µs; state_of_the_art tier confirmed.

qubit_13_T1.profile_notes: T1_avg 589 µs with Q_avg ~14.6e6; among the highest Q averages in the dataset, firmly state_of_the_art.

qubit_14_T1.profile_notes: T1_avg 253 µs; lowest average in cohort but still exceeds 100 µs state_of_the_art threshold; same process as all HV group devices.

qubit_15_T1.profile_notes: T1_avg 322 µs and T1_max 604 µs; state_of_the_art tier confirmed; highest qubit frequency in the cohort at 4.413 GHz.

qubit_16_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta (bcc) is associated with clean-limit transport and low TLS loss. T1_max of 1.27 ms and average T1 of 794 µs place this firmly in state_of_the_art tier.

qubit_17_T1.profile_notes: 100 µm pitch device with T1_max over 1 ms; larger pad pitch noted to reduce surface participation ratio, improving T1.

qubit_18_T1.profile_notes: 100 µm pitch alpha-Ta transmon with T1_max exceeding 1 ms; T1 of 623 µs places this in state_of_the_art tier.

qubit_19_T1.profile_notes: 80 µm pitch device with T1 of 417 µs and T1_max of 834 µs; intermediate pitch between 70 and 100 µm designs.

qubit_20_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta transmon with T1 of 397 µs and T1_max of 607 µs; state_of_the_art by qubit T1 thresholds.

qubit_21_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta transmon with T1 of 482 µs and T1_max of 731 µs; state_of_the_art by qubit T1 thresholds.

qubit_22_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta transmon with T1 of 375 µs and T1_max of 538 µs; state_of_the_art by qubit T1 thresholds.

qubit_23_T1.profile_notes: Higher frequency (5 GHz) alpha-Ta transmon with T1 of 241 µs and T1_max of 416 µs; state_of_the_art by qubit T1 thresholds.

qubit_24_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta transmon with T1 of 534 µs and T1_max of 855 µs; state_of_the_art by qubit T1 thresholds.

qubit_25_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta transmon with T1 of 383 µs and T1_max of 703 µs; state_of_the_art by qubit T1 thresholds.

qubit_26_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta transmon with T1 of 387 µs and T1_max of 716 µs; state_of_the_art by qubit T1 thresholds.

qubit_27_T1.profile_notes: Lower-performing alpha-Ta transmon within the fab_HV group; T1 of 241 µs and T1_max of 307 µs still exceed the 100 µs state_of_the_art threshold.

qubit_28_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta transmon with T1 of 422 µs and T1_max of 622 µs; state_of_the_art by qubit T1 thresholds.

qubit_29_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta transmon with T1 of 363 µs and T1_max of 554 µs; state_of_the_art by qubit T1 thresholds.

qubit_30_T1.profile_notes: UHV junction deposition (base pressure 3e-10 Torr) with Ti getter and high-purity O2 lines distinguishes this sample from fab_HV peers; T1_max of 1.23 ms is among the highest in the dataset, suggesting junction quality contributes meaningfully to coherence.

qubit_31_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta (bcc) is the clean-limit phase; T1_max of 1013 µs far exceeds the 100 µs state_of_the_art threshold. UHV junction fabrication is the key process variable under study.

qubit_32_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta (bcc) clean-limit film; T1_max of 946 µs is well above state_of_the_art threshold. Part of the same UHV junction fabrication group as qubit_31.

qubit_33_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta (bcc) clean-limit film; T1_max of 654 µs exceeds the state_of_the_art threshold. UHV junction group.

qubit_34_T1.profile_notes: This qubit holds the record T1_max of 1681.8 µs (Q_max ~2.5×10^7) reported in the paper, firmly state_of_the_art. UHV junction fabrication is the distinguishing process variable.

qubit_35_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta (bcc) clean-limit film; T1_max of 860 µs is well above the state_of_the_art threshold. Part of the UHV junction fabrication group.

qubit_36_T1.profile_notes: T2E_avg > T1_avg is noted as evidence of UHV junction benefit; T1_max of 735 µs is state_of_the_art. Alpha-Ta clean-limit phase.

qubit_37_T1.profile_notes: T1_max of 452 µs exceeds state_of_the_art threshold despite lower average Q than other qubits in this group. Alpha-Ta (bcc) clean-limit phase.

qubit_38_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta (bcc) clean-limit film; T1_max of 728 µs is state_of_the_art. UHV junction fabrication group.

qubit_39_T1.profile_notes: T2E_avg nearly 2× T1_avg is highlighted as a UHV junction benefit; T1_max of 651 µs is state_of_the_art. Alpha-Ta clean-limit phase.

qubit_40_T1.profile_notes: T2E_avg > T1_avg with UHV junction; T1_max of 832 µs is state_of_the_art. Alpha-Ta (bcc) clean-limit phase.

qubit_41_T1.profile_notes: T2E_avg > T1_avg; T1_max of 772 µs is state_of_the_art. Alpha-Ta (bcc) clean-limit film with UHV junction.

qubit_42_T1.profile_notes: T2E_avg > T1_avg; T1_max of 752 µs is state_of_the_art. Alpha-Ta (bcc) clean-limit film with UHV junction.

qubit_43_T1.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta (bcc) clean-limit film; T1_max of 751 µs is state_of_the_art. UHV junction fabrication group.

qubit_44_T1.profile_notes: T2E_avg > T1_avg with UHV junction; T1_max of 609 µs is state_of_the_art. Alpha-Ta (bcc) clean-limit phase.

qubit_45_T1.profile_notes: T2E_avg > T1_avg with UHV junction; T1_max of 472 µs is state_of_the_art. Alpha-Ta (bcc) clean-limit phase.

qubit_T2_1_drivelineUHV.profile_notes: Alpha-Ta (bcc) with T1 up to 638 µs places this firmly in state_of_the_art tier. Clean_limit inferred from alpha-Ta phase at high deposition temperature and low residual resistivity reported for the fab group.

qubit_T2_2_drivelineUHV.profile_notes: This qubit is the primary subject of CPMG noise spectroscopy and RB; photon shot noise from residual thermal photons and dispersive coupling identified as a significant dephasing channel alongside TLS. T1_max of 729 µs is state_of_the_art.

qubit_T2_3_drivelineUHV.profile_notes: T1_max of 706 µs is state_of_the_art. Part of the same UHV junction fabrication group demonstrating reproducibility across qubits.

qubit_T2_4_drivelineUHV.profile_notes: T1_avg of 440 µs and T1_max of 570 µs; state_of_the_art by qubit T1 thresholds. Part of the multi-qubit UHV chip characterization.

qubit_T2_5_drivelineUHV.profile_notes: T1_avg of 292 µs and T1_max of 383 µs; state_of_the_art. T2E not reported for this qubit.

qubit_T2_6_drivelineUHV.profile_notes: T1_avg of 354 µs and T1_max of 386 µs; state_of_the_art by qubit thresholds.

qubit_T2_7_drivelineUHV.profile_notes: T1_max of 782 µs is the highest in the table, yet T2E is anomalously low (86.5 µs avg, 142 µs max) relative to T1, suggesting a device-specific dephasing mechanism such as flux noise or charge noise.

qubit_T2_8_drivelineUHV.profile_notes: Lower-performing UHV qubit with T1_avg 290 µs; still state_of_the_art. T2E also comparatively low, consistent with device-level variation in dephasing.

qubit_T2_9_drivelineUHV.profile_notes: T1_avg of 333 µs and T1_max of 432 µs; state_of_the_art.

qubit_T2_10_drivelineUHV.profile_notes: T2E_avg (371 µs) exceeds T1_avg (341 µs), which is physically notable; T1_max of 442 µs is state_of_the_art.

qubit_T2_11_drivelineUHV.profile_notes: T1_avg of 411 µs and T1_max of 506 µs; state_of_the_art.

qubit_T2_12_drivelineUHV.profile_notes: T1_avg of 82 µs is dramatically below all other UHV qubits; likely a near-shorted junction fabrication defect rather than a materials limitation, placing it in competitive tier. Unknown is included as a loss mechanism because the anomalous loss source is not formally attributed.

resonator_0.3nm_SiOx.profile_notes: Resonator used to extract surface TLS loss tangent via participation ratio analysis; Q_TLS,0 ranging from ~10^6 to ~10^7 is state_of_the_art. Dominant loss attributed to amorphous TaOx, not SiOx.

resonator_1.5nm_SiOx.profile_notes: Same physical device as resonator_0.3nm_SiOx remeasured after 65 days ambient exposure; statistically identical surface loss tangent confirms SiOx growth does not drive loss, reinforcing TaOx as dominant TLS source.

Ta_film_characterization.profile_notes: Film-only structural characterization via XRD and STEM/EDS; no microwave device measured. Clean_limit inferred from alpha-Ta phase purity, low residual resistivity, and absence of interfacial oxide. Coherence tier is not_applicable.

additional_measurements.description: Magnetic susceptibility vs temperature showing superconducting transition for polycrystalline Mo3Al2C
additional_measurements.value: Tc = 8.5 K (from susceptibility); lower critical field Hc1 estimated at H = 120 Oe at T = 2 K
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Tc sets the operating temperature margin; Hc1 constrains the field range before vortex entry, relevant to vortex-mediated loss in devices operating near these conditions

additional_measurements.description: Four-probe resistance vs temperature measurement on polycrystalline Mo3Al2C from T = 2-300 K
additional_measurements.value: Normal state resistance approximately 0.038 Ohm just above Tc; superconducting transition sharp at 8.99 K

fabrication_details.description: Polycrystalline Mo3Al2C grown by high-temperature flux reaction with excess Al. Mo (99.95%), C (99.95%), Al (99.99%) mixed in 3:4:1 (Mo:Al:C) ratio in sealed alumina tube under 1 bar Ar. Heated at 100 C/hr to 1650 C, held 24 hr, cooled to 1250 C at 5 C/hr, then 100 C/hr to room temperature.

schema_promotion_candidates.description: The chirality (P4132 = right-handed, P4332 = left-handed) of the Mo3Al2C single crystal as determined by single crystal XRD Flack parameter
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: The superconducting diode effect in this system depends critically on having opposite-chirality crystals at the junction interface; tracking crystal handedness is essential for reproducing or extending this result across other chiral superconductors
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Results section and SI Table 5

film_material.source: Results section: 'electrical transport properties of a single crystal of Mo3Al2C (device 1)'

substrate_material.source: Methods section 'Device Fabrication': 'A single crystal of Mo3Al2C was placed on a mica substrate'

junction_present.source: Results section: device 1 is a single crystal device used as comparison, not a pressed junction

Tc_K.source: Results section page 3: 'A drop in the resistance is observed at the known transition temperature of Tc = 9 K'

additional_measurements.description: Critical current of single crystal Mo3Al2C at T = 1.8 K, H = 0 Oe
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Establishes bulk critical current baseline for comparison with junction devices; confirms symmetric Ic+ = |Ic-| in single-chirality single crystal, i.e. absence of intrinsic diode effect

additional_measurements.description: Secondary resistance transition at Tc2 = 3 K attributed to Mo2C inclusions
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Mo2C inclusions alter the effective superconducting volume and may affect transport measurements at very low temperatures; relevant for interpreting device behavior below 3 K

additional_measurements.description: Resistance versus temperature for single crystal device showing two-probe contact resistance
additional_measurements.value: Resistance ~4.4 Ohm above Tc (normal state, read from Figure 2a); finite resistance in superconducting state due to contact resistance
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Contact resistance from two-probe geometry prevents direct observation of true Josephson critical current; authors note this complicates quantitative IcRn analysis

fabrication_details.description: Device fabricated by placing single crystal on mica substrate; immersion oil from scXRD washed off with dichloromethane. DuPont 4922N-100 silver paint used in 'v' shape for contacts; Axis Pro Micromanipulator used to position crystal. Some devices used gold contacts deposited on mica by magnetron sputtering with standard liftoff. Top contact is blank 'v' of silver paint pressed onto crystal.

Transport measured in Quantum Design PPMS with horizontal rotator probe and AC transport option. AC resistance measured from 300 K to 1.8 K with 0.01 mA excitation at 17 Hz. IV curves at base temperature.

film_material.source: Results section and Table 1: device 2 is P4132/P4332 junction

junction_fabrication_method.source: Results section page 4 and Methods 'Device Fabrication'

Tc_K.source: Results page 4: 'All devices show an initial decrease in resistance around Tc = 9 K, followed by a more significant drop at 6 K' — lower transition in device due to insulating barrier

additional_measurements.description: Maximum diode asymmetry alpha = (Ic+ - |Ic-|)/(Ic+ + |Ic-|) x 100%

catchall.free_notes: This paper reports a single NbN kinetic inductance metastructure device (multimode ring resonator). The device is a parametric frequency converter, not a qubit or a simple readout resonator. The Qi reported (3.93×10^5 at 10^5 photons, ~10^4 at single-photon level) describes the internal quality factor of the ring resonator modes, which sets the upper bound on conversion efficiency. No qubit T1/T2 measurements are reported. The paper is highly relevant as a materials/device characterization paper for NbN thin films via ALD used in quantum information processing components. The TLS loss at single-photon level (Qi ~10^4) is a significant finding for NbN ALD films and is consistent with TLS loss from surface oxides. The TLS saturation technique demonstrated here (recovering Qi and conversion efficiency to near-unity with a detuned drive) is a practical mitigation strategy relevant across superconducting circuit platforms.

NbN_metastructure_resonator.profile_notes: Coherence tier is 'competitive' based on the resonator Qi of ~3.93e5 at high power (within 1e5–1e6 range); at single-photon level Qi drops to ~1e4 (early_exploration), but best reported value determines tier. The device is a multimode kinetic inductance ring resonator used as a parametric frequency converter, classified as 'resonator' as the closest vocabulary match; TLS loss from NbN surface oxide is explicitly identified as the dominant loss mechanism at single-photon level.

Q2.profile_notes: Same wafer and film stack as Q1; T1=26 µs places this in the competitive tier. No explicit loss attribution is made in the record.

Q4.profile_notes: Q4 is the control qubit with no LPF; its anomalously low coherence (T1=12 µs) is attributed by the authors to resonant photon leakage through the unfiltered drive port, which maps most closely to radiation loss. Still competitive tier as T1 > 10 µs threshold.

catchall.free_notes: This paper reports material properties (Nb film, 100 nm, ebeam evaporation, UHV) only in the context of an electro-optic transducer device. No qubit coherence metrics (T1, T2), resonator Qi, or standard superconducting material properties (Tc, RRR, sheet resistance) are reported. The Nb resonator is chosen specifically for its negligible kinetic inductance to minimize resonance frequency drift under optical excitation (compared to NbN). The noise performance is currently limited by the small 2.5 µm electrode-to-AlN-ring gap causing piezoelectric-induced heating, not by Nb film quality per se.

catchall.free_notes: Albert and Felix are fabricated by the same process but have different ring radii (60.0 µm vs 61.7 µm) giving different optical FSRs to enable Vernier frequency matching. Albert operates at 4.606 GHz microwave frequency vs Felix at 9.960 GHz. Albert's Nb resonator shows significantly lower intrinsic loss rate (2.4 MHz vs 23.3 MHz for Felix) despite being fabricated identically — this difference warrants investigation and may relate to the different microwave frequency, different gap geometry effects, or statistical variation.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Methods section (Device fabrication) describes a single fabrication process flow for the AlN electro-optic transducers, and Extended Data Fig. 2 shows one process flow diagram labeled 'Fabrication process flow of an AlN transducer.' Both Felix_transducer and Albert_transducer are described as having the same layer stack (1 µm AlN on sapphire, SiO2 cladding, 100 nm Nb by ebeam evaporation in UHV ~10^-9 torr, NMP liftoff, UV laser dicing). The paper does not state explicitly that Felix_transducer and Albert_transducer came from a single physical wafer or deposition run; however, the entire fabrication section describes one unified process without per-device variation, strongly implying shared physical origin. The two devices differ only in ring radius (61.7 µm vs 60.0 µm), which is a lithographic design difference within the same process flow.
fabrication_groups.source: Methods, Device fabrication section (page 10) and Extended Data Fig. 2 (page 12)

Felix_transducer.profile_notes: No RRR, Tc, or mean free path data are reported, so transport regime is unknown. Coherence tier is early_exploration based on the intrinsic loss rate implying Qi ~ ω/κ_in ≈ 9.96GHz/23.3MHz ≈ 427, well below 1e5; the Nb film is used as a low-kinetic-inductance microwave resonator in an electro-optic transducer context, not a standalone superconducting qubit device.

Albert_transducer.profile_notes: Albert's intrinsic loss rate of 2π·2.4 MHz at 4.606 GHz implies Qi ~ 4.606GHz/2.4MHz ≈ 1920, still below 1e5, so early_exploration by strict Qi threshold; however the Nb quality itself is not the focus and no standard Qi sweep is reported — coherence_tier assigned early_exploration for the same reason as Felix. The anomalous noise is attributed to piezoelectric heating from the small electrode-AlN gap geometry, not Nb film quality, so no standard superconducting loss mechanism from the vocabulary is clearly evidenced.

Table II Row 1: Wet etch.profile_notes: RRR=32 for Al indicates clean_limit. Coherence tier is competitive based on tan_delta ~2.53e-3 and Qi in the 1e5-1e6 range implied by the surface loss budget analysis; the paper explicitly decomposes loss into AlOx, hydrocarbon, and MS+SA contributions.

Table II Row 2: H2O2.profile_notes: H2O2 treatment removes adventitious carbon but does not reduce surface loss tangent significantly; authors conclude fabrication-residue hydrocarbons dominate over adventitious carbon in TLS loss.

Table II Row 3: Cryo.profile_notes: RRR=10.41 places this sample between clean and dirty limits (intermediate); cryogenic deposition produces smallest grains and highest roughness, and authors confirm MS interface crystallinity has negligible contribution to surface loss.

Table II Row 4: Dry etch.profile_notes: Chlorine RIE yields ~70% higher surface loss tangent than wet etch despite identical film and oxide thickness; authors attribute excess loss to halogen etch residues not removed by standard solvent strip, implicating an additional TLS source beyond oxide and hydrocarbons.

Table II Row 5: H2O2, 49% HF 5s.profile_notes: HF treatment reduces AlOx from ~2.7 nm to ~1.9 nm and surface loss tangent by ~27% vs untreated; oxide regrows to 1.7-2.1 nm during 2-4 hour ambient exposure before cooldown, demonstrating the kinetic limitation of Al oxide passivation.

Table II Row 6: 49% HF, 3 months.profile_notes: This aged HF-treated chip enables isolation of the intrinsic AlOx loss tangent (1.74±0.7)e-2 by comparing oxide thickness change to loss tangent change vs the fresh HF chip; demonstrates that adventitious hydrocarbon contribution to TLS loss is small.

Table II Row 7: 49% HF 15s.profile_notes: Lowest surface loss tangent (1.68e-3) among sapphire substrates; grouped with 49% HF 5s chip for combined fit yielding tan_delta = (1.77±0.08)e-3 for HF-treated Al devices.

fabrication_details.description: Hall bar geometry used for DC resistivity measurement. Four-probe configuration measured in longitudinal direction. Temperature range: 0.35-295 K with steps of 10 K (5-295 K) and 0.1 K (0.35-2.05 K). Measurement instrument: Quantum Design PPMS DynaCool with Helium-3 insert. Zero applied magnetic field. Average over 25 voltage readings with current-reversal.

STEM imaging: FEI Titan Themis3 300, cross-sectional lamellae prepared by FEI Helios NanoLab G3 UC DualBeam FIB, polished with 2 keV Ga ion beam. 300 kV accelerating voltage, HAADF mode, [110] zone axis.

schema_promotion_candidates.description: London/Pearl magnetic penetration depth λ of the superconducting film in micrometers, extracted from kinetic inductance vs thickness fitting using Lk/□(t) = µ0λ coth(t/λ)
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: λ directly determines sheet kinetic inductance Lk/□(t), which affects resonator frequency design, kinetic inductance fraction α, and is related to superfluid density. For β-Ta with λ~1.78 µm vs α-Ta with λ~0.1 µm, this single parameter determines the entire kinetic inductance behavior and is essential for device design comparison across materials.

fabrication_details.description: Bilayer EBL resist stack for junction: Kayaku MMA(8.5)MAA EL 13 spun at 5000 rpm, 500 rpm/s ramp, 70 s, baked 175°C 2 min; then Allresist AR-P 672.045 950K PMMA spun at 4000 rpm, 500 rpm/s ramp, 68 s, baked 175°C 5 min.
Anti-charging layer: DisChem DisCharge H2O X4, spun at 4000 rpm, 1000 rpm/s ramp, 60 s. Removed after EBL exposure by DI water immersion 60 s at room temperature.
EBL exposure: Elionix ELS-F125 at 125 kV, 1 nA beam current, 500 µm field size, 2.5 nm scan/feed pitch, 2200 µC/cm2 area dose. Lower dose in specific regions for resist undercut.
HMDS vapor priming at 148°C in YES Vacuum Oven before photolithography. AZ 1518 photoresist spun at 4000 rpm, 1000 rpm/s ramp, 40 s, baked 95°C 1 min → 1.9 µm thick.

Direct-write laser photolithography: Heidelberg DWL66+, 10 mm write head, 405 nm laser, 25% attenuation, 70% intensity, optical autofocus with -10% focus offset. Post-exposure bake 110°C 2 min. Developer: AZ 300 MIF, 90 s, DI water rinse 30 s.

Measurement packaging: chips wire-bonded (Questar Q7800) to PCB in Quantum Machines QCage.24 chip carrier (parts Q401, Q402-5, Q403 Al, Q404 Al). On-chip wire bonds added to avoid slotline modes. Assembly wrapped in aluminized Mylar (biaxially oriented PET) for IR reflection. Magnetic shield: Quantum Machines QCage Q428. Refrigerator outer magnetic shield on mixing chamber stage. Dilution refrigerators: Bluefors XLD400 or LD400, base temperature 10-15 mK.
TWPA (MIT Lincoln Laboratory) used for some qubit measurements, installed at mixing chamber stage in dedicated magnetic shield, wired after second isolator on output line.

anomalous_observations.hypothesis: Author hypothesis: non-saturable dielectric loss originating from the MS interface between β-Ta and Si, whose structure differs from the α-Ta-silicon interface. Mechanism not yet identified — requires further investigation.

excluded_candidates.reason: Hall bar was fabricated from Film F6 (263 nm), which is a resonator film (F1-F14). The paper explicitly states Films F15 and F16 are for qubits and F1-F14 for resonators — different physical films from different deposition runs.
Resonators are fabricated from Films F1-F14, explicitly separate physical depositions from qubit Films F15 and F16.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Section S4, Supporting Information states: 'A total of 11 qubits are measured across 2 chips fabricated from films F15 and F16 (Table S1).' The paper does not disclose which of qubit_1 through qubit_11 came from Film F15 versus Film F16 — only that all 11 qubits come from these two films collectively. Films F15 (260 nm) and F16 (262 nm) are listed in Table S1 as distinct films with separate fabrication events (different rows in Table S1), processed identically but in separate depositions. Because the paper does not assign individual qubits to specific films, all 11 are grouped together with individual_assignment_disclosed=false.
fabrication_groups.source: Section S4, Supporting Information, first paragraph; Table S1

Hall_bar_film_F6_263nm.profile_notes: RRR=1.02 and resistivity=180 µΩ·cm firmly place this β-Ta film in the dirty limit, confirmed by the large extracted penetration depth λ=1.78 µm. No microwave device was fabricated from this Hall bar sample; TLS-relevant structural data (oxide thickness, amorphous MS layer) are characterized but not directly measured as loss.

qubit_1.profile_notes: T1=397 µs (time-averaged) from qubit_state measurement places this firmly in state_of_the_art tier (>100 µs). β-Ta dirty-limit assignment follows from RRR=1.02; charge noise identified as additional dephasing mechanism due to OCS regime (EJ/EC=16).

qubit_2.profile_notes: Best qubit in the study with time-averaged T1=585 µs and peak T1=958 µs, clearly state_of_the_art. OCS regime (EJ/EC=19) contributes charge noise dephasing; surface oxide (2.9 nm TaOx) identified as primary TLS source at MA interface.

qubit_3.profile_notes: T1=400 µs (qubit_state) is state_of_the_art; OCS regime (EJ/EC=20) consistent with charge noise contribution to dephasing. Dirty-limit inferred from shared film properties with qubit_1/2 (RRR=1.02, ρn=180 µΩ·cm).

qubit_4.profile_notes: T1=423 µs (qubit_state) is state_of_the_art; OCS regime (EJ/EC=22) with T2,E << T1 indicates charge noise dominates dephasing. Dirty-limit inferred from shared film properties.

qubit_5.profile_notes: T1=329 µs (qubit_state) is state_of_the_art; EJ/EC=28 places qubit at boundary of OCS regime. Dirty-limit inferred from shared film properties.

qubit_6.profile_notes: T1=236 µs (qubit_state) is state_of_the_art; EJ/EC=74 places qubit in deep transmon regime with T2,E > T1 (lifetime-limited), so charge noise is not a primary loss mechanism here. Very long Tφ=1300 µs confirms weak charge noise.

qubit_7.profile_notes: T1=148 µs (qubit_state) is state_of_the_art; EJ/EC=77 in deep transmon regime with very long Tφ=1800 µs confirms lifetime-limited coherence and negligible charge noise.

qubit_8.profile_notes: T1=97 µs (qubit_state) falls in the competitive tier (10–100 µs); EJ/EC=82 in deep transmon regime with T2,E > T1 indicating lifetime-limited coherence.

qubit_9.profile_notes: T1=111 µs (qubit_state) is state_of_the_art; EJ/EC=99 in deep transmon regime. Dirty-limit inferred from shared film properties.

qubit_10.profile_notes: T1=137 µs (qubit_state) is state_of_the_art; EJ/EC=98 in deep transmon regime. Very low T2,R=11 µs suggests a low-frequency noise source but this is not explicitly attributed in the record.

qubit_11.profile_notes: T1=40 µs (qubit_state) falls in competitive tier; this is the highest-frequency qubit (5.804 GHz) with anomalously low Q, and authors hypothesize frequency-dependent radiative coupling to spurious package modes as an additional loss channel.

resonators_F1_to_F14_on_sapphire.profile_notes: Best Qi=1.6×10^6 (CPW) and 4.8×10^6 (LE) at single-photon power; the LE resonator value is state_of_the_art. Authors explicitly show QTLS,0 ∝ 1/pMS (surface TLS dominance) and that tan δ is thickness-independent across 14 films, directly evidencing both surface_oxide_to_Qi and film_thickness_to_loss correlations.

resonators_F17_on_Si.profile_notes: Best Qi=2.8×10^6 is state_of_the_art for a resonator; however performance is limited by a geometry-independent Qother (non-saturable loss) attributed by authors to the β-Ta/Si MS interface, motivating dielectric_substrate as a distinct loss mechanism compared to the sapphire samples.

schema_promotion_candidates.description: The difference in superconducting gap energy between the two junction electrodes, delta-Delta, in GHz (frequency units). Extracted by fitting Arrhenius temperature dependence of parity-switching rates.
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Gap difference is the primary design parameter for gap-engineered qubits; it sets the exponential suppression factor for QP tunneling: exp(-(delta-Delta - h*fq)/kBT). Without this field, the qubit's radiation hardness cannot be characterized or compared across devices. Tracking delta-Delta vs film thickness enables systematic optimization of gap engineering across the corpus.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table S1 and main text throughout

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Dimensionless non-equilibrium quasiparticle density in units of Cooper pair density, x_ne_QP = N_QP / (2*nu0*Delta*V_L). Extracted from temperature-dependent parity-switching rate fits.
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Resident QP density directly determines steady-state parity-switching rate and QP-induced T1 degradation. Comparing x_ne_QP across devices/cooldowns reveals how materials and packaging choices affect non-equilibrium QP levels. Currently no schema field captures this fundamental qubit coherence parameter.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table S1 and Supplementary Section II.B.2, Eq. S13

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Rate of parity-switching events caused by absorption of stray IR photons at the junction, Gamma_ph (in s^-1), separate from QP tunneling contribution. State-dependent: Gamma_ph_0 (ground state) and Gamma_ph_1 (excited state).
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Sets fundamental floor on parity-switching noise independent of QP density; controlled by shielding/filtering quality. Tracking this across devices and filter configurations enables systematic evaluation of IR shielding strategies.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table S1 and Supplementary Section II.C, Eq. S18

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Thickness of the thinner (high-gap) aluminum film forming one electrode of the Josephson junction, in nm. Measured by AFM.
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Thin-film Al gap follows Δ/h = a/d + Δ0/h; controlling thin-film thickness is the primary knob for gap engineering. Without this field, the gap-thickness relationship cannot be tracked systematically across devices and labs.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table S1 film thickness column; Supplementary Section II.D

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Thickness of the thicker (low-gap) aluminum film forming the other electrode of the Josephson junction, in nm. Measured by AFM.
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Complements thin-film thickness; together the two thicknesses determine delta-Delta. Needed for reproducibility of gap-engineering across labs.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table S1 film thickness column

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Rate of detected QP burst events per minute, measured by monitoring excess qubit relaxation events above a threshold in continuous readout.
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Directly quantifies radiation hardness of the device design; gap engineering reduced this rate by 5x in this work. Essential metric for comparing mitigation strategies across papers.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Main text page 3: 'burst detection rate in the big-delta-Delta device (0.57 min^-1) ... small-delta-Delta device (2.76 min^-1)'

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Exponential time constant for recovery of qubit relaxation rate after a QP burst, in ms.
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Sets the duration of correlated errors after a radiation impact; determines how long quantum error correction is compromised. Insensitive to gap engineering in this work (~0.7 ms), suggesting substrate thermalization dominates.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Main text page 4: 'associated time constants ~0.7 ms are insensitive to the gap engineering'; Fig. 2(e)
