B1_cooldown_2022.10.profile_notes: Primary science focus is quasiparticle poisoning and gap engineering via asymmetric Al film thicknesses; T1=197µs qualifies as state_of_the_art. Transport regime is not characterized in this work.

B2_cooldown_2022.12.profile_notes: Same gap-engineering study as B1; T1=150µs is state_of_the_art. QP density and photon-assisted parity-switching rate are the primary tracked quantities.

B2_cooldown_2023.01.profile_notes: Repeat cooldown of device B2; T1=124µs remains state_of_the_art. Variation in x_ne_QP across cooldowns is a key observation.

B3_cooldown_2023.02.profile_notes: Film thickness is an average from wafer companions rather than direct AFM on this device; T1=127µs is state_of_the_art. Large delta-Delta/h=10.8 GHz places this in the big-delta-Delta category.

B4_cooldown_2024.04.profile_notes: Key device for burst measurement and radiation hardness; HERD1 filtering dramatically reduces x_ne_QP vs earlier cooldowns. QP burst rate and phonon thermalization time constants are explicitly correlated with gap engineering outcomes.

M1_cooldown_Ref1.profile_notes: Medium-delta-Delta device from Connolly et al. 2024 PRL included for cross-platform comparison; T1=193µs is state_of_the_art. Film thicknesses are nominal rather than AFM-measured.

M2_cooldown_2022.11.profile_notes: Medium-delta-Delta device with thick thin-film (51 nm) giving delta-Delta/h=3.1 GHz < fq; highest T1 in dataset at 237µs. Elevated Gamma_ph_0 despite CR-112 filter is noted.

M2_cooldown_2022.12.profile_notes: Repeat cooldown of M2; T1=222µs state_of_the_art. Elevated Gamma_ph_0=9.09 s^-1 and higher x_ne_QP compared to M2_2022.11 despite same filter type.

M3_cooldown_2023.03.profile_notes: Medium-delta-Delta device measured across five cooldowns to study filter and environment effects; T1=142µs is state_of_the_art.

M3_cooldown_2023.04.profile_notes: Same device M3 with XMA IR filter; T1=94µs falls just below 100µs threshold, classified competitive. Elevated Gamma_ph_0=7.72 s^-1 correlates with XMA filter use.

M3_cooldown_2023.06.profile_notes: Return to CR-112 filtering restores lower Gamma_ph_0 and x_ne_QP; T1=118µs is state_of_the_art, confirming filter type impact on QP environment.

M3_cooldown_2024.03.profile_notes: HERD1 filter gives lowest x_ne_QP for M3 (1.5e-10) but T1=89µs is competitive; used for burst measurement comparison with B4.

M3_cooldown_2024.04.profile_notes: Medium-delta-Delta device used in main burst comparison; T1=82µs is competitive. QP burst rate (2.08 min^-1) comparable to small-delta-Delta device because delta-Delta - h*fq ~ 50 mK is less than burst-induced temperature ~90 mK.

S1_cooldown_2023.02.profile_notes: Small-delta-Delta control device with near-zero gap difference; highest x_ne_QP (16.9e-10) consistent with absence of QP tunneling suppression. T1=118µs is state_of_the_art despite high QP density.

S1_cooldown_2023.04.profile_notes: Repeat cooldown of S1 with XMA filter; Gamma_ph_0=11.6 s^-1 is among highest in dataset, consistent with poor IR filtering. T1=107µs remains state_of_the_art.

S1_cooldown_2023.05.profile_notes: Primary loss channel is quasiparticle poisoning, evidenced by measured x_ne_QP and photon-assisted parity-switching rate. T1=134 µs qualifies as state_of_the_art under qubit_state thresholds.

S2_cooldown_2024.03.profile_notes: Same fab group and geometry as S2_cooldown_2024.04; T1=92 µs falls in the competitive tier. QP density and parity-switching metrics indicate quasiparticle loss as the primary mechanism.

S2_cooldown_2024.04.profile_notes: This cooldown includes QP burst detection rate and burst decay time, explicitly comparing small-delta-Delta vs big-delta-Delta gap engineering for quasiparticle mitigation. T1=88 µs is competitive tier.

additional_measurements.description: TEM and EDS characterization of MA and MS interfaces confirming absence of native oxide on rhenium film
additional_measurements.value: No native oxide detected at MA interface by TEM (contrast to 3 nm native oxide on Ta); EDS shows no elevated oxygen at MA interface
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Absence of native oxide eliminates one source of TLS loss at the metal-air interface. If MA interface oxide were the dominant loss source, rhenium's oxide-free surface would substantially reduce surface loss factor Γ_surf — the paper finds it does not, suggesting MA loss is not the dominant surface contribution in planar architectures.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Section III paragraph 5 explicitly states: 'Our tripole stripline resonators consist of a rhenium film on a sapphire substrate, and are fabricated on the same wafer in the same process as our transmons.' Section III paragraph 6 states the segmented stripline resonator is 'fabricated on the same wafer as our transmons and measured in the same package.' Appendix A describes a single fabrication process for 4-inch wafers from which all devices (Transmon_1 through Transmon_5, Tripole_1 through Tripole_4, Segmented_1, Segmented_2) are diced. The film characterization sample (Re_film_characterization) is described in Appendix B as 'a 4 mm × 3 mm rhenium on sapphire sample' measured for R vs T; the paper does not explicitly state it comes from the same wafer, but the deposition parameters are identical and it is described in the same fabrication context.
fabrication_groups.source: Section III paragraphs 5-6; Appendix A; Appendix B paragraph 1

Re_film_characterization.profile_notes: RRR=19 places Re between clean and dirty limits (not >50 for clean, not <10 for dirty), so intermediate is most appropriate. No microwave device measured in this sample; TEM/EDS confirms absence of native oxide at MA interface, which is a materials characterization finding relevant to TLS loss identification but no loss mechanism is directly quantified here.

Transmon_1.profile_notes: T1=297 µs exceeds 100 µs threshold for state_of_the_art. Loss mechanisms inferred from the paper's participation matrix framework identifying surface TLS (MS/MA interfaces) and bulk sapphire dielectric as the dominant channels; absence of native oxide on Re is explicitly investigated as a potential TLS source.

Transmon_2.profile_notes: T1=277 µs places this in state_of_the_art tier. Same loss framework as Transmon_1 applies; participation matrix inversion identifies surface and bulk sapphire TLS as dominant loss channels.

Transmon_3.profile_notes: T1=201 µs exceeds 100 µs threshold for state_of_the_art. Fabrication and loss framework identical to other transmons in this batch.

Transmon_4.profile_notes: T1=205 µs exceeds 100 µs threshold for state_of_the_art. Same process and loss attribution framework as other transmons in this study.

Transmon_5.profile_notes: T1=407 µs is the best result in this dataset and clearly state_of_the_art. Qi=13e6 and T2_echo=656 µs further confirm top-tier performance; loss budget analysis implicates surface TLS and bulk sapphire as primary channels.

Tripole_1.profile_notes: Qi_single_photon=1.7e6 for D1 mode; D2 mode reaches 17.2e6, both exceeding 1e6 state_of_the_art threshold. The tripole stripline is used as a participation matrix inversion tool to separate surface TLS, bulk sapphire, and package seam loss contributions.

Tripole_2.profile_notes: Qi_single_photon=1.6e6 (D1 mode); D2 mode reaches 21.9e6. Participation matrix inversion yields surface loss factor Γ_surf=(4.3±0.3)×10^-4, directly attributing loss to surface TLS.

Tripole_3.profile_notes: Qi_single_photon=1.9e6 (D1 mode); D2 mode at 16.4e6. Participation matrix inversion yields Γ_surf=(3.3±0.2)×10^-4 for surface TLS and Γ_bulk=(4.0±0.5)×10^-8 for sapphire bulk loss.

Tripole_4.profile_notes: Qi_single_photon=2.2e6 (D1 mode); D2 mode at 20.1e6. Participation matrix inversion yields Γ_surf=(3.0±0.1)×10^-4, consistent with other tripoles in this batch.

Segmented_1.profile_notes: Segmented resonator is specifically designed to quantify Re-Al interface loss; Γ_Re-Al=(2.4±0.9)×10^-12 Ω·m is extracted via participation matrix inversion, making TLS_interface at the Re-Al junction the primary loss channel under investigation. Qi=2.0e6 is state_of_the_art.

Segmented_2.profile_notes: Identical purpose to Segmented_1; Γ_Re-Al=(3.5±0.9)×10^-12 Ω·m extracted. Qi=1.7e6 is state_of_the_art. The segmented resonator design isolates the Re-Al film interface loss relevant to transmon junction integration.

fabrication_details.description: NbSe2 crystal source: bulk crystal grown by HQ Graphene; mechanically exfoliated and encapsulated with hBN inside an Argon-filled glove box (O2 and H2O < 0.1 ppm) to prevent oxidation
hBN-NbSe2-hBN heterostructure assembled by dry polymer-based transfer technique (hot pick-up method, refs [69-71])

catchall.free_notes: This paper reports MEDIUM relevance material properties (Tc, Rs, sheet kinetic inductance) for NbSe2 films of varying thickness. The primary scientific contribution is characterization of kinetic inductance as a function of NbSe2 layer number. The Al CPW resonator host circuit is a well-established platform (250 nm MBE-Al on high-resistivity Si) while the NbSe2 samples are the materials under study. The Qi values reported (Qi,Al-NbSe2) reflect the combined loss of the Al resonator and NbSe2 termination, not a pure NbSe2 material property. The spectator Al resonator achieves Qi = 5.985×10^6 (Figure S3), representing the baseline Al resonator quality. DC transport measurements (Table S1) provide Rs and Tc for several NbSe2 thicknesses measured on contact-test devices, which are separate from the microwave devices D1-D12.

fabrication_groups.evidence: The paper describes a single fabrication procedure for all NbSe2 devices D1 through D12: mechanical exfoliation of NbSe2 from bulk crystal (HQ Graphene), encapsulation with hBN inside an Argon-filled glove box, dry polymer transfer onto pre-patterned Al CPW chips, and edge-contact formation by RIE + in-situ Ar ion milling + Al evaporation. Table 1 lists all twelve devices (D1-D12) with individually measured thicknesses (AFM), and the main text and supplementary describe one fabrication process producing all devices. No per-device process variation is mentioned; devices differ only in the naturally varying thickness of the mechanically exfoliated NbSe2 flake. Each device is a distinct NbSe2 flake, so while they share a fabrication process, each represents a separate exfoliation event. They are grouped together because the paper presents them as a unified dataset characterized by a single fabrication approach.
fabrication_groups.source: Supplementary Information Section 1; Table 1 (Device IDs D1-D12)

excluded_candidates.reason: D1 through D12 share the Al CPW chip substrate but the characterization target is the NbSe2 termination element; the Al resonator circuit is a host platform, not a distinct NbSe2 sample; grouping them with the Al spectator would conflate the host circuit with the material under study

fabrication_groups.evidence: The Al spectator resonator and all experiment resonators (hosting NbSe2 devices D1-D12) are fabricated from the same 250 nm MBE-grown Al film on high-resistivity Si wafer, patterned on a single chip. The spectator resonator is described as a 'witness to monitor the impact of the vdW materials fabrication process (without incorporating vdW materials)' on the same chip. The Al resonator circuit is a single physical fabrication event; the spectator resonator is one of the Al λ/4 resonators on that chip.
fabrication_groups.source: Main text 'Device Design': 'Two λ/4-resonators, an aluminum spectator resonator and an experiment resonator, are capacitively coupled to a common feedline'; Supplementary Information Section 1

D1.profile_notes: NbSe2 is not in the vocabulary; 'other' is used. Transport regime is dirty_limit based on Lk,sq/Lk,sq,clean = 14.95 >> 1 and high Rs/Tc ratio. Qi = 8000 reflects combined Al+NbSe2 loss, not pure NbSe2; loss mechanism cannot be attributed from the record so 'unknown' is used. NbSe2 was mechanically exfoliated, so growth_method is 'other'.

D2.profile_notes: Lk,sq/Lk,sq,clean = 3.53 and Rs/Tc = 12.5 Ω/K indicate dirty-limit behavior. Qi = 60000 is early_exploration tier for a resonator. NbSe2 exfoliated crystal, growth_method 'other'.

D3.profile_notes: Lk,sq/Lk,sq,clean = 2.39 still indicates dirty-limit dominance. Qi = 7000 is early_exploration. Loss cannot be attributed from the record.

D4.profile_notes: Lk,sq/Lk,sq,clean = 1.79 indicates dirty-limit contribution still present though approaching intermediate. Qi = 24000 is early_exploration.

D5.profile_notes: No Lk,sq/Lk,sq,clean ratio available for D5, but Rs = 19 Ω/sq and trend from surrounding samples supports dirty_limit assignment. Qi = 12000 is early_exploration.

D6.profile_notes: D6 is the primary representative device in the paper; Rs = 19 Ω/sq and context from surrounding samples supports dirty_limit. Qi = 28000 is early_exploration. Depairing current and nonlinearity onset are characterized but do not map directly to a loss mechanism attribution.

D7.profile_notes: No Tc or Rs reported for D7; transport regime inferred as dirty_limit from thickness trend and surrounding samples. Qi = 21000 is early_exploration.

D8.profile_notes: Lk,sq/Lk,sq,clean = 0.71 < 1, suggesting this sample is at or crossing into the clean limit; assigned 'intermediate' as the ratio crosses unity here. Qi = 7000 is early_exploration.

D9.profile_notes: No Lk ratio or transport data provided for D9; intermediate assigned by interpolation from D8 (ratio <1) and increasing thickness trend. Qi = 6000 is early_exploration.

D10.profile_notes: At 25 nm thickness NbSe2 approaches bulk behavior; clean_limit inferred from low Lk,sq and bulk-like Tc trends. Qi = 180000 reaches the competitive tier (1e5–1e6).

D11.profile_notes: At 30 nm, NbSe2 is near bulk; clean_limit inferred from near-zero Lk,sq. Qi = 25000 is early_exploration. The variation in Qi across thick samples is not attributed to a specific loss mechanism.

D12.profile_notes: At 52 nm NbSe2 behaves bulk-like; clean_limit assigned. Qi = 58000 is early_exploration. Loss mechanism not attributed in the record.

Al_spectator_resonator.profile_notes: 250 nm MBE Al on high-resistivity Si; Qi = 5.985e6 is state_of_the_art for a resonator. TLS_unattributed assigned as residual loss in high-Qi Al resonators on Si is generically TLS-dominated even if not explicitly discussed. This resonator serves as a baseline witness device, not the primary subject of the paper.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Section II.A states: 'A 3 nm TaN layer was deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD), immediately followed by physical vapor deposition (PVD) of Ta, in a 300 mm cluster tool capable of in vacuo transfer between the two process chambers. The use of ALD TaN as a seed layer enabled the formation of an α-phase Ta film. Four surfaces were studied: (i) native Ta oxide formed by leaving the Ta thin film in ambient air for three weeks, (ii) chemically formed oxide via CMP, (iii) plasma nitridization of the Ta surface, followed by immediate capping with Nb metal and (iv) plasma nitridization of the Ta surface followed by exposure to ambient air for three weeks, followed by capping with Nb metal.' This language describes four surface treatment variants of a single base film stack fabricated from the same 300 mm wafer deposition process, with each variant (Native_Oxide_3wk, CMP_Oxide_3wk, Nitridized_ImmediateCap, Nitridized_3wk_AirExp_Cap) explicitly enumerated and individually assigned.

catchall.free_notes: This is a tunnel barrier characterization paper — the TaN film is the insulator (I layer) of an S-I-S junction, not the superconducting electrode. No Tc, Qi, T1, or T2 values are reported. The paper explicitly positions ALD TaN as an alternative to AlOx for tantalum-based Josephson junctions, citing advantages of lower bandgap (enabling thicker barriers at same Jc), lower roughness, thermal stability, and wafer-scale uniformity. The companion paper arXiv:2511.20266 (Bhatia et al. 2025) reportedly demonstrates ALD TaN in actual Josephson junctions. Key distinction: conductive ALD TaN (used in CMOS IC as a barrier metal) is different from the insulating ALD TaN characterized here — the insulating character is confirmed by absence of free-carrier IR absorption.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Section II.A states: 'ALD TaN films of different thicknesses (nominally 13 and 25 nm) were deposited on the silicon oxide layer in a 300 mm cluster tool using commercially available, proprietary chemistries.' Both ALD_TaN_13nm and ALD_TaN_25nm are described as being fabricated together in the same deposition campaign on 300 mm wafers in the same tool run (or sequential runs in the same tool with conditioning wafers), with both characterized across the same wafer (center, mid-radius, edge). The paper treats them as a paired set throughout all characterization sections (SE, XRR, XRD, AFM), with both individual assignments to their respective thickness targets explicitly disclosed.
fabrication_groups.source: Section II.A; Sections III.B–III.F throughout, comparing 13 nm and 25 nm films as a paired set from the same deposition campaign

ALD_TaN_13nm.profile_notes: TaN here is the insulating tunnel barrier (I layer), not a superconducting electrode; no microwave device is fabricated or measured, so transport_regime, loss_mechanisms, and coherence_tier are not applicable. The film is confirmed insulating (no free-carrier absorption), so dirty_limit/clean_limit transport classifications are irrelevant.

ALD_TaN_25nm.profile_notes: As with the 13 nm sample, TaN is used as an insulating Josephson junction tunnel barrier, not as the superconducting film; no qubit or resonator device is measured, and no coherence or loss data are reported. Crystal phase, stoichiometry, roughness, and bandgap are characterized purely as materials properties relevant to future junction integration.

fabrication_details.description: Low-temperature electrical transport measured in Quantum Design Dynacool PPMS system using built-in DC resistivity option. Tc defined as midpoint of resistive transition (R/Rn = 0.5, Rn measured at 10 K). RRR = R(300K)/R(10K). Three independent samples characterized under each processing condition.
XRD: Rigaku SmartLab diffractometer with Cu Kα source (λ = 1.5418 Å); GIXRD at 0.5° fixed incidence angle

TEM lamellae prepared by Thermo Fisher Scientific Helios G5 dual-beam FIB with in situ liftout; final thinning to ~50 nm with progressively lower Ga+ beam voltages. TEM on Thermo Fisher Talos X-FEG 200X at 200 kV with Super-X EDS. HAADF-STEM and EELS on Hitachi HD2700C with probe Cs correction at 200 kV.

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Thickness of the self-limiting native oxide layer formed upon air exposure of the superconducting film, measured by TEM (nm)
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Native oxide thickness directly sets the TLS density at the metal-vacuum interface — a primary loss channel in Nb-based qubits. Tracking this across samples and processing conditions would enable systematic comparison of surface passivation strategies and their impact on Qi and T1.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Results section page 5; Supporting Information Appendix B page 25

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Relative fractions of distinct Nb oxidation states (Nb0, Nbδ+, Nb2+, Nb4+, Nb5+) from VEXPS depth-resolved fitting, as a function of surface treatment
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Oxide stoichiometry (not just thickness) determines TLS character; Premkumar et al. [12] showed that suboxide penetration depth and stoichiometry directly control microscopic relaxation pathways. Tracking species fractions would allow correlation with Qi across different surface treatments.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Tables S1, S2, S3, S4 (Supporting Information pages 29-32)

catchall.free_notes: This sample (NbOx/Nb) represents the baseline Nb film after air exposure — it is the starting material for the Pt encapsulation experiment. The paper characterizes both NbOx/Nb and Pt/NbOx/Nb using the same Nb base film, making these two samples directly comparable. The paper notes that the as-deposited Nb film before air exposure was also characterized (same Tc and RRR as NbOx/Nb), but the pre-exposure film is not a separately named sample — NbOx/Nb is the characterization baseline reported in the paper.

additional_measurements.source: Results section page 5: 'the native oxide layer that covered the Nb film prior to the Pt coating is no longer detectable in the EDX mapping'; Figure 2c,d page 18
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Complete removal of concentrated surface oxide layer eliminates primary TLS source at metal-vacuum interface; oxygen dissolved in Nb metal (as interstitials) is less TLS-active than stoichiometric NbOx phases

additional_measurements.description: Sidewall passivation confirmed by cross-sectional HRTEM and STEM-EDX (Figure S13): Pt-Nb alloy forms conformally along etched Nb sidewalls after annealing, though Pt layer is thinner on upper convex sidewall due to line-of-sight deposition geometry

additional_measurements.source: Results section page 11; Supporting Information Appendix F and Figure S13, pages 46-47
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Nb sidewalls have highest electric-field participation ratio in transmon geometries and are most susceptible to oxidation during fabrication; sidewall passivation directly targets the dominant TLS loss channel in patterned Nb devices

additional_measurements.description: GIXRD (incidence 1°) of Pt/NbOx/Nb shows weak, broadened features inconsistent with bulk Pt or Nb phases but partially consistent with NbPt2 and NbPt3 reflections, indicating thin disordered/nanocrystalline Nb-Pt alloy

additional_measurements.source: Supporting Information Appendix A, Figure S1c, page 23-24

anomalous_observations.description: Pt encapsulation with annealing at 750°C produces no degradation of Tc or RRR relative to bare NbOx/Nb (Tc = 9.30 K, RRR = 64 vs 63), despite significant interfacial alloying and oxygen redistribution
anomalous_observations.hypothesis: Author hypothesis: Interfacial alloying is confined to the near-surface Pt/Nb region (~10 nm Pt overlayer); bulk Nb crystal structure and superconducting properties are preserved because the alloying zone is too thin to affect the bulk. Confirmed by Nb K-edge EXAFS showing unchanged bulk bcc structure.

catchall.free_notes: This sample (Pt/NbOx/Nb) is the Pt-encapsulated version of NbOx/Nb, fabricated from the same base Nb deposition. The paper's primary scientific contribution is demonstrating that post-air-exposure Pt deposition + annealing can chemically transform the NbOx surface into a metallic Nb-Pt alloy (NbPt3-dominant) without degrading superconducting transport properties. No microwave measurements (Qi, resonator Q, TLS loss) are reported in this paper — the relevance to qubit performance is asserted through the material mechanism (oxide elimination) rather than direct device measurement. The paper cites [23] (Chattaraj et al., Vacuum, 2025) for a prior related in situ Pt encapsulation result on room-temperature-deposited Nb films.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Methods section A (pages 12-13) describes a single fabrication sequence: Nb film deposited on c-cut sapphire at 700°C → cooled to room temperature → exposed to air for 1 hour (producing NbOx_Nb) → reloaded into deposition chamber → Pt deposited at room temperature → in situ vacuum anneal at 750°C for 2 hours (producing Pt_NbOx_Nb). The two samples NbOx_Nb and Pt_NbOx_Nb share the same physical Nb deposition event; Pt_NbOx_Nb is explicitly the product of further processing of NbOx_Nb.
fabrication_groups.source: Methods section A, pages 12-13; Results section page 5: 'The NbOx/Nb film was subsequently returned to the deposition chamber for deposition of an approximately 10 nm thick Pt overlayer'

NbOx_Nb.profile_notes: RRR=63 clearly places this in the clean limit for Nb. No microwave device is fabricated or measured; the sample is a baseline film characterized by XRD, TEM, and VEXPS — hence film_only and not_applicable for coherence_tier. Loss mechanisms are inferred from the paper's scientific framing around NbOx TLS sources, not from direct Qi measurement.

Pt_NbOx_Nb.profile_notes: No microwave measurements are reported for this sample; coherence_tier is not_applicable. The Pt overlayer drives Nb-Pt alloying and oxide elimination, so loss mechanisms reflect the TLS sources the paper targets rather than measured losses. RRR=64 confirms the bulk Nb remains in the clean limit despite surface alloying.

catchall.free_notes: This paper reports a single NbN KIPA device fabricated from a single 4-inch wafer. The paper does not report Qi directly for the resonator, nor does it report T1 or T2 for any qubit — it is a parametric amplifier demonstration paper. The NbN film characterization (Tc ~12.5 K, thickness 25 nm, sheet kinetic inductance ~10 pH/sq) is reported for the same film used to fabricate the KIPA devices. The paper explicitly compares NbN Tc (~12.5 K) to Al (~1 K) and Ta, noting that the larger superconducting gap enables operation at K-band (23 GHz) without pair-breaking, and also enables elevated-temperature operation. The device is intended as a first-stage amplifier for K-band superconducting qubit readout, not itself a qubit. No junction is present.

NbN_KIPA_film.profile_notes: The device is a kinetic inductance parametric amplifier (KIPA), not a qubit or standard resonator, so coherence_tier is not_applicable; no Qi or T1 is reported. NbN thin films deposited by ALD are canonically in the dirty limit, consistent with the high sheet kinetic inductance (~10 pH/sq) and disordered film character implied by the 25 nm thickness and ALD growth method.

schema_promotion_candidates.description: The per-readout probability that a readout operation causes the qubit to transition from the computational subspace into non-computational leakage states (L↑), measured via repeated readout benchmarking protocol (RILB)
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Readout-induced leakage generates correlated errors that are particularly harmful for quantum error correction — they cannot be corrected by standard stabilizer codes. This is a key figure of merit for readout design that is distinct from readout fidelity. Papers studying nonlinear coupling schemes specifically target reducing this quantity. Tracking it across samples would allow systematic comparison of coupling scheme effectiveness for fault-tolerant operation.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table I, main text; Supplementary Materials, READOUT-INDUCED LEAKAGE BENCHMARKING section

schema_promotion_candidates.description: The per-readout probability that a qubit in a leakage state returns to the computational subspace during a readout operation (L↓), measured via RILB
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Seepage partially mitigates leakage accumulation and must be jointly characterized with leakage rate to predict the steady-state leakage population after repeated measurements. The ratio L↑/L↓ determines the equilibrium leakage fraction. Without seepage, the leakage rate alone overestimates the long-term impact.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table I, main text; Supplementary Materials equation S38

schema_promotion_candidates.description: The anharmonicity of the qubit mode αq/2π in MHz, defined as the detuning between the |g⟩↔|e⟩ and |e⟩↔|f⟩ transition frequencies
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Anharmonicity directly sets the threshold for multiphoton resonances (resonance conditions scale with αq), determines the accessible readout frequency window free from leakage, and sets the speed limit for single-qubit gates. Without this value, the Floquet simulation parameters cannot be interpreted and resonance conditions cannot be predicted.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Supplementary Materials, Pump-probe spectroscopy experiment setup: 'αq/2π = −182.2 MHz'

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Frequency of the auxiliary mediator mode in the dimon circuit, ωm/2π in GHz
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: In mediated cosine-cosine coupling architectures, the mediator mode frequency directly governs which multiphoton resonances appear and their drive-frequency dependence. The density of leakage channels is highly sensitive to this parameter — optimizing it is identified in this paper as the key design requirement for achieving low readout-induced leakage. Tracking this across devices would allow systematic study of mediator mode placement.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Supplementary Materials, Intrinsic multiphoton excitations section: 'ωm/2π = 4.605 GHz'

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Anharmonicity of the auxiliary mediator mode αm/2π in MHz
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Mediator mode anharmonicity determines the matrix elements for multiphoton transitions involving joint qubit-mediator excitations. Linearizing the mediator (reducing its anharmonicity toward zero) is identified as a strategy to suppress higher-order transitions. This parameter must be tracked alongside mediator frequency to characterize the leakage landscape.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Supplementary Materials, Intrinsic multiphoton excitations section: 'αm/2π = −102 MHz'

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Cross-Kerr coupling χqm between qubit mode and mediator mode in MHz
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Cross-Kerr coupling shifts the energy levels of joint qubit-mediator states, directly setting the drive frequencies at which multiphoton resonances occur. It must be characterized to predict and avoid leakage channels. This parameter is specific to multimodal qubit architectures and is not captured by existing schema fields.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Supplementary Materials, Intrinsic multiphoton excitations section: 'cross-Kerr χqm = −273 MHz'

catchall.free_notes: This paper studies a single physical dimon device across three cooldowns. The device implements mediated cosine-cosine coupling (the dimon architecture from Hazra et al., PRL 134, 100601 (2025)). Cooldown I: leakage benchmarking with original readout frequency (Exp 1, ωr/2π = 7.513 GHz). Cooldown II: DUST spectroscopy (same readout frequency). Cooldown III: leakage benchmarking with optimized readout frequency (Exp 2, ωr/2π = 7.025 GHz). The qubit frequency shifts between cooldowns (6.271 → 6.231 → 6.209 GHz) are attributed to Josephson junction aging. The paper's central finding is that readout-induced leakage varies by more than an order of magnitude between Exp 1 and Exp 2 despite less than 7% change in readout frequency, demonstrating that nonlinear coupling architectures require explicit frequency optimization to realize their benefits.

anomalous_observations.description: T2_echo (90 µs) is close to 2×T1 (200 µs theoretical limit), while T2_Ramsey (45 µs) is significantly shorter, suggesting pure dephasing is a significant decoherence mechanism even though the qubit is intrinsically Purcell-protected by symmetry.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Supplementary Materials, Device properties section explicitly states: 'The data shown in the main text consists of experiments from three different cooldowns, viz. the readout-induced leakage benchmarking before the readout frequency optimization is implemented in cooldown I, the characterization of the drive-induced unwanted transitions was performed in cooldown II, and finally, the readout-induced leakage benchmarking experiment with the optimized readout is from cooldown III.' The paper further states that the experimental setup is 'identical to that of the previous work [4]' and refers to 'the device' (singular) throughout, confirming that dimon_cooldown_I, dimon_cooldown_II, and dimon_cooldown_III are all measurements of the same physical device across successive cooldowns.
fabrication_groups.source: Supplementary Materials, Device properties section, paragraph 1

dimon_cooldown_I.profile_notes: Coherence tier is competitive based on qubit T1 ~100 µs (reported in cooldown III for the same device; cooldown I has no explicit T1 but the device is the same). The science focus here is primarily characterizing readout-induced leakage as a loss/error mechanism; TLS-unattributed is noted because DUST spectroscopy in cooldown II identifies resonant TLS exchange as one class of drive-induced transitions. Transport regime is unknown as no RRR or mean-free-path data are reported.

dimon_cooldown_II.profile_notes: This cooldown is dedicated to DUST spectroscopy mapping drive-induced transitions; TLS exchange is explicitly identified as one of three transition classes. Coherence tier assigned competitive by inference from cooldown III T1 on the same physical device, as no T1 is directly reported for cooldown II.

dimon_cooldown_III.profile_notes: T1 = 100 µs places this at the upper boundary of competitive; T2_Ramsey < T2_echo suggests flux or charge noise limits dephasing, justifying flux_noise and charge_noise as loss mechanisms. Science focus includes process_optimization because the readout frequency was deliberately changed to suppress leakage, demonstrating the design optimization finding.

catchall.free_notes: This sample was designed to test whether routing through the Pt2Si intermediate via a controlled two-step anneal could improve final PtSi interface quality. The authors conclude it does not: roughening is intrinsic to the second reaction step (Si diffusing into Pt2Si) regardless of how Pt2Si is formed. This is a key mechanistic finding for PtSi process optimization.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Section II describes a single synthesis process: 'Our synthesis process involved depositing a nominal 10 nm of Pt by sputtering onto silicon substrates that were H-passivated by treatment with buffered oxide etch (BOE) just prior to loading into the vacuum system.' The as-deposited Pt sample, PtSi 600C 2min, and PtSi 600C 10min are all explicitly part of this single deposition-and-anneal study described in Section II, with the as-deposited sample being the same physical film before annealing. Figs. 1 and 2 present these three conditions as a single experimental series from one deposition batch.
fabrication_groups.source: Section II, paragraphs 1-3; Figs. 1, 2, 3

fabrication_groups.evidence: Section III states: 'we examined PtSi formation during 30 s rapid thermal anneals at temperatures ranging between 300–600°C. This series allows direct comparison with the extended 600°C anneals of Section II, isolating the role of temperature from that of annealing duration.' The language 'this series' and the systematic temperature sweep strongly imply a single deposition batch with different anneal conditions applied to different samples from the same deposition. Figs. 4 and the accompanying text treat PtSi 300C 30s, PtSi 400C 30s, PtSi 450C 30s, PtSi 500C 30s, and PtSi 600C 30s as a coherent experimental series.
fabrication_groups.source: Section III, paragraphs 1-5; Figs. 4, 5

fabrication_groups.evidence: Section IV describes a 'series of single-step anneals at temperatures spanning the two reaction thresholds, and a sequential two-step anneal to isolate the intermediate Pt2Si phase before driving the second reaction to completion.' The Pt2Si 270C 30s, mixed-phase 300C 30s, PtSi 340C 30s samples are explicitly part of this single-step anneal series described together in Section IV. The PtSi sequential 280C+360C 30s+30s sample is also described in Section IV as part of the same kinetics investigation. All are treated as a coherent experimental series probing silicidation kinetics and phase boundaries.
fabrication_groups.source: Section IV, paragraphs 1-6; Figs. 6, 7, 8

as-deposited Pt.profile_notes: Pure Pt precursor film before silicidation; no superconducting properties measured and no microwave device fabricated. Classified as 'other' since metallic Pt is not in the vocabulary and is not itself the target superconductor.

PtSi 600C 2min.profile_notes: RRR of 2.0 firmly places this in dirty_limit. TLS_interface is identified as a suspected loss channel via the observed PtSi/Si interfacial roughness increase relative to the Pt precursor, explicitly noted as relevant to Qi and T1.

PtSi 600C 10min.profile_notes: Identical RRR (2.0) and interface roughness to the 600C 2min sample; extended anneal produces no further microstructural change, confirming grain growth saturation.

PtSi 300C 30s.profile_notes: No RRR reported for this sample but silicide family universally shows low RRR; variable phase completion at 300C is flagged as a processing reliability concern. TLS_interface noted due to roughness implications discussed for all PtSi films.

PtSi 400C 30s.profile_notes: RRR of 1.5 with smaller crystallite size (~20 nm) vs 600C samples; authors explicitly correlate smaller grain size to lower RRR via grain boundary scattering, supporting anneal_to_RRR correlation.

PtSi 450C 30s.profile_notes: RRR of 1.5 with intermediate crystallite size (~24 nm); part of systematic temperature series establishing grain size to RRR correlation.

PtSi 500C 30s.profile_notes: No RRR explicitly reported for this sample; crystallite size intermediate between 450C and 600C based on XRD peak width trend. Dirty_limit inferred from silicide material class and low-RRR pattern across all PtSi samples.

PtSi 600C 30s.profile_notes: Tc of 0.9 K confirmed; grain size saturates at ~27 nm same as 600C long-duration samples. No RRR explicitly listed for this specific sample but pattern consistent with RRR ~2.0 from other 600C samples.

Pt2Si 270C 30s.profile_notes: Pt2Si is an intermediate silicide phase not in the vocabulary; classified as 'other'. Smoother interface than PtSi is the key finding, implicating the Pt2Si-to-PtSi conversion as the source of interfacial roughening relevant to TLS loss.

mixed-phase 300C 30s.profile_notes: Mixed Pt2Si/PtSi phase; transport regime unknown due to mixed-phase composition and no electrical measurements reported. crystal_phase_to_loss included because authors explicitly connect phase inhomogeneity to degraded superconducting properties.

PtSi 340C 30s.profile_notes: Single-phase PtSi confirmed at 340C; establishes reliable lower bound for single-step processing. No electrical measurements for this specific sample; dirty_limit inferred from material class pattern.

PtSi sequential 280C+360C 30s+30s.profile_notes: Two-step anneal designed to test whether controlled Pt2Si intermediate improves final PtSi interface quality; authors conclude roughening is intrinsic to the Pt2Si-to-PtSi conversion step regardless of pathway, directly informing TLS_interface loss expectations.

fabrication_details.description: 2D–3D hybrid substrate preparation: CVD monolayer graphene film transferred from copper substrate, or exfoliated hBN flakes placed on SiO2/Si (285 nm SiO2). NbSe2 precursor: 10 nm Nb deposited on SiO2/Si by magnetron sputtering, then oxidized in air at 500°C for 5 h to form niobium oxide.

fabrication_details.description: Oxidation-free transfer using EDL (electrical double layer) force: spin-coat graphene/NbSe2 with PMMA A4 (MW 950,000) at 3,000 rpm for 60 s, bake at 70°C for 5 min (in air; graphene protects NbSe2). Transfer to nitrogen box for delamination in ammonia solution (32 wt%). Rinse with water, place on target substrate, dry naturally ~1 hr in air. Remove PMMA outside glovebox.
fabrication_details.source: Methods section 'Oxidation-free wafer-scale transfer of NbSe2 by EDL force'

fabrication_details.description: Device fabrication: EBL + reactive ion etching to pattern heterostructure; resist removal; second EBL step for metal contacts; etching to expose edges; 160 nm Al deposition by e-beam evaporation. No in situ ion milling required (graphene serves as edge-contact layer). Liftoff. Mounted in Bluefors LD400 dilution refrigerator, cooled to 10 mK base temperature.

For microwave devices: additional post-growth protection layer (monolayer MoS2, CVD-grown) applied on top of graphene/NbSe2 structure before e-beam evaporation step to prevent NbSe2 damage from high-energy metal atoms.
fabrication_details.source: Methods section 'Device fabrication and characterization' and 'Characterization of graphene defects and the impact on long-term air stability'

fabrication_details.description: Transport measurement cryogenic filters: RC π-filter (cut-off 53 kHz) at 4K stage; RC-RF low-pass filter (QDevil) at mixing chamber plate. AC signal from SRS 860 lock-in amplifier; SRS 560 low-noise voltage amplifier (×1000). For differential measurements: RAC = 10 MΩ, RDC = 100 kΩ current bias resistors; QDAC voltage source; Keithley 2100 DMM.

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Sheet kinetic inductance of a superconducting film in nH per square, extracted from microwave resonator frequency comparison with a reference resonator of identical geometry
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Kinetic inductance is the primary figure of merit for 2D superconductors in high-impedance quantum circuits; it directly sets the impedance of inductors in resonators, qubits (fluxonium, superinductance), and parametric amplifiers. Tracking this across materials and thicknesses enables systematic comparison of the design space for compact quantum circuit elements—a capability inaccessible from Tc or Qi alone.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Page 355 and Figure 4i: 'we extract the sheet kinetic inductance of the CVD 1L-NbSe2 to be 0.71 nH □^-1'; Figure 4i benchmarks this against NbN, NbTiN, TiN, gr-Al across thickness and grain size

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Charge density wave transition temperature in Kelvin, extracted from temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy (amplitude mode intensity vs. temperature, fitted to mean-field theory)
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: CDW order coexists and competes with superconductivity in NbSe2 and related SC-TMDs; tracking TCDW alongside Tc characterizes the relative strength of these competing orders, which determines the superconducting condensate density and hence kinetic inductance and superfluid stiffness relevant to qubit design
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Page 352, Figure 2e: TCDW ≈ 177.0 K for graphene/NbSe2; Extended Data Fig. 10c: TCDW ≈ 185.1 K for hBN/NbSe2

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Average grain size of the superconducting film in micrometres, characterizing crystallinity
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Grain size directly determines grain boundary density, which is a major scattering and TLS source in polycrystalline films; the >1 µm grain size of CVD NbSe2 vs. ~8 nm for prior CVD NbSe2 and ~50-100 nm for multilayer SC-TMDs represents orders-of-magnitude improvement that correlates with reduced loss—tracking this across deposition conditions would enable systematic optimization of crystallinity for Qi improvement
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Page 356 and Figure 4i: 'The grain size of 1L-NbSe2 is >1 µm'; referenced comparison with 8.2 nm (ref. 19) and 50-100 nm (ref. 18) for other CVD NbSe2 films

catchall.free_notes: This paper reports two physically distinct device types from CVD 1L-NbSe2: (1) a four-probe transport device (graphene/NbSe2 edge-contacted with Al) used to measure Tc and Jc, and (2) a λ/4 microwave resonator (NbSe2-terminated Al CPW) used to measure Qi and kinetic inductance. These are extracted as separate sample records. The authors explicitly note that the Qi reported for the NbSe2-terminated resonator reflects the entire resonator system, not the intrinsic quality factor of NbSe2 alone ('the reported Qi in this work corresponds to the entire NbSe2-terminated Al resonator, which should not be deemed as the intrinsic quality factor of NbSe2 itself'). The paper benchmarks CVD NbSe2 as a platform technology rather than optimizing Qi, and notes that higher kinetic inductance in disordered films is often accompanied by lower Qi (Supplementary Fig. 21).

The Al portions of the resonator dominate Qi, making the reported value a lower bound on NbSe2's intrinsic microwave performance.

fabrication_details.description: Microwave device heterostructure: MoS2/graphene/NbSe2/hBN layers. MoS2, graphene, NbSe2 are continuous monolayer films by CVD. hBN is exfoliated multilayer. Additional MoS2 protection layer added before e-beam evaporation to prevent NbSe2 damage.

Microwave measurement setup: device at mixing chamber (10 mK) via coax cables. Input attenuated 20 dB at 4K, 10 dB at still (1K), 40 dB at mixing chamber. Output filtered with 3 GHz high-pass + 12 GHz low-pass at mixing chamber. Josephson travelling wave parametric amplifier at mixing chamber; HEMT amplifiers at 4K and room temperature. Keysight N5232A VNA.

Two λ/4 Al CPW resonators capacitively coupled to common feedline connected to VNA. LC filters connected to DC-bias lines (not used in reported measurements). NbSe2 integrated as inductive termination to ground.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Both 1L-NbSe2_graphene_transport_device and 1L-NbSe2_microwave_resonator are described as being fabricated using the same encapsulation-epitaxy CVD process at 950°C on graphene/SiO2 hybrid substrates (Methods section 'Encapsulation epitaxy for growing monolayer NbSe2'). The paper does not explicitly state that both devices were fabricated from the same physical growth run or wafer. However, a single Methods section describes one growth process used throughout the work for all 1L-NbSe2 devices, and no per-device process variation is mentioned. The paper's own statement 'Comparison between CVD 1L-NbSe2 with conventional high-kinetic-inductance materials' treats the CVD NbSe2 as a single material platform. The paper does not disclose which specific growth run supplied which specific device, so individual_assignment_disclosed is set to false.
fabrication_groups.source: Methods section 'Encapsulation epitaxy for growing monolayer NbSe2'; page 354-355 'Integration with superconducting circuit'

The authors explicitly state the reported Qi reflects the entire NbSe2-terminated Al resonator, not intrinsic NbSe2 loss; TLS is implicated but not formally attributed, so TLS_unattributed is used.

additional_measurements.source: Section III.A and Table II (Appendix B): chi_gf/2pi = -11.9±13.8 kHz for Cycle 1

additional_measurements.description: T1 from |f> to |e> transition

additional_measurements.description: Direct relaxation time from |f> to |g>
additional_measurements.source: Section III.A: 'T1^(f->g) = 4 – 6 ms from the fit'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Pauli bit-flip rate within the computational subspace; T1^(f->g) >> T1^(f->e) is the erasure-bias condition; ratio sets erasure fraction

additional_measurements.description: Postselected |f> state lifetime after erasure discarding (peak)
additional_measurements.source: Section III.B and Conclusion: 'peak |f> state lifetime of 5.087±0.685 ms'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Demonstrates 8.4-fold T1 improvement via erasure postselection; upper bound on achievable coherence if erasures are perfectly detected

additional_measurements.description: Postselected Hahn-echo T2E after erasure discarding (peak)
additional_measurements.source: Section III.B: 'maximum value of 620±14 µs at 26 µs cadence'
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: 38% improvement in T2E via postselection; residual dephasing after postselection represents Pauli phase-flip floor

additional_measurements.description: Bare resonator frequency
additional_measurements.source: Table II (Appendix B): Cycle 1 bare resonator frequency f0_res = 7.391 09 GHz
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Sets readout frequency and dispersive coupling regime; determines erasure-check drive detuning

additional_measurements.description: Resonator internal coupling rate (kappa_i/2pi)
additional_measurements.source: Table II (Appendix B): Resonator internal coupling (kappa_i/2pi) = 0.078 MHz for Cycle 1
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Internal loss rate of readout resonator; sets photon lifetime and limits Purcell decay into resonator

additional_measurements.description: Resonator external coupling rate (kappa_c/2pi)
additional_measurements.source: Table II (Appendix B): Resonator external coupling (kappa_c/2pi) = 1.370 MHz for Cycle 1
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Sets readout bandwidth and Purcell decay rate into the transmission line; kappa_c >> kappa_i confirms measurement efficiency

additional_measurements.description: Qubit-resonator coupling g/2pi
additional_measurements.source: Table II (Appendix B): Qubit-resonator coupling g/2pi = 97 MHz for Cycle 1
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Sets dispersive shift magnitude chi; strong coupling enables fast high-fidelity readout and erasure detection

additional_measurements.description: False-positive error rate of erasure check
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Probability of misclassifying a logical state as erasure; contributes directly to unnecessary postselection and effective circuit sampling overhead

additional_measurements.description: False-negative error rate of erasure check
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Missed erasures are converted to undetected Pauli errors; high false-negative rate is the primary limitation on erasure bias in this device

additional_measurements.description: Erasure-check-induced decoherence rate (Delta_Gamma_2E^echeck / 2pi)

additional_measurements.description: Erasure-check-induced gate error per erasure check
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Each erasure check adds this error; 82% of this error is unexplained by estimated incoherent budget, suggesting unknown error mechanism limits performance

additional_measurements.description: Leakage error rate per sqrt(X) gate without erasure checks
additional_measurements.source: Section III.D: 'leakage error rate of 0.022(2)%' from LRB without erasure checks
additional_measurements.suspected_relevance: Intrinsic |f>->|e> leakage rate determines baseline erasure fraction; must be large relative to Pauli error to satisfy erasure-bias condition

additional_measurements.description: Measurement setup dilution refrigerator base temperature

anomalous_observations.description: Erasure-check-induced decoherence rate (374 Hz measured) is ~21x larger than predicted by pure dephasing model (17.6 Hz), despite near-zero chi_gf

anomalous_observations.description: Erasure-check-induced gate error (2.49% per check) is ~5.4x larger than estimated incoherent error budget (0.46%); 82% of induced error is unexplained

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Probability of failing to detect a prepared erasure state during mid-circuit erasure check, in percent

Cycle 1 is the primary measurement session where T1, T2E, and gate benchmarking were performed. Cycle 2 reports slightly different resonator and qubit parameters and additionally includes T2R (Ramsey) measurements not present in Cycle 1. The T2R data in Table II is attributed to Cycle 2 only. Both cycles share the same physical device and fabrication. The sample_id 'integer_fluxonium_cycle1' covers the primary measurements; 'integer_fluxonium_cycle2' covers Cycle 2 distinct measurements.

catchall.free_notes: Cycle 2 is the second cooldown of the same physical device as integer_fluxonium_cycle1. Table II in Appendix B explicitly labels data columns as 'Cycle 1' and 'Cycle 2' and states these are 'two different measurement sessions performed at different cooldown.' Key distinction: Cycle 2 uniquely reports T2R (Ramsey) measurements not present in Cycle 1. The significant increase in resonator internal loss (kappa_i) between cycles is the most notable difference.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Table II in Appendix B explicitly states 'cycle 1 and Cycle 2 refer to the two different measurement sessions performed at different cooldown,' confirming that integer_fluxonium_cycle1 and integer_fluxonium_cycle2 are two cooldowns of the same physical device. The paper reports a single fabricated integer fluxonium device throughout, with no indication that multiple distinct physical devices were studied.
fabrication_groups.source: Table II caption (Appendix B): 'cycle 1 and Cycle 2 refer to the two different measurement sessions performed at different cooldown'

integer_fluxonium_cycle1.profile_notes: Material class assigned as aluminum based on MIT Lincoln Laboratory fluxonium fabrication conventions (Al/AlOx junctions with likely Al or Nb base layer); transport regime is unknown as no film transport data is reported. T1 = 606 µs places this firmly in state_of_the_art tier. The anomalous readout-induced T1 suppression and erasure-check-induced decoherence implicate TLS-interface and quasiparticle mechanisms alongside dephasing channels.

integer_fluxonium_cycle2.profile_notes: Same physical device as Cycle 1 but a distinct cooldown; the ~5.6x increase in resonator internal loss (kappa_i) between cycles implicates TLS or vortex-related loss variation, though no T1 is reported for Cycle 2. Coherence tier is assigned state_of_the_art by association with the same device, but strictly no direct T1 measurement is available for this cooldown — T2R of 357 µs is consistent with high coherence.

schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: This paper demonstrates 2-5× T1 improvement purely from choice of capping material while keeping the base Nb film identical — it is the primary independent variable in the comparison and directly determines surface oxide chemistry and TLS density. Without this field, the corpus cannot systematically compare capping strategies across papers.

schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: The authors find serial sputter deposition may be slightly more effective than ALD or e-beam evaporation at preventing Nb2O5 formation — capturing deposition method separately from the base film deposition method is needed to distinguish these cases
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Main text page 2: 'serial sputter deposition may be slightly more effective at protecting against surface oxidation compared to the other two methods'

Table I Row 1.profile_notes: Baseline Nb qubit with Nb2O5 surface oxide confirmed as primary TLS loss source; T1=54 µs places it in competitive tier. Transport regime not determinable from available data (no RRR reported).

Table I Row 2.profile_notes: Ta-capped Nb on sapphire; average T1=121 µs and best T1=198 µs place this in state_of_the_art tier. The anneal_to_T1 correlation is proxied here by the in-situ capping process reducing Nb2O5 by 1000x and driving the T1 improvement.

Table I Row 3.profile_notes: Al-capped Nb on sapphire with average T1=77.5 µs; competitive tier. Al capping reduces surface oxide relative to baseline but not as effectively as Ta capping.

Table I Row 4.profile_notes: TiN ALD cap on Nb/sapphire; growth_method reflects the ALD cap which is the key process variable distinguishing this sample. Authors explicitly note oxide thickness does not directly predict T1, implicating oxide composition/stoichiometry instead.

Table I Row 5.profile_notes: Au-capped Nb with no detectable surface oxide (surface_oxide_thickness_nm=0); average T1=101.2 µs qualifies as state_of_the_art. Growth method reflects the e-beam evaporation used for the Au cap, the defining process step. Remaining loss attributed to interface TLS since metal-vacuum oxide is eliminated.

Table I Row 6.profile_notes: Baseline Nb on Si substrate using HiPIMS at Rigetti foundry; T1=120 µs is state_of_the_art. Si substrate introduces substrate_to_TLS concern via Nb/Si alloyed interface; cross_platform_comparison reflects the sapphire-vs-Si substrate comparison central to the paper.

Table I Row 7.profile_notes: Ta-capped Nb on Si with average T1=200 µs and best T1=451 µs, firmly state_of_the_art. Authors demonstrate Ta capping improves T1 consistently across both Si and sapphire substrates, confirming Nb2O5 as the primary loss mechanism independent of substrate.

fabrication_details.description: Aluminum patch (bandage) layer deposited in a subsequent lift-off step to connect junctions to Nb circuitry, following Dunsworth et al. [28]

Two chip designs tested: Design 1 = 14 flux-tunable + 2 fixed qubits, uncoupled. Design 2 = 32 flux-tunable qubits with fixed couplers in square-octagon layout (Aspen-9 lattice), measured 24 per die; flip-chip bonded to superconducting cap
Qubit measurements performed at fmax for all qubits. Each qubit's T1, T2, Tφ measured many times over ~4 days. Reported values are median across all measurements.

Measurement setup: dies affixed to PCB on mixing chamber plate, nominal base temperature ≈10 mK. Housed in superconducting and low-permittivity shielding. Input lines: 86 dB total attenuation. Output: 2 double-junction isolators + HEMT at 4K + room-temp LNA.

Resonator measurement setup: 70 dB input attenuation (20 dB at 4K, 10 dB at still/cold plate, 30 dB at MXC). Eccosorb IR filters (QMC-CRYOIRF-002 input, QMC-CRYOIRF-003 output). HEMT LNA (LNF-LNC4_8C) + room-temp LNA (LNF-LNR4_8F) ~80 dB gain. JPA from NIST Advanced Microwave Photonics group for 10-20 dB additional gain at low power.
Resonator power sweep range: average photon number ⟨n⟩ ~ 0.1 to 10^8. Ten CPW resonators per device (each etch condition).

TOF-SIMS performed on witness resonator samples that received same processing as measured devices. No significant differences in F, H, O, C concentration within Nb film between the two etch treatments.

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Ratio of sum of all TLS coupling strengths (g) in a set of qubits to the sum of all tunable qubit frequency ranges (fmax-fmin), in units of 1/GHz or dimensionless if coupling strengths in GHz. Measures frequency-normalized strongly-coupled TLS density across a batch of qubits.
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: SPI normalizes for qubit-to-qubit variation in tunable range and provides a single batch-level metric for strongly-coupled TLS contamination. It directly correlates with gate error from TLS-qubit avoided crossings. Tracking SPI across fabrication processes would enable systematic comparison of TLS reduction strategies in corpus mining.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table 1 and page 6 paragraph 1

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Product of filling factor F and intrinsic TLS loss tangent δ0_TLS extracted from power-dependent Qi fits to the TLS model. Units: dimensionless (~10^-6). Represents the effective TLS loss seen by the resonator mode.
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Fδ0_TLS is the primary output of resonator power-sweep TLS fitting and is directly comparable across samples. Without a dedicated schema field, this quantity — which the paper reports as the main resonator metric — must be buried in the catchall, making cross-paper TLS loss comparisons harder to automate.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table 2 Supplement and main text page 7

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Constant loss term extracted from TLS model fitting of resonator Qi vs photon number. Represents loss mechanisms not saturated by high power (e.g. quasiparticles, vortices, hydrogen in film). Units: dimensionless (~10^-7).
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: δ_PI distinguishes TLS loss from other loss channels in resonators. The paper uses it to rule out hydrogen incorporation differences between the two etch processes. Tracking it alongside Fδ0_TLS across the corpus would allow systematic separation of TLS vs non-TLS loss contributions.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table 2 Supplement and main text page 7

Per-device assignment to specific wafers is not disclosed for 'Table 1 Row 2 (HF_NH4F_qubits)' since the table aggregates across all HF→NH4F-processed devices.
fabrication_groups.source: Table 1 main text; page 4 paragraph 1; Section 6 Device Fabrication

Table 1 Row 1 (BOE_qubits).profile_notes: Transport regime is unknown as no RRR or mean-free-path data is reported; the science focus is surface treatment of the Si substrate at the junction interface region, not the Nb film deposition. Growth method assigned as sputtering as the most common Nb deposition method, but is not explicitly stated in the record — this is a minor uncertainty. The device includes flux-tunable transmon qubits; T1=45 µs places this in the competitive tier.

Table 1 Row 2 (HF_NH4F_qubits).profile_notes: Same Nb/Si transmon platform as BOE sample; HF→NH4F treatment achieves ~32% reduction in both SPI and resonator Fδ0_TLS vs BOE, with XPS confirming suppressed SiOx regrowth as the mechanistic link. T1=55 µs places this in the competitive tier.

schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: This paper demonstrates that grain size is a primary determinant of QP density, QP relaxation time, flux pinning strength, and resonator Qi in Nb films. Systematic tracking of grain size across deposition methods would enable predictive modeling of loss mechanisms. Grain size spans orders of magnitude (44 nm for HiPIMS vs 50 µm for SRF bulk), making it a highly discriminating parameter.

catchall.free_notes: RRR defined in this paper as R(290K)/R(10K), not the standard R(300K)/R(Tc+). The reference temperature of 10K is slightly above Tc=9.3K for Nb, so this is functionally equivalent to the standard definition. Qi reported as median values from box plots of multiple measurement sweeps; significant spread is visible in Figure 4. T1 values are explicitly stated to be upper-limit estimates from resonator-only measurements, not directly measured qubit T1.

Includes total expected interaction rate in events/sec.
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Radiation environment directly determines the rate of quasiparticle poisoning events that cause transient T1 degradation. This paper demonstrates that the same qubit has ~10x different radiation-induced event rates at above-ground vs. underground facilities. Without this field, corpus-level comparison of T1 values across facilities conflates material quality with radiation environment.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Sections I–II and Table I, pages 2–3

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Thickness of a gold capping layer deposited on the superconducting film surface to prevent oxidation, in nm
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Au capping is a distinct surface passivation strategy that modifies the metal-vacuum interface TLS environment. Tracking its thickness enables corpus-level comparison of this technique against other passivation methods (e.g., post-fabrication acid treatments). Referenced as enabling T1 values from tens to hundreds of µs in this paper.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Section I, page 2 and Supplement A, page 11

catchall.free_notes: This paper reports measurements on the same physical qubit chip (Q1) at two different locations: FNAL (above ground, 2025) and LNGS (deep underground, 2023). The T1 values are similar at both sites (~80 µs median), demonstrating radioactivity has negligible effect on average T1 for this coherence regime. The paper's main finding is that a fast decay detection protocol reveals ~10x higher radiation-induced event rates at FNAL vs. LNGS, which is consistent with simulated radiation rates. The chip contains 8 transmons; only Q1 was characterized in detail for this study. Fabrication followed methods of Ref. [45] (Bal et al. 2024, npj Quantum Information).

fabrication_groups.evidence: Section III, page 4 explicitly states: 'Data corresponding to qubit Q1 were collected both underground at LNGS in 2023 (where the chip was also exposed to radioactive sources) and at FNAL in 2025.' Section II, page 3 states: 'we performed standard T1 measurements in both above-ground (FNAL) and underground (LNGS) environments using the same qubit.' Q1_FNAL and Q1_LNGS are thus measurements of the same physical device (same chip, same qubit Q1) at two different locations and times, sharing an identical fabrication origin.

Q1_FNAL.profile_notes: Primary science focus is radiation-induced quasiparticle poisoning as a loss mechanism; surface_oxide is implicated as a motivation for the Au capping layer. T1 of 81 µs places this in the competitive tier. Transport regime cannot be determined from the available data.

Q1_LNGS.profile_notes: Same physical chip as Q1_FNAL measured at deep-underground LNGS facility; cross_platform_comparison is appropriate as the paper explicitly compares above-ground vs. underground radiation environments. No key correlations from the controlled vocabulary are directly evidenced by the paper's data.

catchall.free_notes: This paper is primarily a materials characterization study (APT + TEM + PPMS) rather than a qubit or resonator measurement paper. No T1, T2, Qi, or gate fidelity values are reported. The paper does reference microwave measurements of qubits based on these films (citing [13] = Bal et al. 2024), and states that dielectric losses from surface oxides remain the dominant decoherence mechanism relative to oxygen impurities/GB segregation at current oxygen levels, but that GB segregation could become non-negligible at ~4 at.% O average. Samples 1 and 2 are Nb-only films; Samples 3-5 are Ta/Nb bilayers. Sample 1 (Al2O3) and Sample 2 (Si) are distinct films from different facilities but share the same nominal process (RT DC magnetron sputtering), with the critical difference being the photoresist bake temperature during subsequent processing. The paper explicitly attributes the different oxygen levels to fabrication differences including target purity, sputtering O2 partial pressure, and photoresist bake temperature.

Sample_3.profile_notes: Ta-capped Nb bilayer on sapphire; classified under niobium as the primary superconducting film. Film_only and not_applicable coherence tier apply as no device measurements are reported; the Ta cap is studied as an oxygen diffusion barrier rather than a primary qubit material.

Sample_4.profile_notes: Ta-capped Nb on Si substrate from Rigetti; APT confirms Ta cap partially reduces O enrichment factor in underlying Nb (2.2 vs 2.7 for bare Nb), supporting the oxygen diffusion barrier hypothesis. No device measurements reported.

Sample_5.profile_notes: Ta-capped Nb on sapphire with 800°C/3h post-anneal; anneal drives O concentration in underlying Nb above 2 at.% despite Ta cap, demonstrating that high-temperature thermal processing negates the cap's oxygen-barrier benefit. No device measurements reported.

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Depth of the recess etched into the substrate immediately adjacent to the superconducting metal edge, measured in nm by S/TEM or THz near-field microscopy
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: This paper identifies trench depth as a primary driver of qubit-to-qubit performance variation: Q factor improves logarithmically with trench depth up to ~70 nm saturation, and small (<20 nm) trench depths produce large Q variations. Tracking this systematically across the corpus would enable direct correlation between etch process parameters and qubit Q across labs.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Pages 4-5, 'Relationship between Trench Depth and Performance'; Figure 3

schema_promotion_candidates.description: The angle α of the sidewall at the base of the superconducting film where it meets the substrate, measured in degrees by S/TEM cross-section
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: This paper shows sidewall footer angle correlates with qubit quality factor for devices with large trench depths: devices with α ~30° exhibit surface EPR 15-20% larger than devices with α ~10-15°. Tracking across corpus would allow correlation of etch anisotropy (F-based vs Cl-based, Ar content) with qubit performance.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Pages 4-5, 'Sidewall Geometry'; Figure 4e; Figure 5b

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Identity and thickness of the metal encapsulation layer deposited on top of the base superconducting film (e.g., Ta, Au, AuPd, or none)
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: This study encompasses Nb qubits with 4 distinct surface conditions (uncapped, Ta-capped, Au-capped, AuPd-capped), each with distinct loss mechanisms and oxide behavior. Tracking capping layer systematically across corpus would enable direct comparison of encapsulation strategies on qubit performance.
schema_promotion_candidates.source: Table I, page 14; pages 5-8 discussion of Chips 2, 3, 4 with different capping layers

schema_promotion_candidates.description: Thickness of the metal capping/encapsulation layer in nm
schema_promotion_candidates.why_important: Capping layer thickness determines surface oxide suppression effectiveness; incomplete coverage near sidewall (Chip 3, AuPd) leads to performance variation. Systematic tracking would reveal thickness thresholds for effective encapsulation.

Chip5a_Qubit3.profile_notes: T1 of 208 µs is well above the 100 µs state_of_the_art threshold. Ta capping layer on Nb base film; niobium assigned as primary material class.

Chip5a_Qubit4.profile_notes: T1 of 216 µs is the highest single-qubit value in this record. Same fab group and wafer as Chip5a_Qubit3 with identical capping and substrate.

Chip5b_Qubit3.profile_notes: Same wafer as Chip 5a; T1 of 184 µs exceeds the state_of_the_art threshold. Ta capping layer on 175 nm Nb on Si.

Chip5b_Qubit4.profile_notes: T1 of 184 µs places this sample firmly in state_of_the_art tier. Identical configuration to Chip5b_Qubit3 from the same wafer.

Chip6_Qubit3.profile_notes: Bare Nb with no capping layer; TLS_metal_vacuum included because uncapped Nb surface oxide is an explicit loss channel investigated in this study. T1 of 108 µs exceeds the 100 µs threshold.

Chip6_Qubit4.profile_notes: Bare Nb on Si with no capping layer; sidewall footer angle negatively correlates with Q as explicitly shown in Figure S5. T1 of 138 µs qualifies as state_of_the_art.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Main text page 3 states: 'chips were fabricated in pairs within each run. Both chips were diced from neighboring regions of the same Nb-coated silicon wafer and concurrently processed through lithography, ion beam etching, and post-fabrication chemical treatment... This paired fabrication scheme was repeated across five independent runs, yielding five control chips (C1–C5) and five HMDS-passivated chips (H1–H5).' Each control chip C1, C2, C3, C4, C5 is explicitly named and stated to share a common Nb-coated silicon wafer origin within its respective run, with concurrent processing through lithography and IBE. NOTE: C1 through C5 come from FIVE INDEPENDENT RUNS, each from a different paired wafer. They share a common process but not a single physical wafer or deposition run. Per the fabrication grouping guidance, 'same recipe on separate occasions' is not sufficient for one group. However, the paper does not disclose per-sample wafer assignments beyond the paired structure (C1/H1 from run 1, C2/H2 from run 2, etc.), and the authors explicitly treat C1-C5 as a statistical group for comparison. Since each run's wafer is a distinct physical deposition, strictly each Cn/Hn pair constitutes its own physical fabrication event. The grouping here reflects the paper's own statistical pooling of all control chips; the individual_assignment_disclosed flag is set true because the run-pairing is disclosed (C1 with H1, etc.), and individual_assignment_disclosed refers to run-level assignment.

C1.profile_notes: Qi at ~7 days is approximately 1e5 (early_exploration threshold). The paper explicitly tracks NbOx regrowth over time as the mechanism driving Qi degradation in the unpassivated control.

C2.profile_notes: No individual Qi value reported for C2; paper notes it exhibited particularly low QLP. Coherence tier assigned early_exploration based on this qualitative description and the control group median of ~4.6e5.

C3.profile_notes: Champion resonator QLP = 6.5e5 (competitive tier). STEM-EELS characterization of NbOx depth and substrate-air SiOx provides direct nanoscale evidence linking surface oxide to TLS loss; TLS_interface included for the SA interface SiOx contribution investigated via EELS.

C4.profile_notes: No individual Qi value reported for C4. Coherence tier assigned competitive based on the control group median of (4.6 ± 2.2) × 10^5, which spans the early_exploration/competitive boundary; competitive chosen as the median best estimate.

C5.profile_notes: Control group median QLP = (4.6 ± 2.2) × 10^5 reported here as a group statistic; no individual Qi for C5 alone. Coherence tier set to competitive based on the group median.

H1.profile_notes: HMDS-passivated chip showing retained QLP over 60 days; individual Qi not quantified separately but group median is 8.0e5 (competitive). Stability over ambient exposure is a key finding attributed to suppressed NbOx regrowth.

H2.profile_notes: No individual Qi reported; H2 paired with particularly low-performing C2 and showed pronounced improvement. Coherence tier based on group median of 8.0e5.

H3.profile_notes: Champion resonator QLP = 1.4e6 qualifies as state_of_the_art under resonator Qi thresholds. STEM-EELS directly evidences reduced NbOx at the metal-air interface, and EELS of SA SiOx supports isolation of metal-air interface as dominant loss channel.

H4.profile_notes: No individual Qi reported for H4. Coherence tier based on HMDS group median of 8.0e5 (competitive).

H5.profile_notes: Group median QLP = (8.0 ± 2.6) × 10^5 reported here; no individual Qi for H5. The 1.8-fold improvement over the control group is the key correlation evidenced.

H6.profile_notes: H6 was fabricated solely for EELS characterization and was not included in microwave performance statistics, so device_type is film_only and coherence_tier is not_applicable. STEM-EELS at 2 weeks provides early time-point evidence of HMDS-mediated NbOx suppression.

sample_A_low_Qi.profile_notes: RRR of 66 places this firmly in the clean limit for Nb. Loss mechanisms include vortex motion (flux penetration depth correlation with Qi), quasiparticle (irregular lambda(T) indicating in-gap states), and TLS_unattributed (granular defect structure implicated in sub-gap states). Qi of 140k maps to competitive tier under resonator thresholds.

sample_B_intermediate_Qi.profile_notes: RRR of 72.6 confirms clean limit. Intermediate flux penetration depth and moderate lambda(T) irregularity are consistent with intermediate vortex and quasiparticle loss; Qi of 440k is competitive by resonator thresholds.

sample_C_high_Qi.profile_notes: RRR of 75.9 is clean limit. Best screening (shallowest flux penetration) and regular BCS lambda(T) indicate suppressed vortex and quasiparticle loss; Qi of 520k is competitive but below the state_of_the_art threshold of 1e6. Authors explicitly note Tc, RRR do not predict Qi, so clean_limit_to_vortex_loss is not listed as a key correlation since the paper argues against bulk metrics as predictors.

catchall.free_notes: This paper characterizes six Nb film variants (bare sputtered, PdAu-capped sputtered, Au-capped sputtered x2, bare MBE, Au-capped MBE) using a comprehensive multimodal approach: resistivity, TDR penetration depth, VSM magnetization, magneto-optical imaging, and Campbell penetration depth. No resonator or qubit device measurements are reported — all measurements are bulk film characterization. The key finding is that Au capping affects not just the surface but the entire bulk of the Nb film, substantially reducing disorder (RRR improves from ~5 to ~34). The paper explicitly links bulk disorder to qubit decoherence in the abstract and discussion. TOF-SIMS was performed on sputtered films only; details are referenced to prior publications [17, 34]. Nb/Au-2 is noted as an 'un-optimized' film annealed at 1100°C for 2 h, showing anomalous behavior in the ρ(Tc) vs Tc plot.

fabrication_groups.evidence: Section IV A states 'Niobium films for this study were fabricated on sapphire substrates using either sputtering or molecular beam epitaxy.' The sputtered films (Nb_bare, Nb_PdAu, Nb_Au, Nb_Au_2) are all described as sputtered onto sapphire, with Nb_bare and Nb_PdAu fabricated at FNAL/NIST and Nb_Au and Nb_Au_2 using a sputtering-then-e-beam-Au process. Author Contributions states 'The FNAL team...fabricated, coated, and characterized sputtered films' and 'The NIST team (D.O. and P.H) fabricated sputtered films.' However, the paper does not state that all four sputtered films came from a single physical deposition run or wafer — they were fabricated in different chambers (NIST and FNAL are noted as distinct, with different residual impurities). This grouping reflects shared deposition method (sputtering) and substrate type, not confirmed same physical run. Confidence is low because the paper explicitly notes 'sputtered PdAu-capped and Au-capped films were fabricated in different sputtering chambers.'

Nb_Au.profile_notes: RRR=24 is intermediate — substantially cleaner than bare Nb (RRR=5) but not yet approaching the clean limit (RRR>50); authors note it 'approaches the clean limit' only for Nb/Au-epi (RRR=34). Ar+ ion milling before Au deposition addresses surface oxide.

Nb_Au_2.profile_notes: Labeled 'un-optimized' by authors; the 1100°C anneal produced anomalously high resistivity (highest among all films) indicating increased disorder, placing it in dirty_limit despite Au capping. The anneal_to_RRR correlation is evidenced as a negative result.

Nb_bare_epi.profile_notes: RRR 5-8 despite MBE growth confirms dirty_limit; MBE without encapsulation does not achieve cleanliness of Au-capped films. Included as cross-platform comparison against sputtered bare Nb.

Nb_Au_epi.profile_notes: RRR=34 is the highest in the study and authors state it 'approaches the clean limit,' but does not exceed the >50 threshold; classified as intermediate. Anomalously large λ(0)=140 nm attributed to structural inhomogeneity rather than disorder, consistent with intermediate rather than clean_limit assignment.

catchall.free_notes: The paper's core contribution is a TLS spectroscopy method based on correlated T1e/T1f fluctuations in fixed-frequency transmons. The film_material field is set to Nb (the base metal) with the understanding that Ta capping is an important surface engineering detail not captured by a single film_material field. Both devices are described as fabricated using the same process (reference [11]) and measured in the same cooldown campaign, but the paper does not explicitly state they are from the same wafer or deposition run.

The paper then introduces Device_A and Device_B as 'the two representative transmons' with parameters in Table I. The paper's primary contribution is TLS spectroscopy via correlated T1e/T1f fluctuations, identifying individual TLS defects as the dominant loss mechanism without attributing them to a specific interface.

Device_B.profile_notes: Same fabrication process and material stack as Device A (Ta-capped Nb on sapphire); T1=111 µs places it in state_of_the_art tier. Two-TLS model is identified as governing coherence loss, but TLS interface origin is not attributed, so TLS_unattributed is used.

Device mounted in connectorized Al box with Al wire bonds, cooled to 10 mK on mixing chamber stage of dilution refrigerator
